﴿And make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing (*radiyyan*)﴾. That is: one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and Your destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. It has been said: a prophet, as You made his forefathers prophets.

﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾. Most exegetes said: this call is from God, glorified is He. It has been said that it came from the angels, because of His saying in Surat Al 'Imran, ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ (3:39). There is an omission in the speech: that is, He answered his supplication, and so said, "O Zakariyya." The reason for the name Yahya and Zakariyya has already been given in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-Zajjaj said: he was named Yahya because he was made alive (*hayiya*) by the knowledge and wisdom that he was given.

﴿We have not previously made any namesake for him﴾. (p-883) Most exegetes said: its meaning is that We did not name anyone before him Yahya.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 19, verses 1–11 (part 2 of 2):

Mujahid and a group [of scholars] said: the meaning of ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ is that He did not make for him any equal or peer. On this view the word is derived from *al-musamah* (equality) or *al-sumuww* (exaltedness). This was rejected on the ground that it would imply his being preferred over Abraham and Moses. It was also said: its meaning is that no barren woman had given birth like him. The first view is the better.

In God's (subhanahu) report that no one was named with this name before him is a virtue for him from two aspects. The first: it was God, glorified is He, who Himself chose his name, and did not leave it to his parents.

The second aspect: naming him with a name that had not been given to anyone else indicates his honour and exaltation.

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy?"﴾ That is: how, or from where, can I have a boy? This interrogative does not mean denial; rather it expresses wonder at God's power and the wondrous nature of His creation, since He brings forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. The discussion of this kind of matter has already been presented in Surat Al 'Imran. ﴿And I have reached extreme old age﴾ It is said: *'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'itiyyan* (the old man became decrepit) when his age has advanced and he has grown very old. *Shaykh 'at* (a decrepit old man) is one who has reached a state of dryness and desiccation. The original form is *'utuwwan*, since it is from the *waw*-roots, but they changed it to *ya'* because it is lighter. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

"The youth is excused, but one who has been in the time of decrepitude is not excused."

Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and al-A'mash read *'itiyyan* with a kasra on the 'ayn; the rest read it with a damma on the 'ayn. Both are dialectal variants. The position (i'rab) of the clause ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the speaker. The position of the clause ﴿and I have reached extreme old age﴾ is also accusative as a circumstantial clause. Both clauses serve to reinforce the sense of improbability and wonder conveyed by his words ﴿how can I have a boy?﴾. That is: how can a child be born to us now, when my wife has been barren, not having given birth in her youth or in mine, and she is now an old woman, and I am a frail old man?

Then God, glorified is He, answered this question, which implies wonder and improbability, with His words ﴿He said: "Thus has your Lord said"﴾. The *kaf* (the particle *ka-*, "thus") is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is thus. The demonstrative refers to what preceded in Zakariyya's words. Then He began with the words ﴿your Lord said﴾. It is also possible that its position is accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: he said a saying like that. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to something unspecified, which is explained by His words ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. On the first interpretation, the clause ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ is a new, independent statement aimed at removing Zakariyya's sense of improbability after it had been affirmed; that is: "It is easy for Me, despite its improbability in your view." *Hayyin* is an intensive form (*fay'al*) from *han al-shay'* (the thing became easy): when it is not difficult and does not resist what is intended.

Al-Farra' said: that is, His creating it is easy for Me. ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ This clause confirms what precedes it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the creation of a child for you is like your creation. The meaning is that God created him originally and brought him into existence from pure non-existence, so bringing a child into being for him through ordinary procreation is easier and simpler than that. The verse did not attribute this to Adam, peace be upon him, because he was the one created from nothing in truth, by saying: "And I created your father Adam before, when he was nothing." This is to indicate that every individual of humankind has a share in the origination of Adam from nothing.

The people of Madinah, Makkah, Basra, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿And We created you before﴾ [with "I" as in the verse above]. The rest of the Kufans read *wa-qad khalaqnaka min qablu* ("And We created you before").

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign"﴾ That is: a sign that will show me the occurrence and realisation of what was asked for and the onset of pregnancy. The purpose of this request was to know the time of conception, since the glad tidings were not specific about its timing.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the reason is that his soul yearned for the matter to come quickly, so he asked God for a sign by which he could know that what had been bestowed on him was near. It was also said: he asked for a sign showing that the glad tidings came from God, glorified is He, and not from Satan, because Satan had deceived him with this. Thus said al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound."﴾ The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Al 'Imran. *Sawiyyan* (sound) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: your sign is that you will be unable to speak while you are of sound constitution, with no affliction in you that could prevent you from it. The mention of nights here, and of days in Surat Al 'Imran, indicates that what is meant is three days and their nights.

﴿So he came out to his people from the mihrab﴾ This is his prayer place (the prayer chamber). Its etymology is from *harb* (war), as if the one who keeps to it is fighting Satan. It was also said that it derives from *haraba* (with a fatha), as if the one who keeps to it encounters hardship, fatigue and weariness. ﴿Then he signalled to them to glorify [God] in the morning and the evening﴾ It was said: the meaning of *awha* is *awma'a* (he gestured). This is supported by His words in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿except by gesture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 41]. It was also said: he wrote for them on the ground. The first view was held by al-Kalbi, al-Qurazi, Qatadah and Ibn Munabbih; the second was held by Mujahid. The word *wahy* (revelation) may also be used for writing, as in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Apart from the four dark ones, which are as if they were the remnant of revelation in the pages of the scrolls."

And 'Antarah said:

"Like the writing of scrolls from the era of Kisra, which he sent to a non-Arab with a foreign (*tamtami*) tongue."

The *an* in His words ﴿that glorify﴾ is either the verbal *an* or the explanatory *an*. The meaning: he signalled to them that they should pray, or, that is, "pray." The accusative of *bukratan wa-'ashiyyan* ("in the morning and the evening") is adverbial of time.

Al-Farra' said: *al-'ashi* (evening) may be feminine, and it is permissible to make it masculine when it is indefinite. He said: it is also said that *al-'ashiyy* is the plural of *'ashiyyah*. It was said: what is meant by glorification is the dawn and afternoon prayers. It was also said: what is meant by glorification is the saying "Glory be to God" at both times, that is, exalt your Lord at both ends of the day.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾: "Generous, guide, trustworthy, mighty, truthful." In one wording *kafin* ("sufficient") replaces *kabir* ("great").

'Abd al-Razzaq, Adam ibn Abi Iyas, 'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi in *al-Tawhid*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that he said: *kaf* is from *karim* (generous), *ha* is from *hadi* (guide), *ya* is from *hakim* (wise), *'ayn* is from *'alim* (knowing), and *sad* is from *sadiq* (truthful).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that they are the disjointed letters (*al-hija' al-muqatta'*): the *kaf* is from *al-Malik* (the King), the *ha* is from *Allah*, the *ya* and *'ayn* are from *al-'Aziz* (the Mighty), and the *sad* is from *al-Musawwir* (the Fashioner).

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Kalbi that he was asked about ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ and he related from Abu Salih, from Umm Hani', from (p-٨٨٤) the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Kaf: guide, knowing, truthful."

'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Fatimah daughter of 'Ali, who said: 'Ali used to say: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, forgive me."

Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾, that he said: "The *kaf* is *al-Kafi* (the Sufficient), the *ha* is *al-Hadi* (the Guide), the *'ayn* is *al-'Alim* (the Knowing), and the *sad* is *al-Sadiq* (the Truthful)."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say regarding *Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad*, *Ha Mim*, *Ya Sin* and similar letters: "It is the Greatest Name of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of God's names."

Just as this disagreement arose among the Companions regarding this and similar matters, it also arose among those who came after them, and nothing has been authentically traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a raised (*marfu'*) report on this. Whatever is related from a Companion on this matter has been related from others something that contradicts it, and the same Companion may be related to have given differing and contradictory interpretations of these opening letters. None of this constitutes a proof. Rather, the correct position is to suspend judgement and to refer the knowledge of such matters to God, glorified is He. We have already set out the verification of this in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Zakariyya was a carpenter."

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The last of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Zakariyya ibn Azar ibn Muslim, of the offspring of Ya'qub. He called upon his Lord in secret, ﴿He said: 'My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me'﴾ until His words ﴿and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾" — [in the report] "until His words ﴿I fear the heirs [after me]﴾." He said: "The heirs are the male relatives (*'asabah*) who would inherit from me; they would inherit my prophethood and the prophethood of the family of Ya'qub. So the angels called to him, and he was Jibril: 'Indeed God gives you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya.' When he heard the call, Satan came to him and said: 'O Zakariyya, the voice you heard is not from God; it is from Satan, who mocked you.' So he doubted and said: ﴿How can I have a boy?﴾, meaning: from where can it be, when old age has reached me and my wife is barren?' God said: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾."

al-Firyabi transmitted from him, who said: "Zakariyya had no child, so he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself an heir﴾" and he said: "He will inherit my wealth and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub the prophethood."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ that he said: "A peer."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: "I do not know how the Messenger of God (ﷺ) read this word: *'itiyyan* or *'isiyyan*."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words *'itiyyan* that he said: "He remained for a long time in old age."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "*Harman*" (decrepit).

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound﴾, that he said: "His tongue was tied, without illness." In another wording: "without muteness." Transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So he signalled to them﴾, that he said: "He wrote a book for them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that glorify﴾, that he said: "He commanded them to pray ﴿in the morning and the evening﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 19, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat Maryam was revealed in Makkah." And Ibn Mardawayh recorded the same from Aisha.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dala'il*, recorded from Umm Salama that al-Najashi (the Negus) said to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib: "Do you have with you anything from what he (ﷺ) brought from God?" He said: "Yes." So he recited to him the beginning of (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad). Al-Najashi wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until they wet their scriptures when they heard what he recited to them. Then al-Najashi said: "Indeed, this and what Musa brought come from the same niche (lamp)." Ibn Ishaq related the story in full.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾. Abu Ja'far read these letters separately (pausing between each), while the rest joined them. Abu Amr inclined the *ha'* and opened the *ba'*, and Ibn Amir and Hamza reversed that. Al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Khalaf inclined both. The people of Madinah read them in between the two pronunciations, and the rest read them with a fatha on both.

It is related from Kharija that al-Hasan used to pronounce the *kaf* with a *damma*, and he reported that others pronounced the *ha'* with a *damma*. Abu Hatim said: "It is not permissible to put a *damma* on the *kaf*, the *ha'* or the *ya'*." Al-Nahhas said: "The reading of the people of Madinah is among the best of what is said on this, and inclination (*imalah*, pronouncing a vowel toward *i*) is permissible on *ha'* and on *ya'*." A group has objected to al-Hasan's reading. It has been said that its interpretation is that he gave only a slight *damma* (*ishmam*) on the *raf'* (nominative) position.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Asim and Ya'qub made the *dal* clear in the spelling of *Sad* (*ṣād*), and this is the choice of Abu Ubayda. The rest assimilated it (idgham).

It has been said, in explaining these readings, that *tafkhim* (velarization, the full pronunciation) is the original, and *imalah* is a derivative of it. Whoever read with *tafkhim* on the *ha'* and the *ya'* has acted according to the original; whoever inclined them has acted according to the derivative; and whoever inclined one and velarized the other has acted according to both. The discussion of these letters that occur at the openings of surahs has already been given in full at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. As for the grammatical position of this opening, if it is taken as the name of the surah, as most scholars hold, it is in the nominative (*raf'*) as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is what follows it. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Al-Zajjaj objected to this and said: "This is impossible, because ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾ is not part of what God, Mighty and Majestic, told us about Zakariyya, whereas God, Blessed and Exalted, has informed us about him and about what he was given glad tidings of, and (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) is not part of his story." Or (it is said) it is the predicate of an omitted subject. If the letters are taken as a continuous listing in the manner of enumeration, then his saying ﴿a mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "In what is recited to you is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." Al-Zajjaj said: *dhikr* (mention) is in the nominative by the pronoun (*bi-l-damir*), and the meaning is: "This which we recite to you is a mention of the mercy of your Lord ﴿to His servant Zakariyya﴾," meaning His answering him when he called upon Him and asked Him for a child. The accusative of *'abdahu* (His servant) is, according to al-Akhfash, as an object of *rahmah* (mercy). It has also been said that it is an object of *dhikr*. The meaning of "mention of the mercy" is its reaching and befalling (him), as one says, "The kindness of so-and-so mentioned me," meaning: it reached me.

Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *dhikra* with the accusative. Abu al-Aliya read *'abduhu* with the nominative, on the basis that the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) is in the genitive by being annexed to its object, and the subject of the mention is *'abduhu*. Zakariyya, according to both readings, is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to it or a substitute (*badal*) for it. Al-Kalbi read *dhakara* as a past-tense verb, both with and without doubling of the middle letter, with *'abadahu* as its subject. Ibn Ma'mar read it as an imperative. On this reading, "mercy" refers to Zakariyya himself, because every prophet is a mercy to his community.

﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) "when" is *rahmah* (mercy). It has also been said to be *dhikr* (mention), and it has been said that it is a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from Zakariyya. People differ on why his call was secret. It has been said: because it is further from ostentation (*riya'*). It has been said: he concealed it so that he would not be blamed for asking for a child at a time that was not right, and because it concerned worldly matters. It has been said: he concealed it out of fear of his people. And it has been said: this was from him because he had become weak and decrepit and could not raise his voice.

﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾. This sentence explains his saying "he called upon his Lord." It is said: *wahana yahinu wahnan*, when he became weak, so he is *wahin* (weak). It has been read with all three vowel patterns. He meant that his bones had grown slack and his strength had diminished. He mentioned the bone because it is the pillar of the body, the thing by which it stands, and the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, the rest collapses and its strength falls away. Also, the strongest part of a person is his spine, and when it weakens, what lies beyond it is even weaker. He used the singular "bone" intending the class noun, which conveys the weakening of every individual bone.

﴿And the head has blazed with white hair﴾. Abu Amr read the *sin* as assimilated into the *shin*, and the rest did not. *Al-ishtial* in its original sense is the spreading of the light of fire. So the spreading of the whiteness of hair over its blackness was likened to this, by the common features of whiteness and brightness. Then it was expressed in the form of a metaphor by implication (*isti'arah bi-l-kinayah*), by omitting the thing compared to and the particle of comparison. This metaphor is among the most creative and most beautiful metaphors.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of white hair when it becomes very abundant, "The head of so-and-so has blazed," and he cited Labid:

*"If you see my head has become bright, white hair has taken over it and it has blazed."*

The accusative of *shaybāan* (white hair) is as a specification (*tamyiz*), said al-Zajjaj. Al-Akhfash said its accusative is as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), because the meaning of *ishta'ala* is *shaba* (grew white). Al-Nahhas said: al-Akhfash's view is better, because it is derived from the form *fa'ala*, and the verbal-noun reading is more apparent in cases like this. The original would have been "the white hair of my head blazed," but the blazing was attributed to the head to convey comprehensiveness.

﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord﴾. That is: I have never been disappointed in my calling upon You at any time, but every time I called upon You, You answered me.

The scholars said: It is recommended for a person to combine in his supplication humility and mention of God's blessings upon him, as Zakariyya did here. In His saying ﴿my bones have weakened within me and the head has blazed with white hair﴾ is the utmost humility, abasement, display of weakness, and inability to attain his aims and reach his goals. In His saying ﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord﴾ is a mention of the favour God had accustomed him to, in answering his prayers. It is said *shaqiya bi-kadha*, meaning: he toiled in it and did not obtain his aim from it.

﴿And indeed I have feared the *mawali* (kinsmen) after me﴾. Uthman ibn Affan, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn and his father Ali, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *khaffa* (with the *kha'* vowelled with a fatha, the *fa'* doubled and the *ta'* vowelled with a kasra), with *al-mawali* as its subject. That is: they became few and were unable to bear the responsibility of religion after me, or they died out, from *khaffa al-qawm*, when a people departed. This reading is anomalous and far from correct.

The rest read *khiftu* with a kasra on the *kha'* and a sukun on the *fa'*, so that its subject is a pronoun referring to Zakariyya, its object is *al-mawali*, and *min wara'i* (after me) is connected to an omitted verb, not to *khiftu*. Its implied meaning is: "I feared the conduct of the *mawali* after me."

The majority read *wara'i* with a hamza, a long vowel, and a sukun on the *ya'*. Ibn Kathir read it with a hamza, a long vowel, and a fatha on the *ya'*. It is also reported from him that he read it with a short vowel and a fatha on the *ya'*, like *'asayya* (my staff).

The *mawali* here are the relatives who inherit, and the other male kinsmen, the sons of paternal uncles and the like. The Arabs call these *mawali*. A poet said:

*"Gently, sons of our paternal uncles, gently, our kinsmen! Do not spread among us what was buried."*

It has been said: the *mawali* are those who support him.

They differ on the nature of Zakariyya's fear for his kinsmen after him. It has been said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and he wanted his son to inherit him; so he asked God, glorified is He, to grant him a child. Others said: they were negligent of the affairs of religion, so he feared that religion would be lost at his death, and he asked for a *wali* (guardian) to uphold it after his death. This view is preferable to the first, because prophets do not leave inheritance, and they are too exalted to concern themselves with worldly affairs. So what is meant here is not the inheritance of property but the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, and the upholding of the affairs of religion. It has been firmly established from our Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity."

﴿And my wife has been barren﴾. *Al-'aqir* is the woman who does not bear children because of old age, and also the woman who does not bear children for reasons other than old age; the latter is what is meant here. The term *'aqir* is also used for a man who does not father children, and from it is the saying of Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

*"What a wretched youth you are, if you are one-eyed and barren."*

Ibn Jarir said: the name of his wife was Ashna' daughter of Faqud ibn Mayl, and she was the sister of Hanna, and Hanna was the mother of Maryam. Al-Qutaybi said: she was Ashna' daughter of Imran. On the first view, Yahya ibn Zakariyya would be the maternal cousin of Isa's mother, and on the second, the two would be maternal cousins, as is related in the authentic hadith.

﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir (*waliyyan*)﴾. That is: give me, out of Your bounty, a *wali*. He did not state explicitly that he sought a child, because he knew about himself that he and his wife had reached a state in which a child could not come into being between them and be born of them. It has been said that he was ninety-some years old. It has also been said that he meant by *wali* the one who would be the child he sought. There is no barrier to asking for something like this, which is beyond the ordinary course, since God, glorified is He, may honour His messengers with such things, and this is one of the miracles that testify to their truthfulness.

﴿Who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾. The people of the two holy cities (Makkah and Madinah), al-Hasan, Asim, Hamza, Ibn Muhaysin and Yahya ibn al-Mubarak al-Yazidi read *yarithuni* and *yarithu* both in the nominative, on the basis that they are attributes of the *wali* and not answers (jussive responses) to the supplication. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read both in the jussive, on the basis that they are answers to the supplication. Abu Ubayd preferred the first reading and said: it is more correct in meaning, because he asked for a *wali* with this description, so he said: "Give me one who will be my heir."

Al-Nahhas also preferred this, and said: because the answer to an imperative, according to the grammarians, carries the sense of a condition and consequence. You say: *Obey God, He will admit you into Paradise*, meaning: if you obey Him, He will admit you into Paradise. How could God, glorified is He, inform him of this, I mean that He would grant him an heir who would inherit him, when He is the one who knows about it? Inheritance here is the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, according to the preferred view as already stated.

Most exegetes have held that Ya'qub mentioned here is Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim. Some exegetes claimed that he is Ya'qub son of Mathan, brother of Imran son of Mathan, and this was the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. *Ali Ya'qub* are his closest people, those whose affairs revert to him, by kinship, companionship, or agreement in religion. There were prophets and kings among them. It has also been read *yarithuni warithun min ali Ya'qub* (with *warith* as the subject of *yarithuni*). It has also been read *wa-arithu ali Ya'qub*, that is, "I" will inherit. It has also been read *uwayrithu ali Ya'qub* in the diminutive form, on the basis that this diminutive is the subject of *yarithuni*. These readings are extremely anomalous both in form and in meaning.

﴿And make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing (*radiyyan*)﴾. That is: one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and Your destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. It has been said: a prophet, as You made his forefathers prophets.

﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾. Most exegetes said: this call is from God, glorified is He. It has been said that it came from the angels, because of His saying in Surat Al 'Imran, ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ (3:39). There is an omission in the speech: that is, He answered his supplication, and so said, "O Zakariyya." The reason for the name Yahya and Zakariyya has already been given in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-Zajjaj said: he was named Yahya because he was made alive (*hayiya*) by the knowledge and wisdom that he was given.

﴿We have not previously made any namesake for him﴾. (p-883) Most exegetes said: its meaning is that We did not name anyone before him Yahya.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 19, verses 1–11 (part 2 of 2):

Mujahid and a group [of scholars] said: the meaning of ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ is that He did not make for him any equal or peer. On this view the word is derived from *al-musamah* (equality) or *al-sumuww* (exaltedness). This was rejected on the ground that it would imply his being preferred over Abraham and Moses. It was also said: its meaning is that no barren woman had given birth like him. The first view is the better.

In God's (subhanahu) report that no one was named with this name before him is a virtue for him from two aspects. The first: it was God, glorified is He, who Himself chose his name, and did not leave it to his parents.

The second aspect: naming him with a name that had not been given to anyone else indicates his honour and exaltation.

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy?"﴾ That is: how, or from where, can I have a boy? This interrogative does not mean denial; rather it expresses wonder at God's power and the wondrous nature of His creation, since He brings forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. The discussion of this kind of matter has already been presented in Surat Al 'Imran. ﴿And I have reached extreme old age﴾ It is said: *'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'itiyyan* (the old man became decrepit) when his age has advanced and he has grown very old. *Shaykh 'at* (a decrepit old man) is one who has reached a state of dryness and desiccation. The original form is *'utuwwan*, since it is from the *waw*-roots, but they changed it to *ya'* because it is lighter. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

"The youth is excused, but one who has been in the time of decrepitude is not excused."

Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and al-A'mash read *'itiyyan* with a kasra on the 'ayn; the rest read it with a damma on the 'ayn. Both are dialectal variants. The position (i'rab) of the clause ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the speaker. The position of the clause ﴿and I have reached extreme old age﴾ is also accusative as a circumstantial clause. Both clauses serve to reinforce the sense of improbability and wonder conveyed by his words ﴿how can I have a boy?﴾. That is: how can a child be born to us now, when my wife has been barren, not having given birth in her youth or in mine, and she is now an old woman, and I am a frail old man?

Then God, glorified is He, answered this question, which implies wonder and improbability, with His words ﴿He said: "Thus has your Lord said"﴾. The *kaf* (the particle *ka-*, "thus") is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is thus. The demonstrative refers to what preceded in Zakariyya's words. Then He began with the words ﴿your Lord said﴾. It is also possible that its position is accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: he said a saying like that. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to something unspecified, which is explained by His words ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. On the first interpretation, the clause ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ is a new, independent statement aimed at removing Zakariyya's sense of improbability after it had been affirmed; that is: "It is easy for Me, despite its improbability in your view." *Hayyin* is an intensive form (*fay'al*) from *han al-shay'* (the thing became easy): when it is not difficult and does not resist what is intended.

Al-Farra' said: that is, His creating it is easy for Me. ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ This clause confirms what precedes it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the creation of a child for you is like your creation. The meaning is that God created him originally and brought him into existence from pure non-existence, so bringing a child into being for him through ordinary procreation is easier and simpler than that. The verse did not attribute this to Adam, peace be upon him, because he was the one created from nothing in truth, by saying: "And I created your father Adam before, when he was nothing." This is to indicate that every individual of humankind has a share in the origination of Adam from nothing.

The people of Madinah, Makkah, Basra, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿And We created you before﴾ [with "I" as in the verse above]. The rest of the Kufans read *wa-qad khalaqnaka min qablu* ("And We created you before").

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign"﴾ That is: a sign that will show me the occurrence and realisation of what was asked for and the onset of pregnancy. The purpose of this request was to know the time of conception, since the glad tidings were not specific about its timing.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the reason is that his soul yearned for the matter to come quickly, so he asked God for a sign by which he could know that what had been bestowed on him was near. It was also said: he asked for a sign showing that the glad tidings came from God, glorified is He, and not from Satan, because Satan had deceived him with this. Thus said al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound."﴾ The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Al 'Imran. *Sawiyyan* (sound) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: your sign is that you will be unable to speak while you are of sound constitution, with no affliction in you that could prevent you from it. The mention of nights here, and of days in Surat Al 'Imran, indicates that what is meant is three days and their nights.

﴿So he came out to his people from the mihrab﴾ This is his prayer place (the prayer chamber). Its etymology is from *harb* (war), as if the one who keeps to it is fighting Satan. It was also said that it derives from *haraba* (with a fatha), as if the one who keeps to it encounters hardship, fatigue and weariness. ﴿Then he signalled to them to glorify [God] in the morning and the evening﴾ It was said: the meaning of *awha* is *awma'a* (he gestured). This is supported by His words in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿except by gesture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 41]. It was also said: he wrote for them on the ground. The first view was held by al-Kalbi, al-Qurazi, Qatadah and Ibn Munabbih; the second was held by Mujahid. The word *wahy* (revelation) may also be used for writing, as in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Apart from the four dark ones, which are as if they were the remnant of revelation in the pages of the scrolls."

And 'Antarah said:

"Like the writing of scrolls from the era of Kisra, which he sent to a non-Arab with a foreign (*tamtami*) tongue."

The *an* in His words ﴿that glorify﴾ is either the verbal *an* or the explanatory *an*. The meaning: he signalled to them that they should pray, or, that is, "pray." The accusative of *bukratan wa-'ashiyyan* ("in the morning and the evening") is adverbial of time.

Al-Farra' said: *al-'ashi* (evening) may be feminine, and it is permissible to make it masculine when it is indefinite. He said: it is also said that *al-'ashiyy* is the plural of *'ashiyyah*. It was said: what is meant by glorification is the dawn and afternoon prayers. It was also said: what is meant by glorification is the saying "Glory be to God" at both times, that is, exalt your Lord at both ends of the day.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾: "Generous, guide, trustworthy, mighty, truthful." In one wording *kafin* ("sufficient") replaces *kabir* ("great").

'Abd al-Razzaq, Adam ibn Abi Iyas, 'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi in *al-Tawhid*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that he said: *kaf* is from *karim* (generous), *ha* is from *hadi* (guide), *ya* is from *hakim* (wise), *'ayn* is from *'alim* (knowing), and *sad* is from *sadiq* (truthful).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that they are the disjointed letters (*al-hija' al-muqatta'*): the *kaf* is from *al-Malik* (the King), the *ha* is from *Allah*, the *ya* and *'ayn* are from *al-'Aziz* (the Mighty), and the *sad* is from *al-Musawwir* (the Fashioner).

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Kalbi that he was asked about ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ and he related from Abu Salih, from Umm Hani', from (p-٨٨٤) the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Kaf: guide, knowing, truthful."

'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Fatimah daughter of 'Ali, who said: 'Ali used to say: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, forgive me."

Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾, that he said: "The *kaf* is *al-Kafi* (the Sufficient), the *ha* is *al-Hadi* (the Guide), the *'ayn* is *al-'Alim* (the Knowing), and the *sad* is *al-Sadiq* (the Truthful)."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say regarding *Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad*, *Ha Mim*, *Ya Sin* and similar letters: "It is the Greatest Name of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of God's names."

Just as this disagreement arose among the Companions regarding this and similar matters, it also arose among those who came after them, and nothing has been authentically traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a raised (*marfu'*) report on this. Whatever is related from a Companion on this matter has been related from others something that contradicts it, and the same Companion may be related to have given differing and contradictory interpretations of these opening letters. None of this constitutes a proof. Rather, the correct position is to suspend judgement and to refer the knowledge of such matters to God, glorified is He. We have already set out the verification of this in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Zakariyya was a carpenter."

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The last of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Zakariyya ibn Azar ibn Muslim, of the offspring of Ya'qub. He called upon his Lord in secret, ﴿He said: 'My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me'﴾ until His words ﴿and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾" — [in the report] "until His words ﴿I fear the heirs [after me]﴾." He said: "The heirs are the male relatives (*'asabah*) who would inherit from me; they would inherit my prophethood and the prophethood of the family of Ya'qub. So the angels called to him, and he was Jibril: 'Indeed God gives you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya.' When he heard the call, Satan came to him and said: 'O Zakariyya, the voice you heard is not from God; it is from Satan, who mocked you.' So he doubted and said: ﴿How can I have a boy?﴾, meaning: from where can it be, when old age has reached me and my wife is barren?' God said: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾."

al-Firyabi transmitted from him, who said: "Zakariyya had no child, so he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself an heir﴾" and he said: "He will inherit my wealth and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub the prophethood."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ that he said: "A peer."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: "I do not know how the Messenger of God (ﷺ) read this word: *'itiyyan* or *'isiyyan*."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words *'itiyyan* that he said: "He remained for a long time in old age."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "*Harman*" (decrepit).

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound﴾, that he said: "His tongue was tied, without illness." In another wording: "without muteness." Transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So he signalled to them﴾, that he said: "He wrote a book for them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that glorify﴾, that he said: "He commanded them to pray ﴿in the morning and the evening﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 19, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Nahhas and Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat Maryam was revealed in Makkah." And Ibn Mardawayh recorded the same from Aisha.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dala'il*, recorded from Umm Salama that al-Najashi (the Negus) said to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib: "Do you have with you anything from what he (ﷺ) brought from God?" He said: "Yes." So he recited to him the beginning of (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad). Al-Najashi wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until they wet their scriptures when they heard what he recited to them. Then al-Najashi said: "Indeed, this and what Musa brought come from the same niche (lamp)." Ibn Ishaq related the story in full.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾. Abu Ja'far read these letters separately (pausing between each), while the rest joined them. Abu Amr inclined the *ha'* and opened the *ba'*, and Ibn Amir and Hamza reversed that. Al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Khalaf inclined both. The people of Madinah read them in between the two pronunciations, and the rest read them with a fatha on both.

It is related from Kharija that al-Hasan used to pronounce the *kaf* with a *damma*, and he reported that others pronounced the *ha'* with a *damma*. Abu Hatim said: "It is not permissible to put a *damma* on the *kaf*, the *ha'* or the *ya'*." Al-Nahhas said: "The reading of the people of Madinah is among the best of what is said on this, and inclination (*imalah*, pronouncing a vowel toward *i*) is permissible on *ha'* and on *ya'*." A group has objected to al-Hasan's reading. It has been said that its interpretation is that he gave only a slight *damma* (*ishmam*) on the *raf'* (nominative) position.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Asim and Ya'qub made the *dal* clear in the spelling of *Sad* (*ṣād*), and this is the choice of Abu Ubayda. The rest assimilated it (idgham).

It has been said, in explaining these readings, that *tafkhim* (velarization, the full pronunciation) is the original, and *imalah* is a derivative of it. Whoever read with *tafkhim* on the *ha'* and the *ya'* has acted according to the original; whoever inclined them has acted according to the derivative; and whoever inclined one and velarized the other has acted according to both. The discussion of these letters that occur at the openings of surahs has already been given in full at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. As for the grammatical position of this opening, if it is taken as the name of the surah, as most scholars hold, it is in the nominative (*raf'*) as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is what follows it. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Al-Zajjaj objected to this and said: "This is impossible, because ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾ is not part of what God, Mighty and Majestic, told us about Zakariyya, whereas God, Blessed and Exalted, has informed us about him and about what he was given glad tidings of, and (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) is not part of his story." Or (it is said) it is the predicate of an omitted subject. If the letters are taken as a continuous listing in the manner of enumeration, then his saying ﴿a mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "In what is recited to you is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." Al-Zajjaj said: *dhikr* (mention) is in the nominative by the pronoun (*bi-l-damir*), and the meaning is: "This which we recite to you is a mention of the mercy of your Lord ﴿to His servant Zakariyya﴾," meaning His answering him when he called upon Him and asked Him for a child. The accusative of *'abdahu* (His servant) is, according to al-Akhfash, as an object of *rahmah* (mercy). It has also been said that it is an object of *dhikr*. The meaning of "mention of the mercy" is its reaching and befalling (him), as one says, "The kindness of so-and-so mentioned me," meaning: it reached me.

Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *dhikra* with the accusative. Abu al-Aliya read *'abduhu* with the nominative, on the basis that the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) is in the genitive by being annexed to its object, and the subject of the mention is *'abduhu*. Zakariyya, according to both readings, is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to it or a substitute (*badal*) for it. Al-Kalbi read *dhakara* as a past-tense verb, both with and without doubling of the middle letter, with *'abadahu* as its subject. Ibn Ma'mar read it as an imperative. On this reading, "mercy" refers to Zakariyya himself, because every prophet is a mercy to his community.

﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) "when" is *rahmah* (mercy). It has also been said to be *dhikr* (mention), and it has been said that it is a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from Zakariyya. People differ on why his call was secret. It has been said: because it is further from ostentation (*riya'*). It has been said: he concealed it so that he would not be blamed for asking for a child at a time that was not right, and because it concerned worldly matters. It has been said: he concealed it out of fear of his people. And it has been said: this was from him because he had become weak and decrepit and could not raise his voice.

﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾. This sentence explains his saying "he called upon his Lord." It is said: *wahana yahinu wahnan*, when he became weak, so he is *wahin* (weak). It has been read with all three vowel patterns. He meant that his bones had grown slack and his strength had diminished. He mentioned the bone because it is the pillar of the body, the thing by which it stands, and the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, the rest collapses and its strength falls away. Also, the strongest part of a person is his spine, and when it weakens, what lies beyond it is even weaker. He used the singular "bone" intending the class noun, which conveys the weakening of every individual bone.

﴿And the head has blazed with white hair﴾. Abu Amr read the *sin* as assimilated into the *shin*, and the rest did not. *Al-ishtial* in its original sense is the spreading of the light of fire. So the spreading of the whiteness of hair over its blackness was likened to this, by the common features of whiteness and brightness. Then it was expressed in the form of a metaphor by implication (*isti'arah bi-l-kinayah*), by omitting the thing compared to and the particle of comparison. This metaphor is among the most creative and most beautiful metaphors.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said of white hair when it becomes very abundant, "The head of so-and-so has blazed," and he cited Labid:

*"If you see my head has become bright, white hair has taken over it and it has blazed."*

The accusative of *shaybāan* (white hair) is as a specification (*tamyiz*), said al-Zajjaj. Al-Akhfash said its accusative is as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), because the meaning of *ishta'ala* is *shaba* (grew white). Al-Nahhas said: al-Akhfash's view is better, because it is derived from the form *fa'ala*, and the verbal-noun reading is more apparent in cases like this. The original would have been "the white hair of my head blazed," but the blazing was attributed to the head to convey comprehensiveness.

﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord﴾. That is: I have never been disappointed in my calling upon You at any time, but every time I called upon You, You answered me.

The scholars said: It is recommended for a person to combine in his supplication humility and mention of God's blessings upon him, as Zakariyya did here. In His saying ﴿my bones have weakened within me and the head has blazed with white hair﴾ is the utmost humility, abasement, display of weakness, and inability to attain his aims and reach his goals. In His saying ﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord﴾ is a mention of the favour God had accustomed him to, in answering his prayers. It is said *shaqiya bi-kadha*, meaning: he toiled in it and did not obtain his aim from it.

﴿And indeed I have feared the *mawali* (kinsmen) after me﴾. Uthman ibn Affan, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn and his father Ali, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *khaffa* (with the *kha'* vowelled with a fatha, the *fa'* doubled and the *ta'* vowelled with a kasra), with *al-mawali* as its subject. That is: they became few and were unable to bear the responsibility of religion after me, or they died out, from *khaffa al-qawm*, when a people departed. This reading is anomalous and far from correct.

The rest read *khiftu* with a kasra on the *kha'* and a sukun on the *fa'*, so that its subject is a pronoun referring to Zakariyya, its object is *al-mawali*, and *min wara'i* (after me) is connected to an omitted verb, not to *khiftu*. Its implied meaning is: "I feared the conduct of the *mawali* after me."

The majority read *wara'i* with a hamza, a long vowel, and a sukun on the *ya'*. Ibn Kathir read it with a hamza, a long vowel, and a fatha on the *ya'*. It is also reported from him that he read it with a short vowel and a fatha on the *ya'*, like *'asayya* (my staff).

The *mawali* here are the relatives who inherit, and the other male kinsmen, the sons of paternal uncles and the like. The Arabs call these *mawali*. A poet said:

*"Gently, sons of our paternal uncles, gently, our kinsmen! Do not spread among us what was buried."*

It has been said: the *mawali* are those who support him.

They differ on the nature of Zakariyya's fear for his kinsmen after him. It has been said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and he wanted his son to inherit him; so he asked God, glorified is He, to grant him a child. Others said: they were negligent of the affairs of religion, so he feared that religion would be lost at his death, and he asked for a *wali* (guardian) to uphold it after his death. This view is preferable to the first, because prophets do not leave inheritance, and they are too exalted to concern themselves with worldly affairs. So what is meant here is not the inheritance of property but the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, and the upholding of the affairs of religion. It has been firmly established from our Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity."

﴿And my wife has been barren﴾. *Al-'aqir* is the woman who does not bear children because of old age, and also the woman who does not bear children for reasons other than old age; the latter is what is meant here. The term *'aqir* is also used for a man who does not father children, and from it is the saying of Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

*"What a wretched youth you are, if you are one-eyed and barren."*

Ibn Jarir said: the name of his wife was Ashna' daughter of Faqud ibn Mayl, and she was the sister of Hanna, and Hanna was the mother of Maryam. Al-Qutaybi said: she was Ashna' daughter of Imran. On the first view, Yahya ibn Zakariyya would be the maternal cousin of Isa's mother, and on the second, the two would be maternal cousins, as is related in the authentic hadith.

﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir (*waliyyan*)﴾. That is: give me, out of Your bounty, a *wali*. He did not state explicitly that he sought a child, because he knew about himself that he and his wife had reached a state in which a child could not come into being between them and be born of them. It has been said that he was ninety-some years old. It has also been said that he meant by *wali* the one who would be the child he sought. There is no barrier to asking for something like this, which is beyond the ordinary course, since God, glorified is He, may honour His messengers with such things, and this is one of the miracles that testify to their truthfulness.

﴿Who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾. The people of the two holy cities (Makkah and Madinah), al-Hasan, Asim, Hamza, Ibn Muhaysin and Yahya ibn al-Mubarak al-Yazidi read *yarithuni* and *yarithu* both in the nominative, on the basis that they are attributes of the *wali* and not answers (jussive responses) to the supplication. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read both in the jussive, on the basis that they are answers to the supplication. Abu Ubayd preferred the first reading and said: it is more correct in meaning, because he asked for a *wali* with this description, so he said: "Give me one who will be my heir."

Al-Nahhas also preferred this, and said: because the answer to an imperative, according to the grammarians, carries the sense of a condition and consequence. You say: *Obey God, He will admit you into Paradise*, meaning: if you obey Him, He will admit you into Paradise. How could God, glorified is He, inform him of this, I mean that He would grant him an heir who would inherit him, when He is the one who knows about it? Inheritance here is the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, according to the preferred view as already stated.

Most exegetes have held that Ya'qub mentioned here is Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim. Some exegetes claimed that he is Ya'qub son of Mathan, brother of Imran son of Mathan, and this was the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. *Ali Ya'qub* are his closest people, those whose affairs revert to him, by kinship, companionship, or agreement in religion. There were prophets and kings among them. It has also been read *yarithuni warithun min ali Ya'qub* (with *warith* as the subject of *yarithuni*). It has also been read *wa-arithu ali Ya'qub*, that is, "I" will inherit. It has also been read *uwayrithu ali Ya'qub* in the diminutive form, on the basis that this diminutive is the subject of *yarithuni*. These readings are extremely anomalous both in form and in meaning.

﴿And make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing (*radiyyan*)﴾. That is: one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and Your destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. It has been said: a prophet, as You made his forefathers prophets.

﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾. Most exegetes said: this call is from God, glorified is He. It has been said that it came from the angels, because of His saying in Surat Al 'Imran, ﴿So the angels called out to him﴾ (3:39). There is an omission in the speech: that is, He answered his supplication, and so said, "O Zakariyya." The reason for the name Yahya and Zakariyya has already been given in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-Zajjaj said: he was named Yahya because he was made alive (*hayiya*) by the knowledge and wisdom that he was given.

﴿We have not previously made any namesake for him﴾. (p-883) Most exegetes said: its meaning is that We did not name anyone before him Yahya.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 19, verses 1–11 (part 2 of 2):

Mujahid and a group [of scholars] said: the meaning of ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ is that He did not make for him any equal or peer. On this view the word is derived from *al-musamah* (equality) or *al-sumuww* (exaltedness). This was rejected on the ground that it would imply his being preferred over Abraham and Moses. It was also said: its meaning is that no barren woman had given birth like him. The first view is the better.

In God's (subhanahu) report that no one was named with this name before him is a virtue for him from two aspects. The first: it was God, glorified is He, who Himself chose his name, and did not leave it to his parents.

The second aspect: naming him with a name that had not been given to anyone else indicates his honour and exaltation.

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy?"﴾ That is: how, or from where, can I have a boy? This interrogative does not mean denial; rather it expresses wonder at God's power and the wondrous nature of His creation, since He brings forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. The discussion of this kind of matter has already been presented in Surat Al 'Imran. ﴿And I have reached extreme old age﴾ It is said: *'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'itiyyan* (the old man became decrepit) when his age has advanced and he has grown very old. *Shaykh 'at* (a decrepit old man) is one who has reached a state of dryness and desiccation. The original form is *'utuwwan*, since it is from the *waw*-roots, but they changed it to *ya'* because it is lighter. Similar to what is in the verse is the poet's saying:

"The youth is excused, but one who has been in the time of decrepitude is not excused."

Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and al-A'mash read *'itiyyan* with a kasra on the 'ayn; the rest read it with a damma on the 'ayn. Both are dialectal variants. The position (i'rab) of the clause ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the speaker. The position of the clause ﴿and I have reached extreme old age﴾ is also accusative as a circumstantial clause. Both clauses serve to reinforce the sense of improbability and wonder conveyed by his words ﴿how can I have a boy?﴾. That is: how can a child be born to us now, when my wife has been barren, not having given birth in her youth or in mine, and she is now an old woman, and I am a frail old man?

Then God, glorified is He, answered this question, which implies wonder and improbability, with His words ﴿He said: "Thus has your Lord said"﴾. The *kaf* (the particle *ka-*, "thus") is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is thus. The demonstrative refers to what preceded in Zakariyya's words. Then He began with the words ﴿your Lord said﴾. It is also possible that its position is accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: he said a saying like that. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to something unspecified, which is explained by His words ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. On the first interpretation, the clause ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ is a new, independent statement aimed at removing Zakariyya's sense of improbability after it had been affirmed; that is: "It is easy for Me, despite its improbability in your view." *Hayyin* is an intensive form (*fay'al*) from *han al-shay'* (the thing became easy): when it is not difficult and does not resist what is intended.

Al-Farra' said: that is, His creating it is easy for Me. ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ This clause confirms what precedes it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the creation of a child for you is like your creation. The meaning is that God created him originally and brought him into existence from pure non-existence, so bringing a child into being for him through ordinary procreation is easier and simpler than that. The verse did not attribute this to Adam, peace be upon him, because he was the one created from nothing in truth, by saying: "And I created your father Adam before, when he was nothing." This is to indicate that every individual of humankind has a share in the origination of Adam from nothing.

The people of Madinah, Makkah, Basra, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿And We created you before﴾ [with "I" as in the verse above]. The rest of the Kufans read *wa-qad khalaqnaka min qablu* ("And We created you before").

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign"﴾ That is: a sign that will show me the occurrence and realisation of what was asked for and the onset of pregnancy. The purpose of this request was to know the time of conception, since the glad tidings were not specific about its timing.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the reason is that his soul yearned for the matter to come quickly, so he asked God for a sign by which he could know that what had been bestowed on him was near. It was also said: he asked for a sign showing that the glad tidings came from God, glorified is He, and not from Satan, because Satan had deceived him with this. Thus said al-Dahhak and al-Suddi, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound."﴾ The explanation of this has already been given in full in Surat Al 'Imran. *Sawiyyan* (sound) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: your sign is that you will be unable to speak while you are of sound constitution, with no affliction in you that could prevent you from it. The mention of nights here, and of days in Surat Al 'Imran, indicates that what is meant is three days and their nights.

﴿So he came out to his people from the mihrab﴾ This is his prayer place (the prayer chamber). Its etymology is from *harb* (war), as if the one who keeps to it is fighting Satan. It was also said that it derives from *haraba* (with a fatha), as if the one who keeps to it encounters hardship, fatigue and weariness. ﴿Then he signalled to them to glorify [God] in the morning and the evening﴾ It was said: the meaning of *awha* is *awma'a* (he gestured). This is supported by His words in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿except by gesture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 41]. It was also said: he wrote for them on the ground. The first view was held by al-Kalbi, al-Qurazi, Qatadah and Ibn Munabbih; the second was held by Mujahid. The word *wahy* (revelation) may also be used for writing, as in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Apart from the four dark ones, which are as if they were the remnant of revelation in the pages of the scrolls."

And 'Antarah said:

"Like the writing of scrolls from the era of Kisra, which he sent to a non-Arab with a foreign (*tamtami*) tongue."

The *an* in His words ﴿that glorify﴾ is either the verbal *an* or the explanatory *an*. The meaning: he signalled to them that they should pray, or, that is, "pray." The accusative of *bukratan wa-'ashiyyan* ("in the morning and the evening") is adverbial of time.

Al-Farra' said: *al-'ashi* (evening) may be feminine, and it is permissible to make it masculine when it is indefinite. He said: it is also said that *al-'ashiyy* is the plural of *'ashiyyah*. It was said: what is meant by glorification is the dawn and afternoon prayers. It was also said: what is meant by glorification is the saying "Glory be to God" at both times, that is, exalt your Lord at both ends of the day.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾: "Generous, guide, trustworthy, mighty, truthful." In one wording *kafin* ("sufficient") replaces *kabir* ("great").

'Abd al-Razzaq, Adam ibn Abi Iyas, 'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi in *al-Tawhid*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that he said: *kaf* is from *karim* (generous), *ha* is from *hadi* (guide), *ya* is from *hakim* (wise), *'ayn* is from *'alim* (knowing), and *sad* is from *sadiq* (truthful).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ that they are the disjointed letters (*al-hija' al-muqatta'*): the *kaf* is from *al-Malik* (the King), the *ha* is from *Allah*, the *ya* and *'ayn* are from *al-'Aziz* (the Mighty), and the *sad* is from *al-Musawwir* (the Fashioner).

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Kalbi that he was asked about ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ and he related from Abu Salih, from Umm Hani', from (p-٨٨٤) the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Kaf: guide, knowing, truthful."

'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Fatimah daughter of 'Ali, who said: 'Ali used to say: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, forgive me."

Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾, that he said: "The *kaf* is *al-Kafi* (the Sufficient), the *ha* is *al-Hadi* (the Guide), the *'ayn* is *al-'Alim* (the Knowing), and the *sad* is *al-Sadiq* (the Truthful)."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say regarding *Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad*, *Ha Mim*, *Ya Sin* and similar letters: "It is the Greatest Name of God."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of God's names."

Just as this disagreement arose among the Companions regarding this and similar matters, it also arose among those who came after them, and nothing has been authentically traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a raised (*marfu'*) report on this. Whatever is related from a Companion on this matter has been related from others something that contradicts it, and the same Companion may be related to have given differing and contradictory interpretations of these opening letters. None of this constitutes a proof. Rather, the correct position is to suspend judgement and to refer the knowledge of such matters to God, glorified is He. We have already set out the verification of this in the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Zakariyya was a carpenter."

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The last of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Zakariyya ibn Azar ibn Muslim, of the offspring of Ya'qub. He called upon his Lord in secret, ﴿He said: 'My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me'﴾ until His words ﴿and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾" — [in the report] "until His words ﴿I fear the heirs [after me]﴾." He said: "The heirs are the male relatives (*'asabah*) who would inherit from me; they would inherit my prophethood and the prophethood of the family of Ya'qub. So the angels called to him, and he was Jibril: 'Indeed God gives you glad tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya.' When he heard the call, Satan came to him and said: 'O Zakariyya, the voice you heard is not from God; it is from Satan, who mocked you.' So he doubted and said: ﴿How can I have a boy?﴾, meaning: from where can it be, when old age has reached me and my wife is barren?' God said: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾."

al-Firyabi transmitted from him, who said: "Zakariyya had no child, so he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself an heir﴾" and he said: "He will inherit my wealth and will inherit from the family of Ya'qub the prophethood."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿We have not made for him before [any] namesake﴾ that he said: "A peer."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him, who said: "I do not know how the Messenger of God (ﷺ) read this word: *'itiyyan* or *'isiyyan*."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ata' regarding His words *'itiyyan* that he said: "He remained for a long time in old age."

He also transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: "*Harman*" (decrepit).

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound﴾, that he said: "His tongue was tied, without illness." In another wording: "without muteness." Transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him ﴿So he signalled to them﴾, that he said: "He wrote a book for them."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿that glorify﴾, that he said: "He commanded them to pray ﴿in the morning and the evening﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 12–15:

.

His saying, "Yā Yaḥyā" (O Yahya), here involves an omission, and its implied sense is: Allah said to the newborn, "O Yahya," or: a child was born to him and reached the age at which one may be addressed, and We said to him, "O Yahya."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "So We bestowed him [a son], and We said to him, 'O Yahya.'"

By "the Book" is meant the Tawrat (the Torah), because it was the known scripture at that time. It is also possible that it was a book specific to him, though we do not know of it now. By "taking" it is meant either the literal taking, or taking in the sense of meaning, which is to uphold what is in it as it should be upheld. This is achieved by acquiring a disposition (malakah) that makes it easy to undertake what is commanded and to refrain from what is forbidden. Then he emphasised this with His saying, "with strength" (bi-quwwah), meaning: with earnestness, resolve and diligence.

﴿And We gave him judgment (al-ḥukm) while he was a child﴾. By al-ḥukm is meant al-ḥikmah (wisdom), which is understanding of the Book that he was commanded to take, and understanding of the religious rulings. It has been said that it is knowledge, its preservation and acting upon it. It has been said that it is prophethood. It has been said that it is intellect. There is no barrier to al-ḥukm being suitable for carrying all that has been mentioned. It has been said that Yahya was two years old at the time of this address, and it has been said that he was three years old.

﴿And tenderness (ḥanānan) from Us﴾ is coordinated with al-ḥukm.

The majority of the exegetes said: al-ḥanān is mercy, compassion, kindness and love, and its root is the longing of the soul, derived from the yearning (ḥanīn) of a she-camel for her young.

Abū ʿUbayda said: you say, "Ḥanānuka, O Lord, and ḥanānayka, O Lord," with one meaning, meaning Your mercy. Ṭarafa said:

Abā Mundhir, you have destroyed (us), so spare some of us,
ḥanānayka; some evil is easier than some evil.

And Imru' al-Qays said:

And the Banū Salkh ibn Bakr give them their goats,
"Ḥanānaka, O possessor of tenderness!"

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-Ḥannān, with a shaddah, is one of the attributes of Allah, ʿazza wa-jall, while al-ḥanān, without a shaddah, is affection and mercy, and al-ḥanān is also provision and blessing.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: al-ḥanān in the speech of the Arabs also means that which is great among matters concerning the Essence of Allah. From this is the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl: "By Allah, if you kill this servant, I will surely take his grave as a ḥanān," meaning Bilāl, when he passed by him while he was being tortured. It has been said that the one who said this was Waraqah ibn Nawfal.

Al-Azharī said: the meaning of that is, "I will surely show mercy to him and be tender towards him, because he is among the people of Paradise." Similar to this is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

Be tender towards me, may the King guide you,
for every station has its speech.

The meaning of "from Us" (min ladunnā) is "from Our side." It has been said that it may mean: We gave him mercy from Us, existing in his heart, by which he shows tenderness towards people, including his parents and his relatives, until he rescues them from disbelief.

﴿And purity (zakāh)﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it. Zakāh means purification, blessing, growth and righteousness. That is: We made him blessed for the people, guiding them to good. It has been said: We purified him by praising him well, like the attestation of witnesses. It has been said: it is a charity which We gave on behalf of his parents, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿And he was God-fearing (taqiyyan)﴾ (p-885), meaning: he avoided the disobediences of Allah and was obedient to Him. It has been narrated that he never committed a single act of disobedience.

﴿And dutiful to his parents (barran bi-wālidayh)﴾ is coordinated with (taqiyyan). Al-barr here has the meaning of al-bārr, a form (fa'l) with the meaning of a doer (fā'il). The meaning is: gentle to them both and kind to them.

﴿And he was not arrogant (jabbāran), disobedient (ʿaṣiyyan)﴾, meaning: he was neither proud nor disobedient to his parents or to his Lord. This is a description of him, peace be upon him, of gentleness of manner and lowering of the wing (in humility).

﴿And peace be upon him﴾. Ibn Jarīr and others said: its meaning is: security upon him from Allah. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: in my view the more apparent is that it is the customary greeting, for it is more noble and more distinguished than security, because security is attained for him by the absence of disobedience from him, which is the least of his ranks. The honour lies in Allah greeting him with peace. The meaning of ﴿the day he was born﴾ is that he was secured from Satan and others on that day, or that Allah greeted him on that day. Likewise is the meaning of "the day he dies," and likewise the meaning of ﴿the day he is raised alive﴾. It has been said: the most frightening state for a human being is in three places: the day he is born, because he comes out of what he was in; the day he dies, because he sees people he did not know and rulings for which he has no precedent; and the day he is raised, because he sees the terror of the Day of Resurrection. So Allah, glory be to Him, singled out Yahya with honour and safety in these three places.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid, regarding His saying, "O Yahya, take the Book with strength," that he said: with earnestness. "And We gave him judgment while he was a child," he said: understanding. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: it means, act upon what is in it of obligations. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mālik ibn Dīnār who said: it is intellect (al-lubb). Abū Nuʿaym, al-Daylamī and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying, "And We gave him judgment while he was a child," that he said: "He was given understanding and worship while he was seven years old." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah: "He was a boy, and he was three years old."

Al-Ḥākim in his Tārīkh transmitted through the chain of Nahshal, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The boys said to Yahya ibn Zakariyyā, 'Come, let us play.' Yahya said, 'We were not created for play; go, let us pray.' That is the saying of Allah, 'And We gave him judgment while he was a child.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the Qurʾan before he reaches puberty, he is among those who were given judgment while a child."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās as a mawqūf (a statement ending with a companion). ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqī in al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt transmitted through the chain of ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, "and tenderness," that he said: "I do not know what it is, except that I think He bestows mercy upon His servant." A group of the early generations (al-salaf) explained it as mercy.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, "and purity," that he said: blessing. And regarding His saying, "and he was God-fearing," he said: he was pure, so he did not commit any sin.

Al-Azharī said: the meaning of that is, "I will surely show mercy to him and be tender towards him, because he is among the people of Paradise." Similar to this is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

Be tender towards me, may the King guide you,
for every station has its speech.

It has been said: We purified him by praising him well, like the attestation of witnesses. It has been said: it is a charity which We gave on behalf of his parents, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿And he was God-fearing (taqiyyan)﴾ (p-885), meaning: he avoided the disobediences of Allah and was obedient to Him. It has been narrated that he never committed a single act of disobedience.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: in my view the more apparent is that it is the customary greeting, for it is more noble and more distinguished than security, because security is attained for him by the absence of disobedience from him, which is the least of his ranks. Likewise is the meaning of "the day he dies," and likewise the meaning of ﴿the day he is raised alive﴾.
