Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid, regarding His saying, "O Yahya, take the Book with strength," that he said: with earnestness. "And We gave him judgment while he was a child," he said: understanding. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr who said: it means, act upon what is in it of obligations. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mālik ibn Dīnār who said: it is intellect (al-lubb). Abū Nuʿaym, al-Daylamī and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying, "And We gave him judgment while he was a child," that he said: "He was given understanding and worship while he was seven years old." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in Zawāʾid al-Zuhd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah: "He was a boy, and he was three years old."

Al-Ḥākim in his Tārīkh transmitted through the chain of Nahshal, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The boys said to Yahya ibn Zakariyyā, 'Come, let us play.' Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾: this begins the account of the beginning of the creation of ʿĪsā. What is meant by "the Book" is this surah; that is: mention to the people, O Muḥammad, in this surah, the story of Mary. It is also permissible that "the Book" means the genus of the Qur'an, of which this surah is a part. Since mention does not attach to physical entities, it was necessary to posit a genitive noun to which the mention attaches, namely "the story of Mary" or "the report of Mary." ﴿When she withdrew﴾: the operator in the adverbial phrase is that posited genitive noun. It is also permissible to make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal, substitution of comprehension) for Mary, since times encompass what is in them, and the intended meaning of "Mary" is her report. In this substitution there is an indication of magnifying the matter of the time, because her wondrous story occurred in it. Al-nabdh (withdrawal) means casting away and throwing.

God, glorified is He, said: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187]. The meaning is that she withdrew and moved away. Ibn Qutayba said: she isolated herself; it was said: she went apart; the meanings are close.

They differed regarding the cause of her withdrawal. It was said: so that she might worship God, glorified is He; it was said: so that she might purify herself from her menstruation. "From her people" is connected to "withdrew." The accusative of ﴿a place eastward﴾ is as an object of the mentioned verb, that is: a place on the side of the east. Ash-sharq (with a sukun on the rāʾ) is the place where the sun rises. He specified the place as eastward because they used to venerate the direction of the east, since it is the rising place of lights; Ibn Jarīr related this meaning.

People have differed regarding Mary's prophethood. It was said: she was a prophetess merely by this sending to her and her addressing of the angel. It was said: she was not a prophetess, because the angel only spoke to her in the form of a human. The discussion of this has preceded in Āl ʿImrān.

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾: that is, she took a screen apart from her people which would conceal her from them, so that they would not see her during worship or during purification from menstruation.

Al-ḥijāb (the screen) means a covering and a barrier. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾: it is Jibrīl, peace be upon him. It was said: it is the spirit of ʿĪsā, because God, glorified is He, created the spirits before the bodies; but the first is preferable because of His saying: ﴿So he appeared to her as a man in every way perfect﴾; that is, Jibrīl appeared to her in the form of a man of perfect form, lacking none of the attributes of the children of Ādam. It is said: the reason for the angel's appearing to her as a man is that she could not bear to look at the angel in his own form. When she saw him in the form of a handsome man of complete form, who had breached the screen around her, she thought he intended her harm, so she sought refuge in God from him, and ﴿said: Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears God﴾; that is, one who guards himself against God and fears Him. It was said that "taqiyyan" is the name of a righteous man, so she sought refuge from him in amazement; and it was said that it is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time (p-886). The first is preferable. The answer to the condition is omitted, that is: then do not approach me.

﴿He said: I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾: that is, Jibrīl said to her: I am only the messenger of your Lord, by Whom you have sought refuge, and I am not one from whom what has occurred to your mind of intending evil is to be expected. ﴿To give you a pure son﴾: He attributed the gift to himself, since he was the cause of it, in that the announcement to her came from him, or because the breathing was carried out by him outwardly.

Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh, from Nāfiʿ, read "li-yahaba" (that He may give), meaning: He sent me that He may give you; the rest read with hamza. Al-zakiyy is the one pure from sins who grows in purity and chastity; it was said: the intended meaning of al-zakiyy is the prophet.

﴿She said: How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾: that is, no husband or other has approached me. ﴿And I have not been unchaste﴾: al-baghiyy is the fornicatress who seeks men. Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is baghuwiy on the pattern of faʿūl; the waw was changed to yā', then assimilated into the yā', and the ghayn was kasra for harmony. Ibn Jinnī said: it is faʿīl. The mention of her not having been unchaste, along with her saying "no man has touched me," which encompasses both lawful and unlawful, is for the purpose of emphasis, to declare her innocent from indecency. It was said: she did not find anything in God's power improbable, but she meant: how will the child be—from a husband she will marry in the future, or will God create him directly? It was said: touching is a metaphor for lawful marriage, and on this view there is no need to explain the sense of her saying "and I have not been unchaste." What we have mentioned, that it includes both, is more preferable in the usages of the people of language, and in their discourse there is much that would take long to enumerate. End.

﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾: that is, and that We may make this boy, or his creation without a father, a sign for the people by which they may infer the perfection of power. This is a reason for an omitted motivated clause, the estimate being: We created him so that We might make him (a sign); or it is conjoined to another hidden reason, connected to what is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The sentence ﴿He said: Thus said your Lord, It is easy for Me﴾ is resumptive, and the speaker is the angel; the discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding what preceded of Zakariyyā's saying.

His saying ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ is conjoined to "a sign": that is, and that We may make him a great mercy issuing from Us to the people, for the guidance and abundant good they receive; because every prophet is a mercy to his community. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾: that is, that mentioned matter was something predetermined, which God, glorified is He, had decreed, and the pen had dried over it.

So she conceived him. Here there is an implied statement, and the estimate is: she was reassured by his words, so he approached her and breathed into the collar of her garment, and the breath reached her womb, so she conceived him. It was said: the breath was in her skirt; it was said: in her mouth.

It was said: her delivery was connected to this conception without the passing of a period of gestation. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾; that is, she moved away and isolated herself to a distant place. Al-qaṣiyy is the distant. It was said: this place was behind the mountain; it was said: the farthest place in that abode; it was said: the far end of the valley. It was said: she carried him for six months; it was said: eight months; it was said: seven.

﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾: that is, they compelled her and forced her, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:
"The fear and the hope compelled him."
Shibl read "fājaʾahā" (surprised her), from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness), and this reading is related from ʿĀṣim; al-Ḥasan read without hamza; and in the codex of Ubayy it is "falammā ajāʾahā." In al-Kashshāf he said: ajāʾahā is transferred from jāʾa, except that its usage became specified after the transfer to the meaning of compulsion; and this is far-fetched. The apparent view is that each of the two verbs has its own independent meaning. Al-makhāḍ is the verbal noun of makhadat al-mar'a, tamkhud, makhḍan and makhāḍan, when her delivery drew near.

The majority read with a fatḥa on the mīm, and Ibn Kathīr read with a kasra.

Al-jidhʿ is the trunk of a dry palm tree, as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, just as a pregnant woman clings, due to the severity of labor pains, to something she finds near her. The definite article is either generic or for a known referent. ﴿She said: Would that I had died before this﴾: that is, before this time. She wished for death because she feared that evil would be imputed to her in her religion, or so that people would not fall into slander because of her.

﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾: al-nasy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is of such a kind that it is forgotten, not mentioned, and its loss is not felt, like a peg or a rope; and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:
"Will you make us as a worthless thing for the tribe of Quḍāʿa, while we are not forgotten among Maʿadd nor of little account?"

Al-Farrāʾ said: al-nasy is the rags a woman discards from her menstrual cloths; so Mary says: "a thing forgotten" (nasyan mansiyyan), that is, a discarded menstrual rag. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the nūn, and both are dialects, like al-ḥijr and al-ḥajr, and al-witr and al-watr. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī read "nisāʾan" with hamza and a kasra on the nūn. Nawf al-Bakkālī read with hamza and a fatḥa on the nūn. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "nasiyyan" with a fatḥa on the nūn and shadda on the yā' without hamza. Al-mansiyy is the abandoned one who is not mentioned and does not occur to anyone among the people.

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾: that is, Jibrīl, when he heard her words, and he was lower than her, beneath the mound; it was said: beneath the palm tree; it was said: the caller was ʿĪsā. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the mīm of "min."

His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is an explanation of the calling: that is, do not grieve, or the meaning is "that do not grieve," with the particle being the verbal (maṣdariyya) one. ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾: the majority of the exegetes said: al-sariyy is the small river, and the meaning is: your Lord has placed beneath your feet a river. It was said: it was a river from which the water had ceased; God sent water into it for Mary, and by it He revived that dry trunk on which she had leaned, until it put forth leaves and bore fruit. It was said: the intended meaning of al-sariyy here is ʿĪsā; and al-sariyy means the great one among men, and from it is their saying: "So-and-so is sariyy," that is, great; and "from a people of surāt," that is, great ones.

﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾: al-hazz is moving; it is said: he shook it and it shook; the bāʾ in "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla" is extra for emphasis. Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi." Al-jidhʿ is the lower part of the tree. Quṭrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidhʿ. The meaning of "ilayki" is toward your direction. The original of "tasāqaṭ" is tatasāqaṭ, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the sīn. Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash read "tasāqaṭ" with lightening. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafs, and al-Ḥasan read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and lightening, with a kasra on the qāf. It has been read "tatasāqaṭ" with both tāʾs made apparent. It has been read with a yā' and shadda on the sīn. It has been read "tasquṭ" and "yasquṭ."

The rest read with assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn. Whoever reads with the feminine tāʾ makes the pronoun refer to the palm tree, and whoever reads with the yā' makes the pronoun refer to the trunk. The accusative of "rutaban" in some of these readings is as a specifier, and in the others as the object of "tusāqiṭ."

Al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said: "rutaban" may be accusative by "hazzī," that is: shake toward you dates. ﴿Fresh (janiyyan)﴾ "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla," that is, on its trunk; al-Zamakhsharī weakened this. Al-janiyy is what is picked fresh; it was said: it is what is sought and suitable for picking, and it is a faʿīl in the sense of a maf‌ʿūl. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are one; it was said: it is a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, fresh, good dates.

﴿So eat and drink﴾: that is, from those dates and that water, or from the dates and their juice. She placed eating first though mention of the stream precedes the dates, because a woman in postpartum needs to eat dates more intensely than she needs to drink water. Then He said: ﴿And be cool of eye﴾. The majority read with a fatḥa on the qāf. Ibn Jarīr related that it was read with a kasra, and said: it is the dialect of Najd.

The meaning: be content of soul and cast off grief from yourself. It is derived from al-qarr and al-qurra, and both are coldness; the one who is pleased has a cool heart and still limbs. It was said: the meaning is: cool your eye by seeing the child given to you. Al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is sleep. Abū ʿAmr said: God cooled his eye, that is, made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness.

﴿And if you see any human being﴾: its original is tarʾayīna, like tasmaʿīna; the hamza was softened and the nūn dropped for the jussive, and the yā' of the pronoun for the two sākins after attaching the nūn of emphasis. A similar case without the nūn of emphasis is the saying of Ibn Duraid:
"If you see my head, whose color resembles the dawn's streak under the skirts of the darkness."

Ṭalḥa and Shayba read "tarayna" with a sukūn on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn, lightened. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is anomalous. The answer to the condition is: ﴿then say: Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾; that is, say: if any of the people asks you to speak: indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, that is, silence. It was said: the intended meaning is the legal fast, which is abstaining from things that break the fast; and the first is preferable.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 2 of 2):

It is reported in the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, silence﴾ with the two words joined together (ṣawman ṣamtan without a conjunction), and likewise it is reported from Anas. It is also reported from him that he read ﴿a fast and silence﴾ with the conjunction "wa" (ṣawman wa-ṣamtan). What the majority of the exegetes hold is that the fast here is silence, and what indicates this is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The meaning of ṣawm (fasting) in the lexical sense is broader than the two meanings.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Everyone who refrains from food, speech, or travel is a ṣā’im (one who fasts)."

The reading of Ubayy indicates that what is meant by ṣawm here is silence, because it is an explanation of ṣawm. The reading of Anas indicates that ṣawm here is other than silence, as the conjunction "wa" conveys. The meaning of ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ is that she would not speak to anyone of mankind after informing them of this report, but would only speak to the angels and commune with her Lord. It was also said that she did not inform them here by speech, but by a gesture indicating the vow.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾, that he said: "a place that the sun shaded her, so that none of them could see her."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "The Christians only took the east as a qibla because Maryam withdrew from her family to a place toward the east, so they took her birth-place as a qibla. The Jews only prostrated sideways when the mountain was lifted above them, so they began to tilt while looking at it, fearing that it would fall upon them, and so they prostrated a prostration with which Allah was pleased, and they made it a sunna."

Al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related through the route of al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, both said: "Maryam bint 'Imran went out to the side of the miḥrab because of a menstruation that had befallen her. When she became pure, behold, a man was with her, ﴿and he appeared to her as a well-formed man﴾. She was frightened and ﴿said, 'Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing'﴾. She went out with her outer garment on, and he took hold of her sleeve and blew into the side of her shirt, which was split in front, and the breath entered her chest and she became pregnant. Then her sister, the wife of Zechariah, came to visit her one night, and when she opened the door for her, she embraced her. The wife of Zechariah said: 'O Maryam, do you perceive that I am pregnant?' Maryam said: 'Do you perceive that I am pregnant?' The wife of Zechariah said: 'Indeed I found that what is in my belly prostrated to what is in your belly.' That is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. So the wife of Zechariah gave birth to Yahya. When the time for Maryam to give birth came, she went out to the side of the miḥrab, ﴿and the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree; she said, 'Would that I had died before this'﴾ (the verse). Then Jibril called to her from beneath her, 'Do not grieve.' When she gave birth to him, Satan departed and informed the Children of Israel that Maryam had given birth. When they asked her to speak, she pointed to 'Isa, and he spoke and ﴿said, 'Indeed I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture'﴾ (the verses). When he was born, no idol remained on earth except that it fell upon its face."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding Maryam that he said: "When she became pregnant, she gave birth." Ibn 'Asakir related from him that he said: "She gave birth after eight months."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada regarding His words ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ that he said: "Jibril." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of it from 'Ata' also.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it authentic), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse that he said: "The spirit of 'Isa appeared to her in the form of a human, and she conceived him." He said: "What she conceived is that the one who addressed her entered into her mouth."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿to a distant place﴾ that he said: "Remote."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ that he said: "It was a dry trunk."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him regarding His words ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "I had not been created and I was not a thing."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrima regarding ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "A discarded menstrual cloth."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Mujahid. 'Abd ibn Humayd related the like of it from Nawf al-Bakali and al-Dahhak.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from 'Ikrima regarding His words ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ that he said: "The one who called to her was Jibril."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The one who called to her from beneath her was Jibril, and 'Isa did not speak until she brought him to her people." The reports from the early generations differ as to whether this caller was Jibril or 'Isa.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: "'Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud read ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ with a fatha (naṣb). He said: 'Whoever reads it with a fatha, it is 'Isa, and whoever reads it with a kasra, it is Jibril.'"

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar related from Ibn 'Umar: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the sari (stream) about which Allah said to Maryam ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ is a river that Allah brought forth for her to drink from."

In its chain is Ayyub ibn Nahik al-Jabali, of whom Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "weak"; Abu Zur'a said: "munkar al-hadith"; Abu Fath al-Azdi said: "matruk al-hadith"; and al-Tabarani said after relating this hadith: "It is very strange (gharib)."

Al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and Ibn Mardawayh related "from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ that he said: 'the river.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who declared it authentic), al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara' regarding the verse that he said: "It is the jadwal, which is the small river." Thus it becomes clear that the mawquf (companion's) report is more authentic.

It has been reported from a group of the Successors that the sari is 'Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿fresh ripe dates﴾ that he said: "Fresh."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related regarding His words ﴿Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ that he said: "Silence."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari related from him that he read ﴿ṣawman ṣamtan﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾: this begins the account of the beginning of the creation of ʿĪsā. What is meant by "the Book" is this surah; that is: mention to the people, O Muḥammad, in this surah, the story of Mary. It is also permissible that "the Book" means the genus of the Qur'an, of which this surah is a part. Since mention does not attach to physical entities, it was necessary to posit a genitive noun to which the mention attaches, namely "the story of Mary" or "the report of Mary." ﴿When she withdrew﴾: the operator in the adverbial phrase is that posited genitive noun. It is also permissible to make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal, substitution of comprehension) for Mary, since times encompass what is in them, and the intended meaning of "Mary" is her report. In this substitution there is an indication of magnifying the matter of the time, because her wondrous story occurred in it. Al-nabdh (withdrawal) means casting away and throwing.

God, glorified is He, said: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187]. The meaning is that she withdrew and moved away. Ibn Qutayba said: she isolated herself; it was said: she went apart; the meanings are close.

They differed regarding the cause of her withdrawal. It was said: so that she might worship God, glorified is He; it was said: so that she might purify herself from her menstruation. "From her people" is connected to "withdrew." The accusative of ﴿a place eastward﴾ is as an object of the mentioned verb, that is: a place on the side of the east. Ash-sharq (with a sukun on the rāʾ) is the place where the sun rises. He specified the place as eastward because they used to venerate the direction of the east, since it is the rising place of lights; Ibn Jarīr related this meaning.

People have differed regarding Mary's prophethood. It was said: she was a prophetess merely by this sending to her and her addressing of the angel. It was said: she was not a prophetess, because the angel only spoke to her in the form of a human. The discussion of this has preceded in Āl ʿImrān.

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾: that is, she took a screen apart from her people which would conceal her from them, so that they would not see her during worship or during purification from menstruation.

Al-ḥijāb (the screen) means a covering and a barrier. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾: it is Jibrīl, peace be upon him. It was said: it is the spirit of ʿĪsā, because God, glorified is He, created the spirits before the bodies; but the first is preferable because of His saying: ﴿So he appeared to her as a man in every way perfect﴾; that is, Jibrīl appeared to her in the form of a man of perfect form, lacking none of the attributes of the children of Ādam. It is said: the reason for the angel's appearing to her as a man is that she could not bear to look at the angel in his own form. When she saw him in the form of a handsome man of complete form, who had breached the screen around her, she thought he intended her harm, so she sought refuge in God from him, and ﴿said: Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears God﴾; that is, one who guards himself against God and fears Him. It was said that "taqiyyan" is the name of a righteous man, so she sought refuge from him in amazement; and it was said that it is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time (p-886). The first is preferable. The answer to the condition is omitted, that is: then do not approach me.

﴿He said: I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾: that is, Jibrīl said to her: I am only the messenger of your Lord, by Whom you have sought refuge, and I am not one from whom what has occurred to your mind of intending evil is to be expected. ﴿To give you a pure son﴾: He attributed the gift to himself, since he was the cause of it, in that the announcement to her came from him, or because the breathing was carried out by him outwardly.

Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh, from Nāfiʿ, read "li-yahaba" (that He may give), meaning: He sent me that He may give you; the rest read with hamza. Al-zakiyy is the one pure from sins who grows in purity and chastity; it was said: the intended meaning of al-zakiyy is the prophet.

﴿She said: How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾: that is, no husband or other has approached me. ﴿And I have not been unchaste﴾: al-baghiyy is the fornicatress who seeks men. Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is baghuwiy on the pattern of faʿūl; the waw was changed to yā', then assimilated into the yā', and the ghayn was kasra for harmony. Ibn Jinnī said: it is faʿīl. The mention of her not having been unchaste, along with her saying "no man has touched me," which encompasses both lawful and unlawful, is for the purpose of emphasis, to declare her innocent from indecency. It was said: she did not find anything in God's power improbable, but she meant: how will the child be—from a husband she will marry in the future, or will God create him directly? It was said: touching is a metaphor for lawful marriage, and on this view there is no need to explain the sense of her saying "and I have not been unchaste." What we have mentioned, that it includes both, is more preferable in the usages of the people of language, and in their discourse there is much that would take long to enumerate. End.

﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾: that is, and that We may make this boy, or his creation without a father, a sign for the people by which they may infer the perfection of power. This is a reason for an omitted motivated clause, the estimate being: We created him so that We might make him (a sign); or it is conjoined to another hidden reason, connected to what is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The sentence ﴿He said: Thus said your Lord, It is easy for Me﴾ is resumptive, and the speaker is the angel; the discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding what preceded of Zakariyyā's saying.

His saying ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ is conjoined to "a sign": that is, and that We may make him a great mercy issuing from Us to the people, for the guidance and abundant good they receive; because every prophet is a mercy to his community. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾: that is, that mentioned matter was something predetermined, which God, glorified is He, had decreed, and the pen had dried over it.

So she conceived him. Here there is an implied statement, and the estimate is: she was reassured by his words, so he approached her and breathed into the collar of her garment, and the breath reached her womb, so she conceived him. It was said: the breath was in her skirt; it was said: in her mouth.

It was said: her delivery was connected to this conception without the passing of a period of gestation. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾; that is, she moved away and isolated herself to a distant place. Al-qaṣiyy is the distant. It was said: this place was behind the mountain; it was said: the farthest place in that abode; it was said: the far end of the valley. It was said: she carried him for six months; it was said: eight months; it was said: seven.

﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾: that is, they compelled her and forced her, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:
"The fear and the hope compelled him."
Shibl read "fājaʾahā" (surprised her), from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness), and this reading is related from ʿĀṣim; al-Ḥasan read without hamza; and in the codex of Ubayy it is "falammā ajāʾahā." In al-Kashshāf he said: ajāʾahā is transferred from jāʾa, except that its usage became specified after the transfer to the meaning of compulsion; and this is far-fetched. The apparent view is that each of the two verbs has its own independent meaning. Al-makhāḍ is the verbal noun of makhadat al-mar'a, tamkhud, makhḍan and makhāḍan, when her delivery drew near.

The majority read with a fatḥa on the mīm, and Ibn Kathīr read with a kasra.

Al-jidhʿ is the trunk of a dry palm tree, as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, just as a pregnant woman clings, due to the severity of labor pains, to something she finds near her. The definite article is either generic or for a known referent. ﴿She said: Would that I had died before this﴾: that is, before this time. She wished for death because she feared that evil would be imputed to her in her religion, or so that people would not fall into slander because of her.

﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾: al-nasy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is of such a kind that it is forgotten, not mentioned, and its loss is not felt, like a peg or a rope; and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:
"Will you make us as a worthless thing for the tribe of Quḍāʿa, while we are not forgotten among Maʿadd nor of little account?"

Al-Farrāʾ said: al-nasy is the rags a woman discards from her menstrual cloths; so Mary says: "a thing forgotten" (nasyan mansiyyan), that is, a discarded menstrual rag. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the nūn, and both are dialects, like al-ḥijr and al-ḥajr, and al-witr and al-watr. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī read "nisāʾan" with hamza and a kasra on the nūn. Nawf al-Bakkālī read with hamza and a fatḥa on the nūn. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "nasiyyan" with a fatḥa on the nūn and shadda on the yā' without hamza. Al-mansiyy is the abandoned one who is not mentioned and does not occur to anyone among the people.

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾: that is, Jibrīl, when he heard her words, and he was lower than her, beneath the mound; it was said: beneath the palm tree; it was said: the caller was ʿĪsā. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the mīm of "min."

His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is an explanation of the calling: that is, do not grieve, or the meaning is "that do not grieve," with the particle being the verbal (maṣdariyya) one. ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾: the majority of the exegetes said: al-sariyy is the small river, and the meaning is: your Lord has placed beneath your feet a river. It was said: it was a river from which the water had ceased; God sent water into it for Mary, and by it He revived that dry trunk on which she had leaned, until it put forth leaves and bore fruit. It was said: the intended meaning of al-sariyy here is ʿĪsā; and al-sariyy means the great one among men, and from it is their saying: "So-and-so is sariyy," that is, great; and "from a people of surāt," that is, great ones.

﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾: al-hazz is moving; it is said: he shook it and it shook; the bāʾ in "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla" is extra for emphasis. Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi." Al-jidhʿ is the lower part of the tree. Quṭrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidhʿ. The meaning of "ilayki" is toward your direction. The original of "tasāqaṭ" is tatasāqaṭ, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the sīn. Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash read "tasāqaṭ" with lightening. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafs, and al-Ḥasan read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and lightening, with a kasra on the qāf. It has been read "tatasāqaṭ" with both tāʾs made apparent. It has been read with a yā' and shadda on the sīn. It has been read "tasquṭ" and "yasquṭ."

The rest read with assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn. Whoever reads with the feminine tāʾ makes the pronoun refer to the palm tree, and whoever reads with the yā' makes the pronoun refer to the trunk. The accusative of "rutaban" in some of these readings is as a specifier, and in the others as the object of "tusāqiṭ."

Al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said: "rutaban" may be accusative by "hazzī," that is: shake toward you dates. ﴿Fresh (janiyyan)﴾ "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla," that is, on its trunk; al-Zamakhsharī weakened this. Al-janiyy is what is picked fresh; it was said: it is what is sought and suitable for picking, and it is a faʿīl in the sense of a maf‌ʿūl. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are one; it was said: it is a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, fresh, good dates.

﴿So eat and drink﴾: that is, from those dates and that water, or from the dates and their juice. She placed eating first though mention of the stream precedes the dates, because a woman in postpartum needs to eat dates more intensely than she needs to drink water. Then He said: ﴿And be cool of eye﴾. The majority read with a fatḥa on the qāf. Ibn Jarīr related that it was read with a kasra, and said: it is the dialect of Najd.

The meaning: be content of soul and cast off grief from yourself. It is derived from al-qarr and al-qurra, and both are coldness; the one who is pleased has a cool heart and still limbs. It was said: the meaning is: cool your eye by seeing the child given to you. Al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is sleep. Abū ʿAmr said: God cooled his eye, that is, made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness.

﴿And if you see any human being﴾: its original is tarʾayīna, like tasmaʿīna; the hamza was softened and the nūn dropped for the jussive, and the yā' of the pronoun for the two sākins after attaching the nūn of emphasis. A similar case without the nūn of emphasis is the saying of Ibn Duraid:
"If you see my head, whose color resembles the dawn's streak under the skirts of the darkness."

Ṭalḥa and Shayba read "tarayna" with a sukūn on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn, lightened. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is anomalous. The answer to the condition is: ﴿then say: Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾; that is, say: if any of the people asks you to speak: indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, that is, silence. It was said: the intended meaning is the legal fast, which is abstaining from things that break the fast; and the first is preferable.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 2 of 2):

It is reported in the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, silence﴾ with the two words joined together (ṣawman ṣamtan without a conjunction), and likewise it is reported from Anas. It is also reported from him that he read ﴿a fast and silence﴾ with the conjunction "wa" (ṣawman wa-ṣamtan). What the majority of the exegetes hold is that the fast here is silence, and what indicates this is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The meaning of ṣawm (fasting) in the lexical sense is broader than the two meanings.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Everyone who refrains from food, speech, or travel is a ṣā’im (one who fasts)."

The reading of Ubayy indicates that what is meant by ṣawm here is silence, because it is an explanation of ṣawm. The reading of Anas indicates that ṣawm here is other than silence, as the conjunction "wa" conveys. The meaning of ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ is that she would not speak to anyone of mankind after informing them of this report, but would only speak to the angels and commune with her Lord. It was also said that she did not inform them here by speech, but by a gesture indicating the vow.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾, that he said: "a place that the sun shaded her, so that none of them could see her."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "The Christians only took the east as a qibla because Maryam withdrew from her family to a place toward the east, so they took her birth-place as a qibla. The Jews only prostrated sideways when the mountain was lifted above them, so they began to tilt while looking at it, fearing that it would fall upon them, and so they prostrated a prostration with which Allah was pleased, and they made it a sunna."

Al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related through the route of al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, both said: "Maryam bint 'Imran went out to the side of the miḥrab because of a menstruation that had befallen her. When she became pure, behold, a man was with her, ﴿and he appeared to her as a well-formed man﴾. She was frightened and ﴿said, 'Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing'﴾. She went out with her outer garment on, and he took hold of her sleeve and blew into the side of her shirt, which was split in front, and the breath entered her chest and she became pregnant. Then her sister, the wife of Zechariah, came to visit her one night, and when she opened the door for her, she embraced her. The wife of Zechariah said: 'O Maryam, do you perceive that I am pregnant?' Maryam said: 'Do you perceive that I am pregnant?' The wife of Zechariah said: 'Indeed I found that what is in my belly prostrated to what is in your belly.' That is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. So the wife of Zechariah gave birth to Yahya. When the time for Maryam to give birth came, she went out to the side of the miḥrab, ﴿and the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree; she said, 'Would that I had died before this'﴾ (the verse). Then Jibril called to her from beneath her, 'Do not grieve.' When she gave birth to him, Satan departed and informed the Children of Israel that Maryam had given birth. When they asked her to speak, she pointed to 'Isa, and he spoke and ﴿said, 'Indeed I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture'﴾ (the verses). When he was born, no idol remained on earth except that it fell upon its face."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding Maryam that he said: "When she became pregnant, she gave birth." Ibn 'Asakir related from him that he said: "She gave birth after eight months."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada regarding His words ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ that he said: "Jibril." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of it from 'Ata' also.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it authentic), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse that he said: "The spirit of 'Isa appeared to her in the form of a human, and she conceived him." He said: "What she conceived is that the one who addressed her entered into her mouth."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿to a distant place﴾ that he said: "Remote."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ that he said: "It was a dry trunk."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him regarding His words ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "I had not been created and I was not a thing."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrima regarding ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "A discarded menstrual cloth."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Mujahid. 'Abd ibn Humayd related the like of it from Nawf al-Bakali and al-Dahhak.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from 'Ikrima regarding His words ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ that he said: "The one who called to her was Jibril."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The one who called to her from beneath her was Jibril, and 'Isa did not speak until she brought him to her people." The reports from the early generations differ as to whether this caller was Jibril or 'Isa.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: "'Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud read ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ with a fatha (naṣb). He said: 'Whoever reads it with a fatha, it is 'Isa, and whoever reads it with a kasra, it is Jibril.'"

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar related from Ibn 'Umar: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the sari (stream) about which Allah said to Maryam ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ is a river that Allah brought forth for her to drink from."

In its chain is Ayyub ibn Nahik al-Jabali, of whom Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "weak"; Abu Zur'a said: "munkar al-hadith"; Abu Fath al-Azdi said: "matruk al-hadith"; and al-Tabarani said after relating this hadith: "It is very strange (gharib)."

Al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and Ibn Mardawayh related "from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ that he said: 'the river.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who declared it authentic), al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara' regarding the verse that he said: "It is the jadwal, which is the small river." Thus it becomes clear that the mawquf (companion's) report is more authentic.

It has been reported from a group of the Successors that the sari is 'Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿fresh ripe dates﴾ that he said: "Fresh."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related regarding His words ﴿Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ that he said: "Silence."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari related from him that he read ﴿ṣawman ṣamtan﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾: this begins the account of the beginning of the creation of ʿĪsā. What is meant by "the Book" is this surah; that is: mention to the people, O Muḥammad, in this surah, the story of Mary. It is also permissible that "the Book" means the genus of the Qur'an, of which this surah is a part. Since mention does not attach to physical entities, it was necessary to posit a genitive noun to which the mention attaches, namely "the story of Mary" or "the report of Mary." ﴿When she withdrew﴾: the operator in the adverbial phrase is that posited genitive noun. It is also permissible to make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal, substitution of comprehension) for Mary, since times encompass what is in them, and the intended meaning of "Mary" is her report. In this substitution there is an indication of magnifying the matter of the time, because her wondrous story occurred in it. Al-nabdh (withdrawal) means casting away and throwing.

God, glorified is He, said: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187]. The meaning is that she withdrew and moved away. Ibn Qutayba said: she isolated herself; it was said: she went apart; the meanings are close.

They differed regarding the cause of her withdrawal. It was said: so that she might worship God, glorified is He; it was said: so that she might purify herself from her menstruation. "From her people" is connected to "withdrew." The accusative of ﴿a place eastward﴾ is as an object of the mentioned verb, that is: a place on the side of the east. Ash-sharq (with a sukun on the rāʾ) is the place where the sun rises. He specified the place as eastward because they used to venerate the direction of the east, since it is the rising place of lights; Ibn Jarīr related this meaning.

People have differed regarding Mary's prophethood. It was said: she was a prophetess merely by this sending to her and her addressing of the angel. It was said: she was not a prophetess, because the angel only spoke to her in the form of a human. The discussion of this has preceded in Āl ʿImrān.

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾: that is, she took a screen apart from her people which would conceal her from them, so that they would not see her during worship or during purification from menstruation.

Al-ḥijāb (the screen) means a covering and a barrier. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾: it is Jibrīl, peace be upon him. It was said: it is the spirit of ʿĪsā, because God, glorified is He, created the spirits before the bodies; but the first is preferable because of His saying: ﴿So he appeared to her as a man in every way perfect﴾; that is, Jibrīl appeared to her in the form of a man of perfect form, lacking none of the attributes of the children of Ādam. It is said: the reason for the angel's appearing to her as a man is that she could not bear to look at the angel in his own form. When she saw him in the form of a handsome man of complete form, who had breached the screen around her, she thought he intended her harm, so she sought refuge in God from him, and ﴿said: Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears God﴾; that is, one who guards himself against God and fears Him. It was said that "taqiyyan" is the name of a righteous man, so she sought refuge from him in amazement; and it was said that it is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time (p-886). The first is preferable. The answer to the condition is omitted, that is: then do not approach me.

﴿He said: I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾: that is, Jibrīl said to her: I am only the messenger of your Lord, by Whom you have sought refuge, and I am not one from whom what has occurred to your mind of intending evil is to be expected. ﴿To give you a pure son﴾: He attributed the gift to himself, since he was the cause of it, in that the announcement to her came from him, or because the breathing was carried out by him outwardly.

Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh, from Nāfiʿ, read "li-yahaba" (that He may give), meaning: He sent me that He may give you; the rest read with hamza. Al-zakiyy is the one pure from sins who grows in purity and chastity; it was said: the intended meaning of al-zakiyy is the prophet.

﴿She said: How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾: that is, no husband or other has approached me. ﴿And I have not been unchaste﴾: al-baghiyy is the fornicatress who seeks men. Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is baghuwiy on the pattern of faʿūl; the waw was changed to yā', then assimilated into the yā', and the ghayn was kasra for harmony. Ibn Jinnī said: it is faʿīl. The mention of her not having been unchaste, along with her saying "no man has touched me," which encompasses both lawful and unlawful, is for the purpose of emphasis, to declare her innocent from indecency. It was said: she did not find anything in God's power improbable, but she meant: how will the child be—from a husband she will marry in the future, or will God create him directly? It was said: touching is a metaphor for lawful marriage, and on this view there is no need to explain the sense of her saying "and I have not been unchaste." What we have mentioned, that it includes both, is more preferable in the usages of the people of language, and in their discourse there is much that would take long to enumerate. End.

﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾: that is, and that We may make this boy, or his creation without a father, a sign for the people by which they may infer the perfection of power. This is a reason for an omitted motivated clause, the estimate being: We created him so that We might make him (a sign); or it is conjoined to another hidden reason, connected to what is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The sentence ﴿He said: Thus said your Lord, It is easy for Me﴾ is resumptive, and the speaker is the angel; the discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding what preceded of Zakariyyā's saying.

His saying ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ is conjoined to "a sign": that is, and that We may make him a great mercy issuing from Us to the people, for the guidance and abundant good they receive; because every prophet is a mercy to his community. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾: that is, that mentioned matter was something predetermined, which God, glorified is He, had decreed, and the pen had dried over it.

So she conceived him. Here there is an implied statement, and the estimate is: she was reassured by his words, so he approached her and breathed into the collar of her garment, and the breath reached her womb, so she conceived him. It was said: the breath was in her skirt; it was said: in her mouth.

It was said: her delivery was connected to this conception without the passing of a period of gestation. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾; that is, she moved away and isolated herself to a distant place. Al-qaṣiyy is the distant. It was said: this place was behind the mountain; it was said: the farthest place in that abode; it was said: the far end of the valley. It was said: she carried him for six months; it was said: eight months; it was said: seven.

﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾: that is, they compelled her and forced her, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:
"The fear and the hope compelled him."
Shibl read "fājaʾahā" (surprised her), from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness), and this reading is related from ʿĀṣim; al-Ḥasan read without hamza; and in the codex of Ubayy it is "falammā ajāʾahā." In al-Kashshāf he said: ajāʾahā is transferred from jāʾa, except that its usage became specified after the transfer to the meaning of compulsion; and this is far-fetched. The apparent view is that each of the two verbs has its own independent meaning. Al-makhāḍ is the verbal noun of makhadat al-mar'a, tamkhud, makhḍan and makhāḍan, when her delivery drew near.

The majority read with a fatḥa on the mīm, and Ibn Kathīr read with a kasra.

Al-jidhʿ is the trunk of a dry palm tree, as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, just as a pregnant woman clings, due to the severity of labor pains, to something she finds near her. The definite article is either generic or for a known referent. ﴿She said: Would that I had died before this﴾: that is, before this time. She wished for death because she feared that evil would be imputed to her in her religion, or so that people would not fall into slander because of her.

﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾: al-nasy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is of such a kind that it is forgotten, not mentioned, and its loss is not felt, like a peg or a rope; and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:
"Will you make us as a worthless thing for the tribe of Quḍāʿa, while we are not forgotten among Maʿadd nor of little account?"

Al-Farrāʾ said: al-nasy is the rags a woman discards from her menstrual cloths; so Mary says: "a thing forgotten" (nasyan mansiyyan), that is, a discarded menstrual rag. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the nūn, and both are dialects, like al-ḥijr and al-ḥajr, and al-witr and al-watr. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī read "nisāʾan" with hamza and a kasra on the nūn. Nawf al-Bakkālī read with hamza and a fatḥa on the nūn. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "nasiyyan" with a fatḥa on the nūn and shadda on the yā' without hamza. Al-mansiyy is the abandoned one who is not mentioned and does not occur to anyone among the people.

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾: that is, Jibrīl, when he heard her words, and he was lower than her, beneath the mound; it was said: beneath the palm tree; it was said: the caller was ʿĪsā. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the mīm of "min."

His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is an explanation of the calling: that is, do not grieve, or the meaning is "that do not grieve," with the particle being the verbal (maṣdariyya) one. ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾: the majority of the exegetes said: al-sariyy is the small river, and the meaning is: your Lord has placed beneath your feet a river. It was said: it was a river from which the water had ceased; God sent water into it for Mary, and by it He revived that dry trunk on which she had leaned, until it put forth leaves and bore fruit. It was said: the intended meaning of al-sariyy here is ʿĪsā; and al-sariyy means the great one among men, and from it is their saying: "So-and-so is sariyy," that is, great; and "from a people of surāt," that is, great ones.

﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾: al-hazz is moving; it is said: he shook it and it shook; the bāʾ in "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla" is extra for emphasis. Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi." Al-jidhʿ is the lower part of the tree. Quṭrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidhʿ. The meaning of "ilayki" is toward your direction. The original of "tasāqaṭ" is tatasāqaṭ, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the sīn. Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash read "tasāqaṭ" with lightening. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafs, and al-Ḥasan read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and lightening, with a kasra on the qāf. It has been read "tatasāqaṭ" with both tāʾs made apparent. It has been read with a yā' and shadda on the sīn. It has been read "tasquṭ" and "yasquṭ."

The rest read with assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn. Whoever reads with the feminine tāʾ makes the pronoun refer to the palm tree, and whoever reads with the yā' makes the pronoun refer to the trunk. The accusative of "rutaban" in some of these readings is as a specifier, and in the others as the object of "tusāqiṭ."

Al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said: "rutaban" may be accusative by "hazzī," that is: shake toward you dates. ﴿Fresh (janiyyan)﴾ "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla," that is, on its trunk; al-Zamakhsharī weakened this. Al-janiyy is what is picked fresh; it was said: it is what is sought and suitable for picking, and it is a faʿīl in the sense of a maf‌ʿūl. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are one; it was said: it is a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, fresh, good dates.

﴿So eat and drink﴾: that is, from those dates and that water, or from the dates and their juice. She placed eating first though mention of the stream precedes the dates, because a woman in postpartum needs to eat dates more intensely than she needs to drink water. Then He said: ﴿And be cool of eye﴾. The majority read with a fatḥa on the qāf. Ibn Jarīr related that it was read with a kasra, and said: it is the dialect of Najd.

The meaning: be content of soul and cast off grief from yourself. It is derived from al-qarr and al-qurra, and both are coldness; the one who is pleased has a cool heart and still limbs. It was said: the meaning is: cool your eye by seeing the child given to you. Al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is sleep. Abū ʿAmr said: God cooled his eye, that is, made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness.

﴿And if you see any human being﴾: its original is tarʾayīna, like tasmaʿīna; the hamza was softened and the nūn dropped for the jussive, and the yā' of the pronoun for the two sākins after attaching the nūn of emphasis. A similar case without the nūn of emphasis is the saying of Ibn Duraid:
"If you see my head, whose color resembles the dawn's streak under the skirts of the darkness."

Ṭalḥa and Shayba read "tarayna" with a sukūn on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn, lightened. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is anomalous. The answer to the condition is: ﴿then say: Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾; that is, say: if any of the people asks you to speak: indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, that is, silence. It was said: the intended meaning is the legal fast, which is abstaining from things that break the fast; and the first is preferable.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 2 of 2):

It is reported in the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, silence﴾ with the two words joined together (ṣawman ṣamtan without a conjunction), and likewise it is reported from Anas. It is also reported from him that he read ﴿a fast and silence﴾ with the conjunction "wa" (ṣawman wa-ṣamtan). What the majority of the exegetes hold is that the fast here is silence, and what indicates this is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The meaning of ṣawm (fasting) in the lexical sense is broader than the two meanings.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Everyone who refrains from food, speech, or travel is a ṣā’im (one who fasts)."

The reading of Ubayy indicates that what is meant by ṣawm here is silence, because it is an explanation of ṣawm. The reading of Anas indicates that ṣawm here is other than silence, as the conjunction "wa" conveys. The meaning of ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ is that she would not speak to anyone of mankind after informing them of this report, but would only speak to the angels and commune with her Lord. It was also said that she did not inform them here by speech, but by a gesture indicating the vow.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾, that he said: "a place that the sun shaded her, so that none of them could see her."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "The Christians only took the east as a qibla because Maryam withdrew from her family to a place toward the east, so they took her birth-place as a qibla. The Jews only prostrated sideways when the mountain was lifted above them, so they began to tilt while looking at it, fearing that it would fall upon them, and so they prostrated a prostration with which Allah was pleased, and they made it a sunna."

Al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related through the route of al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, both said: "Maryam bint 'Imran went out to the side of the miḥrab because of a menstruation that had befallen her. When she became pure, behold, a man was with her, ﴿and he appeared to her as a well-formed man﴾. She was frightened and ﴿said, 'Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing'﴾. She went out with her outer garment on, and he took hold of her sleeve and blew into the side of her shirt, which was split in front, and the breath entered her chest and she became pregnant. Then her sister, the wife of Zechariah, came to visit her one night, and when she opened the door for her, she embraced her. The wife of Zechariah said: 'O Maryam, do you perceive that I am pregnant?' Maryam said: 'Do you perceive that I am pregnant?' The wife of Zechariah said: 'Indeed I found that what is in my belly prostrated to what is in your belly.' That is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. So the wife of Zechariah gave birth to Yahya. When the time for Maryam to give birth came, she went out to the side of the miḥrab, ﴿and the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree; she said, 'Would that I had died before this'﴾ (the verse). Then Jibril called to her from beneath her, 'Do not grieve.' When she gave birth to him, Satan departed and informed the Children of Israel that Maryam had given birth. When they asked her to speak, she pointed to 'Isa, and he spoke and ﴿said, 'Indeed I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Scripture'﴾ (the verses). When he was born, no idol remained on earth except that it fell upon its face."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding Maryam that he said: "When she became pregnant, she gave birth." Ibn 'Asakir related from him that he said: "She gave birth after eight months."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada regarding His words ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ that he said: "Jibril." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of it from 'Ata' also.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who declared it authentic), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b regarding the verse that he said: "The spirit of 'Isa appeared to her in the form of a human, and she conceived him." He said: "What she conceived is that the one who addressed her entered into her mouth."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿to a distant place﴾ that he said: "Remote."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His words ﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ that he said: "It was a dry trunk."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him regarding His words ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "I had not been created and I was not a thing."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrima regarding ﴿and I was a thing forgotten, forgotten﴾ that he said: "A discarded menstrual cloth."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of it from Mujahid. 'Abd ibn Humayd related the like of it from Nawf al-Bakali and al-Dahhak.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from 'Ikrima regarding His words ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ that he said: "The one who called to her was Jibril."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The one who called to her from beneath her was Jibril, and 'Isa did not speak until she brought him to her people." The reports from the early generations differ as to whether this caller was Jibril or 'Isa.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash that he said: "'Asim ibn Abi al-Nujud read ﴿then he called to her from beneath her﴾ with a fatha (naṣb). He said: 'Whoever reads it with a fatha, it is 'Isa, and whoever reads it with a kasra, it is Jibril.'"

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar related from Ibn 'Umar: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the sari (stream) about which Allah said to Maryam ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ is a river that Allah brought forth for her to drink from."

In its chain is Ayyub ibn Nahik al-Jabali, of whom Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "weak"; Abu Zur'a said: "munkar al-hadith"; Abu Fath al-Azdi said: "matruk al-hadith"; and al-Tabarani said after relating this hadith: "It is very strange (gharib)."

Al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and Ibn Mardawayh related "from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ that he said: 'the river.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim (who declared it authentic), al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Bara' regarding the verse that he said: "It is the jadwal, which is the small river." Thus it becomes clear that the mawquf (companion's) report is more authentic.

It has been reported from a group of the Successors that the sari is 'Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿fresh ripe dates﴾ that he said: "Fresh."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related regarding His words ﴿Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ that he said: "Silence."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari related from him that he read ﴿ṣawman ṣamtan﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾: this begins the account of the beginning of the creation of ʿĪsā. What is meant by "the Book" is this surah; that is: mention to the people, O Muḥammad, in this surah, the story of Mary. It is also permissible that "the Book" means the genus of the Qur'an, of which this surah is a part. Since mention does not attach to physical entities, it was necessary to posit a genitive noun to which the mention attaches, namely "the story of Mary" or "the report of Mary." ﴿When she withdrew﴾: the operator in the adverbial phrase is that posited genitive noun. It is also permissible to make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal, substitution of comprehension) for Mary, since times encompass what is in them, and the intended meaning of "Mary" is her report. In this substitution there is an indication of magnifying the matter of the time, because her wondrous story occurred in it. Al-nabdh (withdrawal) means casting away and throwing.

God, glorified is He, said: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187]. The meaning is that she withdrew and moved away. Ibn Qutayba said: she isolated herself; it was said: she went apart; the meanings are close.

They differed regarding the cause of her withdrawal. It was said: so that she might worship God, glorified is He; it was said: so that she might purify herself from her menstruation. "From her people" is connected to "withdrew." The accusative of ﴿a place eastward﴾ is as an object of the mentioned verb, that is: a place on the side of the east. Ash-sharq (with a sukun on the rāʾ) is the place where the sun rises. He specified the place as eastward because they used to venerate the direction of the east, since it is the rising place of lights; Ibn Jarīr related this meaning.

People have differed regarding Mary's prophethood. It was said: she was a prophetess merely by this sending to her and her addressing of the angel. It was said: she was not a prophetess, because the angel only spoke to her in the form of a human. The discussion of this has preceded in Āl ʿImrān.

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾: that is, she took a screen apart from her people which would conceal her from them, so that they would not see her during worship or during purification from menstruation.

Al-ḥijāb (the screen) means a covering and a barrier. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾: it is Jibrīl, peace be upon him. It was said: it is the spirit of ʿĪsā, because God, glorified is He, created the spirits before the bodies; but the first is preferable because of His saying: ﴿So he appeared to her as a man in every way perfect﴾; that is, Jibrīl appeared to her in the form of a man of perfect form, lacking none of the attributes of the children of Ādam. It is said: the reason for the angel's appearing to her as a man is that she could not bear to look at the angel in his own form. When she saw him in the form of a handsome man of complete form, who had breached the screen around her, she thought he intended her harm, so she sought refuge in God from him, and ﴿said: Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears God﴾; that is, one who guards himself against God and fears Him. It was said that "taqiyyan" is the name of a righteous man, so she sought refuge from him in amazement; and it was said that it is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time (p-886). The first is preferable. The answer to the condition is omitted, that is: then do not approach me.

﴿He said: I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾: that is, Jibrīl said to her: I am only the messenger of your Lord, by Whom you have sought refuge, and I am not one from whom what has occurred to your mind of intending evil is to be expected. ﴿To give you a pure son﴾: He attributed the gift to himself, since he was the cause of it, in that the announcement to her came from him, or because the breathing was carried out by him outwardly.

Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh, from Nāfiʿ, read "li-yahaba" (that He may give), meaning: He sent me that He may give you; the rest read with hamza. Al-zakiyy is the one pure from sins who grows in purity and chastity; it was said: the intended meaning of al-zakiyy is the prophet.

﴿She said: How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾: that is, no husband or other has approached me. ﴿And I have not been unchaste﴾: al-baghiyy is the fornicatress who seeks men. Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is baghuwiy on the pattern of faʿūl; the waw was changed to yā', then assimilated into the yā', and the ghayn was kasra for harmony. Ibn Jinnī said: it is faʿīl. The mention of her not having been unchaste, along with her saying "no man has touched me," which encompasses both lawful and unlawful, is for the purpose of emphasis, to declare her innocent from indecency. It was said: she did not find anything in God's power improbable, but she meant: how will the child be—from a husband she will marry in the future, or will God create him directly? It was said: touching is a metaphor for lawful marriage, and on this view there is no need to explain the sense of her saying "and I have not been unchaste." What we have mentioned, that it includes both, is more preferable in the usages of the people of language, and in their discourse there is much that would take long to enumerate. End.

﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾: that is, and that We may make this boy, or his creation without a father, a sign for the people by which they may infer the perfection of power. This is a reason for an omitted motivated clause, the estimate being: We created him so that We might make him (a sign); or it is conjoined to another hidden reason, connected to what is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The sentence ﴿He said: Thus said your Lord, It is easy for Me﴾ is resumptive, and the speaker is the angel; the discussion regarding it is like the discussion regarding what preceded of Zakariyyā's saying.

His saying ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾ is conjoined to "a sign": that is, and that We may make him a great mercy issuing from Us to the people, for the guidance and abundant good they receive; because every prophet is a mercy to his community. ﴿And it was a matter decreed﴾: that is, that mentioned matter was something predetermined, which God, glorified is He, had decreed, and the pen had dried over it.

So she conceived him. Here there is an implied statement, and the estimate is: she was reassured by his words, so he approached her and breathed into the collar of her garment, and the breath reached her womb, so she conceived him. It was said: the breath was in her skirt; it was said: in her mouth.

It was said: her delivery was connected to this conception without the passing of a period of gestation. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾; that is, she moved away and isolated herself to a distant place. Al-qaṣiyy is the distant. It was said: this place was behind the mountain; it was said: the farthest place in that abode; it was said: the far end of the valley. It was said: she carried him for six months; it was said: eight months; it was said: seven.

﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾: that is, they compelled her and forced her, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:
"The fear and the hope compelled him."
Shibl read "fājaʾahā" (surprised her), from al-mufājaʾa (suddenness), and this reading is related from ʿĀṣim; al-Ḥasan read without hamza; and in the codex of Ubayy it is "falammā ajāʾahā." In al-Kashshāf he said: ajāʾahā is transferred from jāʾa, except that its usage became specified after the transfer to the meaning of compulsion; and this is far-fetched. The apparent view is that each of the two verbs has its own independent meaning. Al-makhāḍ is the verbal noun of makhadat al-mar'a, tamkhud, makhḍan and makhāḍan, when her delivery drew near.

The majority read with a fatḥa on the mīm, and Ibn Kathīr read with a kasra.

Al-jidhʿ is the trunk of a dry palm tree, as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, just as a pregnant woman clings, due to the severity of labor pains, to something she finds near her. The definite article is either generic or for a known referent. ﴿She said: Would that I had died before this﴾: that is, before this time. She wished for death because she feared that evil would be imputed to her in her religion, or so that people would not fall into slander because of her.

﴿And I had been a thing forgotten﴾: al-nasy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is of such a kind that it is forgotten, not mentioned, and its loss is not felt, like a peg or a rope; and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:
"Will you make us as a worthless thing for the tribe of Quḍāʿa, while we are not forgotten among Maʿadd nor of little account?"

Al-Farrāʾ said: al-nasy is the rags a woman discards from her menstrual cloths; so Mary says: "a thing forgotten" (nasyan mansiyyan), that is, a discarded menstrual rag. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the nūn, and both are dialects, like al-ḥijr and al-ḥajr, and al-witr and al-watr. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī read "nisāʾan" with hamza and a kasra on the nūn. Nawf al-Bakkālī read with hamza and a fatḥa on the nūn. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "nasiyyan" with a fatḥa on the nūn and shadda on the yā' without hamza. Al-mansiyy is the abandoned one who is not mentioned and does not occur to anyone among the people.

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾: that is, Jibrīl, when he heard her words, and he was lower than her, beneath the mound; it was said: beneath the palm tree; it was said: the caller was ʿĪsā. It has been read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the mīm of "min."

His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is an explanation of the calling: that is, do not grieve, or the meaning is "that do not grieve," with the particle being the verbal (maṣdariyya) one. ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾: the majority of the exegetes said: al-sariyy is the small river, and the meaning is: your Lord has placed beneath your feet a river. It was said: it was a river from which the water had ceased; God sent water into it for Mary, and by it He revived that dry trunk on which she had leaned, until it put forth leaves and bore fruit. It was said: the intended meaning of al-sariyy here is ʿĪsā; and al-sariyy means the great one among men, and from it is their saying: "So-and-so is sariyy," that is, great; and "from a people of surāt," that is, great ones.

﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾: al-hazz is moving; it is said: he shook it and it shook; the bāʾ in "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla" is extra for emphasis. Al-Farrāʾ said: the Arabs say "hazzahu" and "hazza bihi." Al-jidhʿ is the lower part of the tree. Quṭrub said: every piece of wood at the base of a tree is a jidhʿ. The meaning of "ilayki" is toward your direction. The original of "tasāqaṭ" is tatasāqaṭ, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the sīn. Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash read "tasāqaṭ" with lightening. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafs, and al-Ḥasan read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ and lightening, with a kasra on the qāf. It has been read "tatasāqaṭ" with both tāʾs made apparent. It has been read with a yā' and shadda on the sīn. It has been read "tasquṭ" and "yasquṭ."

The rest read with assimilation of the tāʾ into the sīn. Whoever reads with the feminine tāʾ makes the pronoun refer to the palm tree, and whoever reads with the yā' makes the pronoun refer to the trunk. The accusative of "rutaban" in some of these readings is as a specifier, and in the others as the object of "tusāqiṭ."

Al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said: "rutaban" may be accusative by "hazzī," that is: shake toward you dates. ﴿Fresh (janiyyan)﴾ "bi-jidhʿi al-nakhla," that is, on its trunk; al-Zamakhsharī weakened this. Al-janiyy is what is picked fresh; it was said: it is what is sought and suitable for picking, and it is a faʿīl in the sense of a maf‌ʿūl. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-janiyy and al-majniyy are one; it was said: it is a faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, that is, fresh, good dates.

﴿So eat and drink﴾: that is, from those dates and that water, or from the dates and their juice. She placed eating first though mention of the stream precedes the dates, because a woman in postpartum needs to eat dates more intensely than she needs to drink water. Then He said: ﴿And be cool of eye﴾. The majority read with a fatḥa on the qāf. Ibn Jarīr related that it was read with a kasra, and said: it is the dialect of Najd.

The meaning: be content of soul and cast off grief from yourself. It is derived from al-qarr and al-qurra, and both are coldness; the one who is pleased has a cool heart and still limbs. It was said: the meaning is: cool your eye by seeing the child given to you. Al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is sleep. Abū ʿAmr said: God cooled his eye, that is, made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness.

﴿And if you see any human being﴾: its original is tarʾayīna, like tasmaʿīna; the hamza was softened and the nūn dropped for the jussive, and the yā' of the pronoun for the two sākins after attaching the nūn of emphasis. A similar case without the nūn of emphasis is the saying of Ibn Duraid:
"If you see my head, whose color resembles the dawn's streak under the skirts of the darkness."

Ṭalḥa and Shayba read "tarayna" with a sukūn on the yā' and a fatḥa on the nūn, lightened. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is anomalous. The answer to the condition is: ﴿then say: Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾; that is, say: if any of the people asks you to speak: indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, that is, silence. It was said: the intended meaning is the legal fast, which is abstaining from things that break the fast; and the first is preferable.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 2 of 2):

It is reported in the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, silence﴾ with the two words joined together (ṣawman ṣamtan without a conjunction), and likewise it is reported from Anas. It is also reported from him that he read ﴿a fast and silence﴾ with the conjunction "wa" (ṣawman wa-ṣamtan). What the majority of the exegetes hold is that the fast here is silence, and what indicates this is ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The meaning of ṣawm (fasting) in the lexical sense is broader than the two meanings.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "Everyone who refrains from food, speech, or travel is a ṣā’im (one who fasts)."
