It was also said that He described him with messengerhood because Ibrahim sent him to Jurhum.

﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾. It was said: by "his family" here is meant his community. It was said: Jurhum. It was said: his clan, as in His saying: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214]. By "prayer and zakat" here are meant the two legal acts of worship. It is also permissible that their linguistic meanings are intended. ﴿And he was with his Lord pleasing (mardiyyan)﴾. That is, content (radiyyan), pure, righteous.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: whoever says "mardiyy" has formed it from "radītu" (I was pleased). They said: the people of the Hijaz say "mardu."

﴿And mention in the Book Idris﴾. The name of Idris is Akhnukh. It was said he is the grandfather of Nuh, for Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh. On this basis, he would be the grandfather of Nuh's father. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and others. It has been said that this is an error, and that Idris is not declined (diptotic) because of being non-Arabic and a proper noun.

He was the first to write with the pen, to look into the stars and calculation, and the first to sew garments. It was said: he was the first of the children of Adam to be given prophethood.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. It was said: Allah raised him to the fourth heaven. It was said: to the sixth. It was said: to the second.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), in which it says: "Among them was Idris in the second." But this is an error in the narration of Sharik ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Namir.

The correct view is that he was in the fourth heaven, as narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said that what is meant by raising him to a high station is the noble rank of prophethood that he was given. It was said that he was raised to Paradise.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has favored among the prophets﴾. The reference is to those mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here. The relative clause is its description. "Among the prophets" is an explanation of the relative. ﴿From the descendants of Adam﴾ is a substitute for it, with the preposition repeated. It was also said that "min" in "from the descendants" of Adam is partitive. ﴿And of those We carried with Nuh﴾. That is, of the descendants of those We carried with him, who are other than Idris, for Ibrahim was of the descendants of Sam son of Nuh. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, and they are the rest, ﴿and Isra'il﴾. That is, and of the descendants of Isra'il, among whom are Musa, Harun, Yahya, and Isa. It was also said that by His saying: ﴿from the descendants of Adam﴾ He meant Idris alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of those We carried with Nuh﴾ He meant Ibrahim alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾ He meant Isma'il, Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim and Isra'il﴾ He meant Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, and Isa. ﴿And of those We guided﴾. That is, among those We guided to Islam ﴿and chose﴾ by faith. ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down in prostration and weeping﴾. This is the predicate of "those" (ulā'ika). It is also permissible that the predicate is "those whom Allah has favored." This is a resumptive sentence explaining their humility before Allah and their fear of Him.

The meaning of ﴿fell down in prostration﴾ has already been explained in Surah al-Isra'. It is said: bakā yabkī bukā'an wa bukiyyan (he wept).

Al-Khalil said: when you shorten "bukā'" (weeping) it becomes like "ḥuzn" (sorrow), meaning there is no sound with it. From it is the saying of the poet:

"My eye wept, and rightly so for its weeping, though weeping and wailing profit nothing."

"Sujjadan" (prostrating) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has made clear that the prophets, when they heard the verses of Allah, would weep and prostrate. This verse has been cited as evidence for the legislated nature of the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa).

When He praised these prophets with these attributes, to encourage others to follow them and adopt their way, He mentioned their opposites, to deter people from their way. So He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors﴾. That is, a bad posterity. The people of language said: a good posterity is called "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, and a bad posterity is called "khalf" with a sukun on the lam. We have already discussed this at the end of Surah al-A'raf. ﴿who neglected prayer﴾. Most said: the meaning of that is that they delayed it beyond its time. It was said: they wasted the time. It was said: they disbelieved in it and denied its obligation. It was said: they did not perform it in the legislated manner.

The apparent meaning is that whoever delays prayer beyond its time, or abandons one of its obligations, or one of its conditions, or one of its pillars, has neglected it. Included under neglect is whoever abandons it entirely or denies it, by primary inclusion.

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: the Jews. It was said: the Christians. It was said: a people of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who will come at the end of time. The meaning of ﴿and followed desires﴾ is that they did what their souls desired and inclined to of the forbidden things, such as drinking wine and fornication. ﴿So they will meet with ghayy﴾. Ghayy, according to the people of language, is evil, just as khayr is guidance (rashad). The meaning is that they will meet with evil, not good. It was said: ghayy is error. It was said: it is loss. It was said: it is the name of a valley in Hell. It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: they will meet the recompense of ghayy. So said al-Zajjaj. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿He will meet a penalty (athām)﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning the recompense of a penalty.

﴿Except one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾. That is, one who repents of what he committed of wasting the prayers and following desires, returns to obedience to Allah, believes in Him, and does righteous work. In this exception there is evidence that the verse is about disbelievers, not Muslims. ﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu ʿAmr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read yudkhalūna with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the khā' (they will be admitted). The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the khā' (they enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in the least﴾. That is, nothing will be reduced from their rewards, even if it is little, for Allah, glory be to Him, pays them their rewards in full.

The accusative of ﴿gardens of perpetual residence (jannāt ʿadn)﴾ is by substitution for "Paradise," a partial substitution, since the gardens of perpetual residence are a part of Paradise.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "jannātu ʿadnin" in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'). It has been read that way.

Abu Hatim said: were it not for the script, it would be "jannata ʿadnin," meaning the singular in place of the plural. This is nothing, for "Paradise" is a name for the collection of gardens, which are like types with respect to the genus.

It has also been read with the accusative "jannāt" as praise. It has been read "jannata" in the singular.

﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾. This clause is a qualifier of "jannāt ʿadn." "In the unseen" (bil-ghayb) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the gardens or of His servants. That is, while they are unseen, or while they are unseen to them. It has been read with "ʿadn" having tanwin (ṣarf) and without it (manʿ), as it is a proper noun for the meaning of ʿadn, which is residence, or a proper noun for the land of Paradise. ﴿Indeed, His promise has always been fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾. That is, what was promised is general, so the gardens enter it by primary inclusion. Al-Farra' said: He did not say ātiyan (coming), because whatever comes to you, you have come to it. Al-Zajjaj said likewise.

﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech﴾. Ill speech (laghw) is idle talk of speech that is discarded and has no benefit. It is a metaphor for their not uttering ill speech. It was said: laghw is everything in which there is no mention of Allah. ﴿Except "Peace"﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning the peace of some of them upon others, or the peace of the angels upon them.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-salam is a comprehensive name for good, because it includes safety. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will not hear what pains them, but will only hear what gives them peace. ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The commentators said: there is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are given their provision in proportion to what they know of breakfast and dinner.

﴿That is Paradise which We will give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah﴾. That is, this is the Paradise whose conditions We have described, which We give as inheritance to those who were among the people of piety, as property remains for the heir after its former owner.

Ya'qub read nūwarrithu with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the rā'. The rest read it with the light form. It was said: there is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the implied meaning is: We give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾, that he said: "The prophet is one who is spoken to and revealed to, but not sent. The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim is: 'The prophets who are not messengers are those to whom revelation is given but who are not sent to anyone. The messengers are the prophets to whom revelation is given and who are sent.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿the right side of the mount﴾, that he said: "the right side of the mountain." ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. He said: "He was saved by his truthfulness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pen." Something similar was narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "Until he heard the scratching of the pen writing on the Preserved Tablet." Al-Daylami narrated it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun﴾, that he said: Harun was older than Musa, but He only granted him prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾, that he said: Idris was a tailor. He would not make a single stitch without saying, "Glory be to Allah." When evening came, there was no one on earth with better deeds than him. An angel asked his Lord for permission, saying, "My Lord, permit me to descend to Idris." He was permitted, so he came to Idris and said, "I have come to serve you." Idris said, "How can you serve me when you are an angel and I am a human?" Then Idris said, "Is there any relationship between you and the Angel of Death?" The angel said, "He is my brother among the angels." Idris said, "Can you benefit me?" The angel said, "He cannot delay or advance anything, but I will speak to him on your behalf, so that he will be gentle with you at death." Then the angel said, "Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended to the highest heaven, where he met the Angel of Death while Idris was between the angel's wings. The angel said to him, "I have a need concerning you." He replied, "I know your need. You want to speak to me about Idris. His name has been erased from the register, and only half a blink of an eye remains of his term." Idris died between the wings of the angel.

Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Masahif and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: I asked Ka'b, and he related something similar. This is among the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) that Ka'b transmits.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Idris was raised to the sixth heaven.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When I was taken up on the Night Journey, I saw Idris in the fourth heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: Idris was raised as Isa was raised, and he did not die.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: Idris is Ilyas. Al-Suyuti graded it as fair (hasan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ to the end, that he said: These are the names of the prophets He mentioned. From the offspring of Adam: Idris and Nuh. Of those carried with Nuh: Ibrahim. From the offspring of Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. From the offspring of Isra'il: Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾, that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: They are from this Ummah. They ride upon the roads as cattle ride, not ashamed before people, and not fearing Allah in the sky.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾, that he said: Neglecting it does not mean abandoning it. A person may neglect a thing without abandoning it. Rather, neglecting it means not performing it at its time.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed desires﴾ to the end," and he said: "There will come after sixty years a succession who neglect the prayer and follow desires, ﴿so they will meet error (ghayy)﴾. Then there will come a succession who recite the Qur'an without it passing beyond their throats. The Qur'an will be recited by three: a believer, a hypocrite, and a wicked person."

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Uqba ibn Amir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Among my Ummah will be destroyed the People of the Book and the People of Milk.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the People of the Book?' He said, 'A people who learn the Book and argue with it against those who believe.' I said, 'Who are the People of Milk?' He said, 'A people who follow desires and neglect the prayers.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Aisha that she used to send charity to the people entitled to it and say: "Do not give from it to a Berber man or a Berber woman, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'They are the successors (khalf) of whom Allah said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: loss.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: Ghayy is a river or a valley in Jahannam, of pus, deep in its bottom and foul in taste, into which those who follow desires will be thrown.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said that it is a valley in Jahannam, and Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated this from him. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Even if a rock weighing ten awqiyah were thrown from the edge of Jahannam, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it would reach ghayy and athām." I said, "What are ghayy and athām?" He said: "Two rivers at the bottom of Jahannam, in which flows the pus of the people of the Fire. They are the two that Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾ and ﴿Whoever does that will meet athām﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Ghayy is a valley in Jahannam."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿They will hear therein no vain speech﴾, that he said: falsehood.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿Morning and evening﴾, that he said: They will be brought it in the Hereafter in the same measure as they were brought it in this world.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul narrated through the route of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba, who both said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What has prompted you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah mention in the Book: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾. So I said: night is part of morning and evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there. Rather, there is light and radiance, the morning returns upon the afternoon and the afternoon upon the morning. Gifts from Allah come to them at the times of the prayers they used to perform in the world, and the angels greet them.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no morning among the mornings of Paradise, and all of Paradise is mornings, except that there will be brought to the friend of Allah therein a wife from the Houris with large eyes, and the nearest of them is the one created from saffron." After narrating it, he said: Abu Muhammad said: This is a munkar (rejected) hadith.

(p-٨٩٢).

God, glory be to Him, followed the story of Ibrahim with the story of Musa, because Musa is next to him in nobility. He placed Musa before Isma'il so that Isma'il would not separate him from the mention of Ya'qub. That is, recite to them from the Qur'an the story of Musa. ﴿Indeed, he was chosen (mukhlasan)﴾. The people of Kufa read the lam with a fatha (mukhlasan, meaning "We made him chosen and purified him"). The rest read it with a kasra (mukhlisan, meaning "he made his worship and monotheism sincerely for Allah, not showing off to the servants"). ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. That is, Allah sent him to His servants, and he informed them about Allah through the laws that He had prescribed for them. This is the reason for mentioning "prophet" after "messenger," given that being a messenger entails being a prophet. It seems that by "messenger" he meant its linguistic sense, not its technical sense. And Allah knows best.

Al-Naysaburi said: "The messenger is one who has a scripture from among the prophets, and the prophet is one who reports from Allah, mighty and majestic, even if he does not have a scripture. It would have been appropriate to mention the more general before the more specific, but the requirement of the rhyme (fasila) required the reverse, as in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿by the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 70]." End of quote.

﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount﴾. That is, We spoke to him from the side of the mount. The mount (al-Tur) is a mountain between Egypt and Madyan, named Zubayr. The meaning of "right" (al-ayman) is that this side was on Musa's right, since the tree was on that side and the call came from it. It does not mean the right side of the mountain itself, for mountains have no right or left. It was also said that the meaning of "al-ayman" is "the blessed," and that the meaning of "the call" is that speech was presented to him from that side. ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. That is, We drew him close by raising his rank until We spoke to him. The word najiyy (confidant) has the meaning of "one who converses privately," like "companion" or "boon companion." So the drawing near here is a drawing near of honor and esteem. His condition is depicted as the condition of one whom a king brings near for private conversation.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He brought him near in rank, until he heard his private conversation." It was also said: "Allah, glory be to Him, lifted him up until he heard the scratching of the pen." This was narrated from some of the early generation (al-salaf).

﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy﴾. That is, out of Our blessing. It was also said: "for the sake of Our mercy." Harun is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan), and "a prophet" is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of him. This was when he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29–30].

Allah, glory be to Him, described Isma'il with truthfulness of promise, although all the prophets were like that, because he was famous for it and exceeded in it. Consider that he promised himself patience over being slaughtered and fulfilled that. He would wait for whoever had promised him something for days and nights, until it was said that he waited for one of those who had promised him for a full year.

By "Isma'il" here is meant Isma'il son of Ibrahim. No one disputed this except one whose opinion is not considered, who said: he is Isma'il son of Huzayqil, whom Allah sent to his people. They flayed the skin of his head, so Allah gave him the choice of whatever punishment he wished for them. He asked Him to pardon them and was content with His reward. The verse ﴿and he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ has been cited regarding Isma'il as evidence that a messenger does not have to be the bearer of a sharia, for the children of Ibrahim were upon his sharia. It was also said that He described him with messengerhood because Ibrahim sent him to Jurhum.

﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾. It was said: by "his family" here is meant his community. It was said: Jurhum. It was said: his clan, as in His saying: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214]. By "prayer and zakat" here are meant the two legal acts of worship. It is also permissible that their linguistic meanings are intended. ﴿And he was with his Lord pleasing (mardiyyan)﴾. That is, content (radiyyan), pure, righteous.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: whoever says "mardiyy" has formed it from "radītu" (I was pleased). They said: the people of the Hijaz say "mardu."

﴿And mention in the Book Idris﴾. The name of Idris is Akhnukh. It was said he is the grandfather of Nuh, for Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh. On this basis, he would be the grandfather of Nuh's father. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and others. It has been said that this is an error, and that Idris is not declined (diptotic) because of being non-Arabic and a proper noun.

He was the first to write with the pen, to look into the stars and calculation, and the first to sew garments. It was said: he was the first of the children of Adam to be given prophethood.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. It was said: Allah raised him to the fourth heaven. It was said: to the sixth. It was said: to the second.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), in which it says: "Among them was Idris in the second." But this is an error in the narration of Sharik ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Namir.

The correct view is that he was in the fourth heaven, as narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said that what is meant by raising him to a high station is the noble rank of prophethood that he was given. It was said that he was raised to Paradise.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has favored among the prophets﴾. The reference is to those mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here. The relative clause is its description. "Among the prophets" is an explanation of the relative. ﴿From the descendants of Adam﴾ is a substitute for it, with the preposition repeated. It was also said that "min" in "from the descendants" of Adam is partitive. ﴿And of those We carried with Nuh﴾. That is, of the descendants of those We carried with him, who are other than Idris, for Ibrahim was of the descendants of Sam son of Nuh. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, and they are the rest, ﴿and Isra'il﴾. That is, and of the descendants of Isra'il, among whom are Musa, Harun, Yahya, and Isa. It was also said that by His saying: ﴿from the descendants of Adam﴾ He meant Idris alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of those We carried with Nuh﴾ He meant Ibrahim alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾ He meant Isma'il, Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim and Isra'il﴾ He meant Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, and Isa. ﴿And of those We guided﴾. That is, among those We guided to Islam ﴿and chose﴾ by faith. ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down in prostration and weeping﴾. This is the predicate of "those" (ulā'ika). It is also permissible that the predicate is "those whom Allah has favored." This is a resumptive sentence explaining their humility before Allah and their fear of Him.

The meaning of ﴿fell down in prostration﴾ has already been explained in Surah al-Isra'. It is said: bakā yabkī bukā'an wa bukiyyan (he wept).

Al-Khalil said: when you shorten "bukā'" (weeping) it becomes like "ḥuzn" (sorrow), meaning there is no sound with it. From it is the saying of the poet:

"My eye wept, and rightly so for its weeping, though weeping and wailing profit nothing."

"Sujjadan" (prostrating) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has made clear that the prophets, when they heard the verses of Allah, would weep and prostrate. This verse has been cited as evidence for the legislated nature of the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa).

When He praised these prophets with these attributes, to encourage others to follow them and adopt their way, He mentioned their opposites, to deter people from their way. So He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors﴾. That is, a bad posterity. The people of language said: a good posterity is called "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, and a bad posterity is called "khalf" with a sukun on the lam. We have already discussed this at the end of Surah al-A'raf. ﴿who neglected prayer﴾. Most said: the meaning of that is that they delayed it beyond its time. It was said: they wasted the time. It was said: they disbelieved in it and denied its obligation. It was said: they did not perform it in the legislated manner.

The apparent meaning is that whoever delays prayer beyond its time, or abandons one of its obligations, or one of its conditions, or one of its pillars, has neglected it. Included under neglect is whoever abandons it entirely or denies it, by primary inclusion.

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: the Jews. It was said: the Christians. It was said: a people of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who will come at the end of time. The meaning of ﴿and followed desires﴾ is that they did what their souls desired and inclined to of the forbidden things, such as drinking wine and fornication. ﴿So they will meet with ghayy﴾. Ghayy, according to the people of language, is evil, just as khayr is guidance (rashad). The meaning is that they will meet with evil, not good. It was said: ghayy is error. It was said: it is loss. It was said: it is the name of a valley in Hell. It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: they will meet the recompense of ghayy. So said al-Zajjaj. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿He will meet a penalty (athām)﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning the recompense of a penalty.

﴿Except one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾. That is, one who repents of what he committed of wasting the prayers and following desires, returns to obedience to Allah, believes in Him, and does righteous work. In this exception there is evidence that the verse is about disbelievers, not Muslims. ﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu ʿAmr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read yudkhalūna with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the khā' (they will be admitted). The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the khā' (they enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in the least﴾. That is, nothing will be reduced from their rewards, even if it is little, for Allah, glory be to Him, pays them their rewards in full.

The accusative of ﴿gardens of perpetual residence (jannāt ʿadn)﴾ is by substitution for "Paradise," a partial substitution, since the gardens of perpetual residence are a part of Paradise.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "jannātu ʿadnin" in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'). It has been read that way.

Abu Hatim said: were it not for the script, it would be "jannata ʿadnin," meaning the singular in place of the plural. This is nothing, for "Paradise" is a name for the collection of gardens, which are like types with respect to the genus.

It has also been read with the accusative "jannāt" as praise. It has been read "jannata" in the singular.

﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾. This clause is a qualifier of "jannāt ʿadn." "In the unseen" (bil-ghayb) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the gardens or of His servants. That is, while they are unseen, or while they are unseen to them. It has been read with "ʿadn" having tanwin (ṣarf) and without it (manʿ), as it is a proper noun for the meaning of ʿadn, which is residence, or a proper noun for the land of Paradise. ﴿Indeed, His promise has always been fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾. That is, what was promised is general, so the gardens enter it by primary inclusion. Al-Farra' said: He did not say ātiyan (coming), because whatever comes to you, you have come to it. Al-Zajjaj said likewise.

﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech﴾. Ill speech (laghw) is idle talk of speech that is discarded and has no benefit. It is a metaphor for their not uttering ill speech. It was said: laghw is everything in which there is no mention of Allah. ﴿Except "Peace"﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning the peace of some of them upon others, or the peace of the angels upon them.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-salam is a comprehensive name for good, because it includes safety. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will not hear what pains them, but will only hear what gives them peace. ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The commentators said: there is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are given their provision in proportion to what they know of breakfast and dinner.

﴿That is Paradise which We will give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah﴾. That is, this is the Paradise whose conditions We have described, which We give as inheritance to those who were among the people of piety, as property remains for the heir after its former owner.

Ya'qub read nūwarrithu with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the rā'. The rest read it with the light form. It was said: there is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the implied meaning is: We give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾, that he said: "The prophet is one who is spoken to and revealed to, but not sent. The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim is: 'The prophets who are not messengers are those to whom revelation is given but who are not sent to anyone. The messengers are the prophets to whom revelation is given and who are sent.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿the right side of the mount﴾, that he said: "the right side of the mountain." ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. He said: "He was saved by his truthfulness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pen." Something similar was narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "Until he heard the scratching of the pen writing on the Preserved Tablet." Al-Daylami narrated it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun﴾, that he said: Harun was older than Musa, but He only granted him prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾, that he said: Idris was a tailor. He would not make a single stitch without saying, "Glory be to Allah." When evening came, there was no one on earth with better deeds than him. An angel asked his Lord for permission, saying, "My Lord, permit me to descend to Idris." He was permitted, so he came to Idris and said, "I have come to serve you." Idris said, "How can you serve me when you are an angel and I am a human?" Then Idris said, "Is there any relationship between you and the Angel of Death?" The angel said, "He is my brother among the angels." Idris said, "Can you benefit me?" The angel said, "He cannot delay or advance anything, but I will speak to him on your behalf, so that he will be gentle with you at death." Then the angel said, "Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended to the highest heaven, where he met the Angel of Death while Idris was between the angel's wings. The angel said to him, "I have a need concerning you." He replied, "I know your need. You want to speak to me about Idris. His name has been erased from the register, and only half a blink of an eye remains of his term." Idris died between the wings of the angel.

Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Masahif and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: I asked Ka'b, and he related something similar. This is among the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) that Ka'b transmits.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Idris was raised to the sixth heaven.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When I was taken up on the Night Journey, I saw Idris in the fourth heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: Idris was raised as Isa was raised, and he did not die.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: Idris is Ilyas. Al-Suyuti graded it as fair (hasan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ to the end, that he said: These are the names of the prophets He mentioned. From the offspring of Adam: Idris and Nuh. Of those carried with Nuh: Ibrahim. From the offspring of Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. From the offspring of Isra'il: Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾, that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: They are from this Ummah. They ride upon the roads as cattle ride, not ashamed before people, and not fearing Allah in the sky.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾, that he said: Neglecting it does not mean abandoning it. A person may neglect a thing without abandoning it. Rather, neglecting it means not performing it at its time.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed desires﴾ to the end," and he said: "There will come after sixty years a succession who neglect the prayer and follow desires, ﴿so they will meet error (ghayy)﴾. Then there will come a succession who recite the Qur'an without it passing beyond their throats. The Qur'an will be recited by three: a believer, a hypocrite, and a wicked person."

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Uqba ibn Amir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Among my Ummah will be destroyed the People of the Book and the People of Milk.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the People of the Book?' He said, 'A people who learn the Book and argue with it against those who believe.' I said, 'Who are the People of Milk?' He said, 'A people who follow desires and neglect the prayers.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Aisha that she used to send charity to the people entitled to it and say: "Do not give from it to a Berber man or a Berber woman, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'They are the successors (khalf) of whom Allah said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: loss.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: Ghayy is a river or a valley in Jahannam, of pus, deep in its bottom and foul in taste, into which those who follow desires will be thrown.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said that it is a valley in Jahannam, and Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated this from him. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Even if a rock weighing ten awqiyah were thrown from the edge of Jahannam, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it would reach ghayy and athām." I said, "What are ghayy and athām?" He said: "Two rivers at the bottom of Jahannam, in which flows the pus of the people of the Fire. They are the two that Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾ and ﴿Whoever does that will meet athām﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Ghayy is a valley in Jahannam."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿They will hear therein no vain speech﴾, that he said: falsehood.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿Morning and evening﴾, that he said: They will be brought it in the Hereafter in the same measure as they were brought it in this world.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul narrated through the route of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba, who both said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What has prompted you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah mention in the Book: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾. So I said: night is part of morning and evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there. Rather, there is light and radiance, the morning returns upon the afternoon and the afternoon upon the morning. Gifts from Allah come to them at the times of the prayers they used to perform in the world, and the angels greet them.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no morning among the mornings of Paradise, and all of Paradise is mornings, except that there will be brought to the friend of Allah therein a wife from the Houris with large eyes, and the nearest of them is the one created from saffron." After narrating it, he said: Abu Muhammad said: This is a munkar (rejected) hadith.

(p-٨٩٢).

God, glory be to Him, followed the story of Ibrahim with the story of Musa, because Musa is next to him in nobility. He placed Musa before Isma'il so that Isma'il would not separate him from the mention of Ya'qub. That is, recite to them from the Qur'an the story of Musa. ﴿Indeed, he was chosen (mukhlasan)﴾. The people of Kufa read the lam with a fatha (mukhlasan, meaning "We made him chosen and purified him"). The rest read it with a kasra (mukhlisan, meaning "he made his worship and monotheism sincerely for Allah, not showing off to the servants"). ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. That is, Allah sent him to His servants, and he informed them about Allah through the laws that He had prescribed for them. This is the reason for mentioning "prophet" after "messenger," given that being a messenger entails being a prophet. It seems that by "messenger" he meant its linguistic sense, not its technical sense. And Allah knows best.

Al-Naysaburi said: "The messenger is one who has a scripture from among the prophets, and the prophet is one who reports from Allah, mighty and majestic, even if he does not have a scripture. It would have been appropriate to mention the more general before the more specific, but the requirement of the rhyme (fasila) required the reverse, as in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿by the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 70]." End of quote.

﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount﴾. That is, We spoke to him from the side of the mount. The mount (al-Tur) is a mountain between Egypt and Madyan, named Zubayr. The meaning of "right" (al-ayman) is that this side was on Musa's right, since the tree was on that side and the call came from it. It does not mean the right side of the mountain itself, for mountains have no right or left. It was also said that the meaning of "al-ayman" is "the blessed," and that the meaning of "the call" is that speech was presented to him from that side. ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. That is, We drew him close by raising his rank until We spoke to him. The word najiyy (confidant) has the meaning of "one who converses privately," like "companion" or "boon companion." So the drawing near here is a drawing near of honor and esteem. His condition is depicted as the condition of one whom a king brings near for private conversation.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He brought him near in rank, until he heard his private conversation." It was also said: "Allah, glory be to Him, lifted him up until he heard the scratching of the pen." This was narrated from some of the early generation (al-salaf).

﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy﴾. That is, out of Our blessing. It was also said: "for the sake of Our mercy." Harun is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan), and "a prophet" is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of him. This was when he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29–30].

Allah, glory be to Him, described Isma'il with truthfulness of promise, although all the prophets were like that, because he was famous for it and exceeded in it. Consider that he promised himself patience over being slaughtered and fulfilled that. He would wait for whoever had promised him something for days and nights, until it was said that he waited for one of those who had promised him for a full year.

By "Isma'il" here is meant Isma'il son of Ibrahim. No one disputed this except one whose opinion is not considered, who said: he is Isma'il son of Huzayqil, whom Allah sent to his people. They flayed the skin of his head, so Allah gave him the choice of whatever punishment he wished for them. He asked Him to pardon them and was content with His reward. The verse ﴿and he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ has been cited regarding Isma'il as evidence that a messenger does not have to be the bearer of a sharia, for the children of Ibrahim were upon his sharia. It was also said that He described him with messengerhood because Ibrahim sent him to Jurhum.

﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾. It was said: by "his family" here is meant his community. It was said: Jurhum. It was said: his clan, as in His saying: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214]. By "prayer and zakat" here are meant the two legal acts of worship. It is also permissible that their linguistic meanings are intended. ﴿And he was with his Lord pleasing (mardiyyan)﴾. That is, content (radiyyan), pure, righteous.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: whoever says "mardiyy" has formed it from "radītu" (I was pleased). They said: the people of the Hijaz say "mardu."

﴿And mention in the Book Idris﴾. The name of Idris is Akhnukh. It was said he is the grandfather of Nuh, for Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh. On this basis, he would be the grandfather of Nuh's father. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and others. It has been said that this is an error, and that Idris is not declined (diptotic) because of being non-Arabic and a proper noun.

He was the first to write with the pen, to look into the stars and calculation, and the first to sew garments. It was said: he was the first of the children of Adam to be given prophethood.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. It was said: Allah raised him to the fourth heaven. It was said: to the sixth. It was said: to the second.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), in which it says: "Among them was Idris in the second." But this is an error in the narration of Sharik ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Namir.

The correct view is that he was in the fourth heaven, as narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said that what is meant by raising him to a high station is the noble rank of prophethood that he was given. It was said that he was raised to Paradise.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has favored among the prophets﴾. The reference is to those mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here. The relative clause is its description. "Among the prophets" is an explanation of the relative. ﴿From the descendants of Adam﴾ is a substitute for it, with the preposition repeated. It was also said that "min" in "from the descendants" of Adam is partitive. ﴿And of those We carried with Nuh﴾. That is, of the descendants of those We carried with him, who are other than Idris, for Ibrahim was of the descendants of Sam son of Nuh. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, and they are the rest, ﴿and Isra'il﴾. That is, and of the descendants of Isra'il, among whom are Musa, Harun, Yahya, and Isa. It was also said that by His saying: ﴿from the descendants of Adam﴾ He meant Idris alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of those We carried with Nuh﴾ He meant Ibrahim alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾ He meant Isma'il, Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim and Isra'il﴾ He meant Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, and Isa. ﴿And of those We guided﴾. That is, among those We guided to Islam ﴿and chose﴾ by faith. ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down in prostration and weeping﴾. This is the predicate of "those" (ulā'ika). It is also permissible that the predicate is "those whom Allah has favored." This is a resumptive sentence explaining their humility before Allah and their fear of Him.

The meaning of ﴿fell down in prostration﴾ has already been explained in Surah al-Isra'. It is said: bakā yabkī bukā'an wa bukiyyan (he wept).

Al-Khalil said: when you shorten "bukā'" (weeping) it becomes like "ḥuzn" (sorrow), meaning there is no sound with it. From it is the saying of the poet:

"My eye wept, and rightly so for its weeping, though weeping and wailing profit nothing."

"Sujjadan" (prostrating) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has made clear that the prophets, when they heard the verses of Allah, would weep and prostrate. This verse has been cited as evidence for the legislated nature of the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa).

When He praised these prophets with these attributes, to encourage others to follow them and adopt their way, He mentioned their opposites, to deter people from their way. So He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors﴾. That is, a bad posterity. The people of language said: a good posterity is called "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, and a bad posterity is called "khalf" with a sukun on the lam. We have already discussed this at the end of Surah al-A'raf. ﴿who neglected prayer﴾. Most said: the meaning of that is that they delayed it beyond its time. It was said: they wasted the time. It was said: they disbelieved in it and denied its obligation. It was said: they did not perform it in the legislated manner.

The apparent meaning is that whoever delays prayer beyond its time, or abandons one of its obligations, or one of its conditions, or one of its pillars, has neglected it. Included under neglect is whoever abandons it entirely or denies it, by primary inclusion.

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: the Jews. It was said: the Christians. It was said: a people of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who will come at the end of time. The meaning of ﴿and followed desires﴾ is that they did what their souls desired and inclined to of the forbidden things, such as drinking wine and fornication. ﴿So they will meet with ghayy﴾. Ghayy, according to the people of language, is evil, just as khayr is guidance (rashad). The meaning is that they will meet with evil, not good. It was said: ghayy is error. It was said: it is loss. It was said: it is the name of a valley in Hell. It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: they will meet the recompense of ghayy. So said al-Zajjaj. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿He will meet a penalty (athām)﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning the recompense of a penalty.

﴿Except one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾. That is, one who repents of what he committed of wasting the prayers and following desires, returns to obedience to Allah, believes in Him, and does righteous work. In this exception there is evidence that the verse is about disbelievers, not Muslims. ﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu ʿAmr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read yudkhalūna with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the khā' (they will be admitted). The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the khā' (they enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in the least﴾. That is, nothing will be reduced from their rewards, even if it is little, for Allah, glory be to Him, pays them their rewards in full.

The accusative of ﴿gardens of perpetual residence (jannāt ʿadn)﴾ is by substitution for "Paradise," a partial substitution, since the gardens of perpetual residence are a part of Paradise.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "jannātu ʿadnin" in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'). It has been read that way.

Abu Hatim said: were it not for the script, it would be "jannata ʿadnin," meaning the singular in place of the plural. This is nothing, for "Paradise" is a name for the collection of gardens, which are like types with respect to the genus.

It has also been read with the accusative "jannāt" as praise. It has been read "jannata" in the singular.

﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾. This clause is a qualifier of "jannāt ʿadn." "In the unseen" (bil-ghayb) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the gardens or of His servants. That is, while they are unseen, or while they are unseen to them. It has been read with "ʿadn" having tanwin (ṣarf) and without it (manʿ), as it is a proper noun for the meaning of ʿadn, which is residence, or a proper noun for the land of Paradise. ﴿Indeed, His promise has always been fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾. That is, what was promised is general, so the gardens enter it by primary inclusion. Al-Farra' said: He did not say ātiyan (coming), because whatever comes to you, you have come to it. Al-Zajjaj said likewise.

﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech﴾. Ill speech (laghw) is idle talk of speech that is discarded and has no benefit. It is a metaphor for their not uttering ill speech. It was said: laghw is everything in which there is no mention of Allah. ﴿Except "Peace"﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning the peace of some of them upon others, or the peace of the angels upon them.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-salam is a comprehensive name for good, because it includes safety. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will not hear what pains them, but will only hear what gives them peace. ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The commentators said: there is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are given their provision in proportion to what they know of breakfast and dinner.

﴿That is Paradise which We will give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah﴾. That is, this is the Paradise whose conditions We have described, which We give as inheritance to those who were among the people of piety, as property remains for the heir after its former owner.

Ya'qub read nūwarrithu with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the rā'. The rest read it with the light form. It was said: there is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the implied meaning is: We give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾, that he said: "The prophet is one who is spoken to and revealed to, but not sent. The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim is: 'The prophets who are not messengers are those to whom revelation is given but who are not sent to anyone. The messengers are the prophets to whom revelation is given and who are sent.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿the right side of the mount﴾, that he said: "the right side of the mountain." ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. He said: "He was saved by his truthfulness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pen." Something similar was narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "Until he heard the scratching of the pen writing on the Preserved Tablet." Al-Daylami narrated it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun﴾, that he said: Harun was older than Musa, but He only granted him prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾, that he said: Idris was a tailor. He would not make a single stitch without saying, "Glory be to Allah." When evening came, there was no one on earth with better deeds than him. An angel asked his Lord for permission, saying, "My Lord, permit me to descend to Idris." He was permitted, so he came to Idris and said, "I have come to serve you." Idris said, "How can you serve me when you are an angel and I am a human?" Then Idris said, "Is there any relationship between you and the Angel of Death?" The angel said, "He is my brother among the angels." Idris said, "Can you benefit me?" The angel said, "He cannot delay or advance anything, but I will speak to him on your behalf, so that he will be gentle with you at death." Then the angel said, "Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended to the highest heaven, where he met the Angel of Death while Idris was between the angel's wings. The angel said to him, "I have a need concerning you." He replied, "I know your need. You want to speak to me about Idris. His name has been erased from the register, and only half a blink of an eye remains of his term." Idris died between the wings of the angel.

Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Masahif and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: I asked Ka'b, and he related something similar. This is among the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) that Ka'b transmits.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Idris was raised to the sixth heaven.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When I was taken up on the Night Journey, I saw Idris in the fourth heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: Idris was raised as Isa was raised, and he did not die.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: Idris is Ilyas. Al-Suyuti graded it as fair (hasan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ to the end, that he said: These are the names of the prophets He mentioned. From the offspring of Adam: Idris and Nuh. Of those carried with Nuh: Ibrahim. From the offspring of Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. From the offspring of Isra'il: Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾, that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: They are from this Ummah. They ride upon the roads as cattle ride, not ashamed before people, and not fearing Allah in the sky.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾, that he said: Neglecting it does not mean abandoning it. A person may neglect a thing without abandoning it. Rather, neglecting it means not performing it at its time.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed desires﴾ to the end," and he said: "There will come after sixty years a succession who neglect the prayer and follow desires, ﴿so they will meet error (ghayy)﴾. Then there will come a succession who recite the Qur'an without it passing beyond their throats. The Qur'an will be recited by three: a believer, a hypocrite, and a wicked person."

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Uqba ibn Amir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Among my Ummah will be destroyed the People of the Book and the People of Milk.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the People of the Book?' He said, 'A people who learn the Book and argue with it against those who believe.' I said, 'Who are the People of Milk?' He said, 'A people who follow desires and neglect the prayers.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Aisha that she used to send charity to the people entitled to it and say: "Do not give from it to a Berber man or a Berber woman, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'They are the successors (khalf) of whom Allah said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: loss.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: Ghayy is a river or a valley in Jahannam, of pus, deep in its bottom and foul in taste, into which those who follow desires will be thrown.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said that it is a valley in Jahannam, and Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated this from him. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Even if a rock weighing ten awqiyah were thrown from the edge of Jahannam, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it would reach ghayy and athām." I said, "What are ghayy and athām?" He said: "Two rivers at the bottom of Jahannam, in which flows the pus of the people of the Fire. They are the two that Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾ and ﴿Whoever does that will meet athām﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Ghayy is a valley in Jahannam."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿They will hear therein no vain speech﴾, that he said: falsehood.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿Morning and evening﴾, that he said: They will be brought it in the Hereafter in the same measure as they were brought it in this world.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul narrated through the route of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba, who both said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What has prompted you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah mention in the Book: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾. So I said: night is part of morning and evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there. Rather, there is light and radiance, the morning returns upon the afternoon and the afternoon upon the morning. Gifts from Allah come to them at the times of the prayers they used to perform in the world, and the angels greet them.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no morning among the mornings of Paradise, and all of Paradise is mornings, except that there will be brought to the friend of Allah therein a wife from the Houris with large eyes, and the nearest of them is the one created from saffron." After narrating it, he said: Abu Muhammad said: This is a munkar (rejected) hadith.

(p-٨٩٢).

God, glory be to Him, followed the story of Ibrahim with the story of Musa, because Musa is next to him in nobility. He placed Musa before Isma'il so that Isma'il would not separate him from the mention of Ya'qub. That is, recite to them from the Qur'an the story of Musa. ﴿Indeed, he was chosen (mukhlasan)﴾. The people of Kufa read the lam with a fatha (mukhlasan, meaning "We made him chosen and purified him"). The rest read it with a kasra (mukhlisan, meaning "he made his worship and monotheism sincerely for Allah, not showing off to the servants"). ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. That is, Allah sent him to His servants, and he informed them about Allah through the laws that He had prescribed for them. This is the reason for mentioning "prophet" after "messenger," given that being a messenger entails being a prophet. It seems that by "messenger" he meant its linguistic sense, not its technical sense. And Allah knows best.

Al-Naysaburi said: "The messenger is one who has a scripture from among the prophets, and the prophet is one who reports from Allah, mighty and majestic, even if he does not have a scripture. It would have been appropriate to mention the more general before the more specific, but the requirement of the rhyme (fasila) required the reverse, as in His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿by the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 70]." End of quote.

﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount﴾. That is, We spoke to him from the side of the mount. The mount (al-Tur) is a mountain between Egypt and Madyan, named Zubayr. The meaning of "right" (al-ayman) is that this side was on Musa's right, since the tree was on that side and the call came from it. It does not mean the right side of the mountain itself, for mountains have no right or left. It was also said that the meaning of "al-ayman" is "the blessed," and that the meaning of "the call" is that speech was presented to him from that side. ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. That is, We drew him close by raising his rank until We spoke to him. The word najiyy (confidant) has the meaning of "one who converses privately," like "companion" or "boon companion." So the drawing near here is a drawing near of honor and esteem. His condition is depicted as the condition of one whom a king brings near for private conversation.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He brought him near in rank, until he heard his private conversation." It was also said: "Allah, glory be to Him, lifted him up until he heard the scratching of the pen." This was narrated from some of the early generation (al-salaf).

﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy﴾. That is, out of Our blessing. It was also said: "for the sake of Our mercy." Harun is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan), and "a prophet" is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of him. This was when he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun, my brother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29–30].

Allah, glory be to Him, described Isma'il with truthfulness of promise, although all the prophets were like that, because he was famous for it and exceeded in it. Consider that he promised himself patience over being slaughtered and fulfilled that. He would wait for whoever had promised him something for days and nights, until it was said that he waited for one of those who had promised him for a full year.

By "Isma'il" here is meant Isma'il son of Ibrahim. No one disputed this except one whose opinion is not considered, who said: he is Isma'il son of Huzayqil, whom Allah sent to his people. They flayed the skin of his head, so Allah gave him the choice of whatever punishment he wished for them. He asked Him to pardon them and was content with His reward. The verse ﴿and he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ has been cited regarding Isma'il as evidence that a messenger does not have to be the bearer of a sharia, for the children of Ibrahim were upon his sharia. It was also said that He described him with messengerhood because Ibrahim sent him to Jurhum.

﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾. It was said: by "his family" here is meant his community. It was said: Jurhum. It was said: his clan, as in His saying: ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 214]. By "prayer and zakat" here are meant the two legal acts of worship. It is also permissible that their linguistic meanings are intended. ﴿And he was with his Lord pleasing (mardiyyan)﴾. That is, content (radiyyan), pure, righteous.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: whoever says "mardiyy" has formed it from "radītu" (I was pleased). They said: the people of the Hijaz say "mardu."

﴿And mention in the Book Idris﴾. The name of Idris is Akhnukh. It was said he is the grandfather of Nuh, for Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh. On this basis, he would be the grandfather of Nuh's father. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and others. It has been said that this is an error, and that Idris is not declined (diptotic) because of being non-Arabic and a proper noun.

He was the first to write with the pen, to look into the stars and calculation, and the first to sew garments. It was said: he was the first of the children of Adam to be given prophethood.

There has been disagreement about the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾. It was said: Allah raised him to the fourth heaven. It was said: to the sixth. It was said: to the second.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), in which it says: "Among them was Idris in the second." But this is an error in the narration of Sharik ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Namir.

The correct view is that he was in the fourth heaven, as narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said that what is meant by raising him to a high station is the noble rank of prophethood that he was given. It was said that he was raised to Paradise.

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has favored among the prophets﴾. The reference is to those mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here. The relative clause is its description. "Among the prophets" is an explanation of the relative. ﴿From the descendants of Adam﴾ is a substitute for it, with the preposition repeated. It was also said that "min" in "from the descendants" of Adam is partitive. ﴿And of those We carried with Nuh﴾. That is, of the descendants of those We carried with him, who are other than Idris, for Ibrahim was of the descendants of Sam son of Nuh. ﴿And of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾, and they are the rest, ﴿and Isra'il﴾. That is, and of the descendants of Isra'il, among whom are Musa, Harun, Yahya, and Isa. It was also said that by His saying: ﴿from the descendants of Adam﴾ He meant Idris alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of those We carried with Nuh﴾ He meant Ibrahim alone, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim﴾ He meant Isma'il, Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and by His saying: ﴿and of the descendants of Ibrahim and Isra'il﴾ He meant Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya, and Isa. ﴿And of those We guided﴾. That is, among those We guided to Islam ﴿and chose﴾ by faith. ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down in prostration and weeping﴾. This is the predicate of "those" (ulā'ika). It is also permissible that the predicate is "those whom Allah has favored." This is a resumptive sentence explaining their humility before Allah and their fear of Him.

The meaning of ﴿fell down in prostration﴾ has already been explained in Surah al-Isra'. It is said: bakā yabkī bukā'an wa bukiyyan (he wept).

Al-Khalil said: when you shorten "bukā'" (weeping) it becomes like "ḥuzn" (sorrow), meaning there is no sound with it. From it is the saying of the poet:

"My eye wept, and rightly so for its weeping, though weeping and wailing profit nothing."

"Sujjadan" (prostrating) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has made clear that the prophets, when they heard the verses of Allah, would weep and prostrate. This verse has been cited as evidence for the legislated nature of the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa).

When He praised these prophets with these attributes, to encourage others to follow them and adopt their way, He mentioned their opposites, to deter people from their way. So He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors﴾. That is, a bad posterity. The people of language said: a good posterity is called "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam, and a bad posterity is called "khalf" with a sukun on the lam. We have already discussed this at the end of Surah al-A'raf. ﴿who neglected prayer﴾. Most said: the meaning of that is that they delayed it beyond its time. It was said: they wasted the time. It was said: they disbelieved in it and denied its obligation. It was said: they did not perform it in the legislated manner.

The apparent meaning is that whoever delays prayer beyond its time, or abandons one of its obligations, or one of its conditions, or one of its pillars, has neglected it. Included under neglect is whoever abandons it entirely or denies it, by primary inclusion.

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. It was said: the Jews. It was said: the Christians. It was said: a people of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who will come at the end of time. The meaning of ﴿and followed desires﴾ is that they did what their souls desired and inclined to of the forbidden things, such as drinking wine and fornication. ﴿So they will meet with ghayy﴾. Ghayy, according to the people of language, is evil, just as khayr is guidance (rashad). The meaning is that they will meet with evil, not good. It was said: ghayy is error. It was said: it is loss. It was said: it is the name of a valley in Hell. It was said: there is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: they will meet the recompense of ghayy. So said al-Zajjaj. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿He will meet a penalty (athām)﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], meaning the recompense of a penalty.

﴿Except one who repents and believes and does righteous work﴾. That is, one who repents of what he committed of wasting the prayers and following desires, returns to obedience to Allah, believes in Him, and does righteous work. In this exception there is evidence that the verse is about disbelievers, not Muslims. ﴿Those will enter Paradise﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu ʿAmr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr read yudkhalūna with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the khā' (they will be admitted). The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the khā' (they enter). ﴿And they will not be wronged in the least﴾. That is, nothing will be reduced from their rewards, even if it is little, for Allah, glory be to Him, pays them their rewards in full.

The accusative of ﴿gardens of perpetual residence (jannāt ʿadn)﴾ is by substitution for "Paradise," a partial substitution, since the gardens of perpetual residence are a part of Paradise.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "jannātu ʿadnin" in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'). It has been read that way.

Abu Hatim said: were it not for the script, it would be "jannata ʿadnin," meaning the singular in place of the plural. This is nothing, for "Paradise" is a name for the collection of gardens, which are like types with respect to the genus.

It has also been read with the accusative "jannāt" as praise. It has been read "jannata" in the singular.

﴿Which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen﴾. This clause is a qualifier of "jannāt ʿadn." "In the unseen" (bil-ghayb) is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the gardens or of His servants. That is, while they are unseen, or while they are unseen to them. It has been read with "ʿadn" having tanwin (ṣarf) and without it (manʿ), as it is a proper noun for the meaning of ʿadn, which is residence, or a proper noun for the land of Paradise. ﴿Indeed, His promise has always been fulfilled (ma'tiyyan)﴾. That is, what was promised is general, so the gardens enter it by primary inclusion. Al-Farra' said: He did not say ātiyan (coming), because whatever comes to you, you have come to it. Al-Zajjaj said likewise.

﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech﴾. Ill speech (laghw) is idle talk of speech that is discarded and has no benefit. It is a metaphor for their not uttering ill speech. It was said: laghw is everything in which there is no mention of Allah. ﴿Except "Peace"﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning the peace of some of them upon others, or the peace of the angels upon them.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-salam is a comprehensive name for good, because it includes safety. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will not hear what pains them, but will only hear what gives them peace. ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾. The commentators said: there is no morning or evening in Paradise, but they are given their provision in proportion to what they know of breakfast and dinner.

﴿That is Paradise which We will give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah﴾. That is, this is the Paradise whose conditions We have described, which We give as inheritance to those who were among the people of piety, as property remains for the heir after its former owner.

Ya'qub read nūwarrithu with a fatha on the waw and shadda on the rā'. The rest read it with the light form. It was said: there is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the implied meaning is: We give as inheritance to those of Our servants who were mindful of Allah.

Ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾, that he said: "The prophet is one who is spoken to and revealed to, but not sent. The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim is: 'The prophets who are not messengers are those to whom revelation is given but who are not sent to anyone. The messengers are the prophets to whom revelation is given and who are sent.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿the right side of the mount﴾, that he said: "the right side of the mountain." ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. He said: "He was saved by his truthfulness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "He brought him near until he heard the scratching of the pen." Something similar was narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: "Until he heard the scratching of the pen writing on the Preserved Tablet." Al-Daylami narrated it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun﴾, that he said: Harun was older than Musa, but He only granted him prophethood.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾, that he said: Idris was a tailor. He would not make a single stitch without saying, "Glory be to Allah." When evening came, there was no one on earth with better deeds than him. An angel asked his Lord for permission, saying, "My Lord, permit me to descend to Idris." He was permitted, so he came to Idris and said, "I have come to serve you." Idris said, "How can you serve me when you are an angel and I am a human?" Then Idris said, "Is there any relationship between you and the Angel of Death?" The angel said, "He is my brother among the angels." Idris said, "Can you benefit me?" The angel said, "He cannot delay or advance anything, but I will speak to him on your behalf, so that he will be gentle with you at death." Then the angel said, "Ride between my wings." Idris rode, and he ascended to the highest heaven, where he met the Angel of Death while Idris was between the angel's wings. The angel said to him, "I have a need concerning you." He replied, "I know your need. You want to speak to me about Idris. His name has been erased from the register, and only half a blink of an eye remains of his term." Idris died between the wings of the angel.
