Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Masahif and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: I asked Ka'b, and he related something similar. This is among the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin) that Ka'b transmits.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: Idris was raised to the sixth heaven.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When I was taken up on the Night Journey, I saw Idris in the fourth heaven."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: Idris was raised as Isa was raised, and he did not die.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: Idris is Ilyas. Al-Suyuti graded it as fair (hasan).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾ to the end, that he said: These are the names of the prophets He mentioned. From the offspring of Adam: Idris and Nuh. Of those carried with Nuh: Ibrahim. From the offspring of Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. From the offspring of Isra'il: Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾, that he said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid, regarding the verse, that he said: They are from this Ummah. They ride upon the roads as cattle ride, not ashamed before people, and not fearing Allah in the sky.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They neglected the prayer﴾, that he said: Neglecting it does not mean abandoning it. A person may neglect a thing without abandoning it. Rather, neglecting it means not performing it at its time.

Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed desires﴾ to the end," and he said: "There will come after sixty years a succession who neglect the prayer and follow desires, ﴿so they will meet error (ghayy)﴾. Then there will come a succession who recite the Qur'an without it passing beyond their throats. The Qur'an will be recited by three: a believer, a hypocrite, and a wicked person."

Ahmad and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Uqba ibn Amir: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Among my Ummah will be destroyed the People of the Book and the People of Milk.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the People of the Book?' He said, 'A people who learn the Book and argue with it against those who believe.' I said, 'Who are the People of Milk?' He said, 'A people who follow desires and neglect the prayers.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, narrated from Aisha that she used to send charity to the people entitled to it and say: "Do not give from it to a Berber man or a Berber woman, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'They are the successors (khalf) of whom Allah said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: loss.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾, that he said: Ghayy is a river or a valley in Jahannam, of pus, deep in its bottom and foul in taste, into which those who follow desires will be thrown.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said that it is a valley in Jahannam, and Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated this from him. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Even if a rock weighing ten awqiyah were thrown from the edge of Jahannam, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it would reach ghayy and athām." I said, "What are ghayy and athām?" He said: "Two rivers at the bottom of Jahannam, in which flows the pus of the people of the Fire. They are the two that Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿They will meet ghayy﴾ and ﴿Whoever does that will meet athām﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Ghayy is a valley in Jahannam."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿They will hear therein no vain speech﴾, that he said: falsehood.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿Morning and evening﴾, that he said: They will be brought it in the Hereafter in the same measure as they were brought it in this world.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul narrated through the route of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba, who both said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What has prompted you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah mention in the Book: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾. So I said: night is part of morning and evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there. Rather, there is light and radiance, the morning returns upon the afternoon and the afternoon upon the morning. Gifts from Allah come to them at the times of the prayers they used to perform in the world, and the angels greet them.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no morning among the mornings of Paradise, and all of Paradise is mornings, except that there will be brought to the friend of Allah therein a wife from the Houris with large eyes, and the nearest of them is the one created from saffron." After narrating it, he said: Abu Muhammad said: This is a munkar (rejected) hadith.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. That is, Allah the Most High said: Say, O Jibril, "And we do not descend..." This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow in receiving the descent of Jibril, so Jibril was commanded to inform him that the angels do not descend upon him except by the command of Allah.

It was said: Jibril withheld himself from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for forty days. It was said: fifteen; it was said: twelve; it was said: three days. It was also said: this is a report about the people of Paradise, who say upon entering it: "And we do not descend [into] these gardens ﴿except by the command of your Lord﴾." The first view is more preferable by the indication of what precedes it. Its meaning admits of two aspects:

The first: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, who commands us to descend."

The second: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, which commands you with what He has legislated for you and for your community." And tanazzul (descending) is descent gradually (ʿalā mahl), though it may also be applied to descent in general.

Then Jibril confirmed what he had informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of, so he said: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that﴾. That is: of directions and places, or of past and future times, and what is between them of the time or place in which we are. So we are not able to move from one direction to another, or from one time to another, except by the command and will of your Lord. It was said: the meaning is: to Him belongs what has passed of the affairs of this world, what is to come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between them, which is what lies between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). It was said: the earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth. It was said: what has passed of our lifetimes, what has changed of them, and the state in which we presently are.

According to all these statements the meaning is that Allah the Most High is the One who encompasses everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and not an atom's weight escapes His knowledge; so we do not proceed to any matter except by His permission. He said "and what is between that" and did not say "between those two" because the intended meaning is "and what is between what we have mentioned," as in His saying: ﴿neither too old nor too young; but between that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 68]. ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾: that is, He has not forgotten you, even if revelation has been delayed from you. It was said: the meaning is that He knows all things and forgets none of them. It was said: the meaning is: your Lord would never forget the sending to you at the time at which He sends His messengers.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾: that is, their Creator and the Creator of what is between them, and their Owner and the Owner of what is between them; and whoever is thus, forgetfulness is impossible for Him.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to worship Him and to be patient in it, so He said: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾. The fa' here indicates causation, because His being Lord of the worlds is a cause necessitating that He be worshipped. The verb "be steadfast" (iṣṭabir) is transitive with lām rather than ʿalā, which it takes with its usual construction, because it includes the meaning of perseverance. ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ The interrogation is for denial.

The meaning: He has no like or equal such that he would share with Him in worship, for that would entail that worship would not be sincerely devoted to Him, the Glorified. So, when the sharer is negated, Allah the Glorified deserves to be singled out for worship and for it to be made purely His. This is based on the view that what is meant by samiyy (namesake) is a partner in the named (the essence). It was also said: what is meant is a partner in the name, as is apparent from the usage of the Arabic language. Thus it was said: the meaning is that no one among the idols or others has ever been named "Allah," meaning after the addition of the alif and lām which replaced the hamzah and became obligatory. It was also said: what is meant is: do you know anyone named "al-Raḥmān" other than Him?

Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation, and Allah knows best: "Do you know of a namesake for Him?" — one who deserves to be called Creator, Powerful, and Knowing of what has been and what will be? On this basis, there is no namesake for Allah in all His names, because others, even if named with some of His names, Allah the Glorified has the true reality of that attribute. The negation of knowledge derived from the interrogation here means the negation of the known in the most eloquent and complete manner.

﴿And man says: "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ The majority read it as an interrogative; Ibn Dhakwan read "idha ma mitu" as a declarative. The "man" here refers to the disbeliever, because this interrogation is for denial, mockery, and denial of resurrection. It was said: the lām in "al-insan" is for the whole species, even though only some, namely the disbelievers, uttered this statement, since what is done by one of them may be attributed to the group. What is meant by "ukhraj" is: from the grave. The element governing the adverbial phrase is a verb indicated by "ukhraj," because what follows the lām does not govern what precedes it.

﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ The hamzah is for reproachful denial, and the waw is for conjoining the clause that follows to the clause that precedes. What is meant by "remember" here is exercising thought: that is, does this denier not reflect upon his first creation and so infer the return from the beginning? The beginning is more wondrous and more strange than the return, because the first creation is the bringing of these created things from non-existence into existence by origination and invention, and nothing preceded it that could serve as an example for it; whereas for the later creation, the first creation has preceded it, so it is like an example for it. The meaning of "before" is: before the state in which he now is. The clause ﴿and he was nothing﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, the state was that he was then not anything among things at all; so his return after he was an existing thing is easier and simpler.

The people of Makkah, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, and the people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "awa-lā yadhdhakkaru" with shaddah; its origin is "yatadhakkaru." Shaybah, Nafiʿ, ʿĀsim, and Ibn ʿĀmir read "yadhkuru" with a lighter form. In the reading of Ubayy: "awa-lā yatadhakkaru."

Then, when the Glorified and Exalted brought this argument, upon which the intelligent have agreed that among the arguments for resurrection there is no stronger argument than it, He confirmed it with an oath by His name, the Glorified, joined to His Messenger, as an honour and exaltation for him, so He said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾. The meaning of "lanahsurannahum" is: We will surely drive them to the place of gathering after bringing them out of their graves alive as they were. The waw in His saying "and the devils" is for conjunction with the object, or is in the sense of "together with."

The meaning: these deniers, Allah will gather them together with their devils who misled and led them astray. This is apparent if the lām in "al-insan" is for the specific (the known disbelieving man). As for taking it to be for the genus, then there exists within the genus someone who will be gathered with his devil.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, on their knees.﴾ "Jithiyy" is the plural of jathin, from their saying: "jathā ʿalā rukbatayhi yajthū juthūwan," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial: that is, kneeling on their knees because of the terror of the station and the awe of the reckoning; or because kneeling is the condition of the people of the station, as in His saying: ﴿And you will see every community kneeling﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. It was also said: what is meant by His saying "jithiyy" is groups, and its origin is the plural of jathwah, and a jathwah is a heap of dust or stones.

Ṭarafah said:
"I see two heaps of dust, upon them slabs, hard, of flat stone, arranged in order."

﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect﴾. The shiʿah is the group that followed a religion among the religions. Al-Zamakhshari specified it, saying: it is the party that followed (shāʿat) a misguided one among the misguided. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ [al-Anʿam: 159]. The meaning of ﴿which of them is most insolent against the Most Merciful﴾ is: whoever was most disobedient to Allah and most defiant. For He draws out from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most disobedient and most defiant of them; then, when they are gathered, He casts them into Hell. The ʿitiyy here is a verbal noun like ʿutuww, which is rebellion in disobedience. It was said: the meaning is: We will draw out from the people of every religion their leaders and chiefs in evil. The reciters agreed on reading "ayyuhum" with a ḍammah except Hārūn al-Ghāzī, who read it with a fatḥah.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding the case of "ayyuhum" there are three views. The first is the view of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: that it is marfūʿ by way of ḥikāyah (quotation). The meaning: then We will surely draw out from every sect those who are said of them: "Which of them is more..." Al-Khalil recited in this regard the poet's verse:

"I have spent a night from the girl in a place, so I have spent (the night) neither in a state of distress nor deprived."

That is: so I have spent the night in the position of one who is said of him: "he is neither distressed nor deprived."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq, meaning al-Zajjaj, preferring this view and considering it good.

The second view is that of Yunus: that "lanazaʿanna" is like verbs that are annulled and suspended (ta'līq), so this verb is, in his view, suspended from acting upon "ayy." Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others restricted suspension to verbs of doubt and the like, which are not certain to occur.

The third view is that of Sibawayh: that "ayyuhum" here is built on ḍammah, because it differs from its sisters in the elision (of the noun). Many grammarians have considered Sibawayh's statement erroneous; indeed al-Zajjaj said: it has not become clear to me that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. The grammarians have a lengthy discussion about the i'rab of "ayyuhum" in this context.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing of those who most deserve to burn therein.﴾ It is said: ṣalā yaṣlā ṣuliyyan, like maḍā al-shay' yamḍī muḍiyyan. Al-Jawhari said: it is said "ṣalaytu al-rajul nāran" when you cause him to enter the fire and make him burn in it; if you throw him in as though intending burning, you say "aṣlaytuhu" with alif, and "ṣallaytahu" and "tuṣlīhi," and from it is His saying: ﴿and he will burn in a blaze﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 12]. Whoever reads it lightly does so from their saying: "ṣaliya fulān al-nār" with kasrah, yaṣlā ṣuliyyan: he was burned. Allah the Most High said: ﴿those who most deserve to burn therein﴾. Al-ʿAjjaj said: "By God, were it not for the fire that you would burn in it..."

The meaning of the verse: those who are most insolent against the Most Merciful are those most deserving of its burning, or their burning is most deserving of the fire.

﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it.﴾ The address is to the people without a shift in grammatical person, or it is to the mentioned man, in which case it is an iltifāt (shift); that is: there is none of you, of any one, but he will come to it, that is, reach it.

People have differed about this coming (wurūd). It was said: the wurūd is entering, and it will be cool and safe upon the believers, as it was upon Ibrahim. A group said: the wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ. It was said: wurūd is not entering; it is as one says: "I came to Basra but did not enter it." Many scholars held back from definitively determining this wurūd and took it according to its apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. They said: then whoever Allah has guaranteed to keep far from it does not enter the Fire. Among what indicates that wurūd does not necessarily imply entering is His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], for what is meant is that he arrived at it, not that he entered it. From the same usage is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So when they came to the water, bluish of its pigeons, they set down the staves of the settled one who had pitched camp."

It is not hidden that the view that wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ, or wurūd upon Hell while it is extinguished, combines the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah; so this verse should be understood accordingly, since the combination is achieved by understanding wurūd as entering the Fire together with the one who enters being among the believers kept far from its punishment, or by understanding it as passing over the bridge erected over it, which is the ṣirāṭ.

﴿It was a decree decided by your Lord.﴾ That is: that their mentioned coming was a matter decreed, which Allah the Glorified had determined that it must occur without fail. The Muʿtazilah have used this verse to argue that punishment is obligatory upon Allah; but according to the Ashʿariyyah, this is likened to what is obligatory, from the aspect of the impossibility of any breach of it occurring.

﴿Then We will deliver those who were pious﴾: that is, those who guarded against what necessitates the Fire, which is disbelief in Allah and His disobedience, and abandoning what He legislated and made obligatory to act upon.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 2 of 2):

ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra read ﴿نُنْجِي﴾ (*nunjī*) with a light (*takhfīf*) pronunciation, from *anjā*. Ḥumayd, Yaʿqūb and al-Kisāʾī also read it this way. The rest read it with the emphatic (*tashdīd*) form. Ibn Abī Layla read ﴿ثَمَّ نَذَرُ﴾ with a fatḥa on the *thāʾ* of *thamma*. By "the wrongdoers" (*al-ẓālimīn*) is meant those who wronged themselves by doing what makes the Fire obligatory, or who wronged others with an injustice against their person, property or honour. *Al-Jithiyy* is the plural of *jāthin* (kneeling). The explanation and grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of *al-jithiyy* were given shortly before.

Al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibrīl: 'What prevents you from visiting us more often than you visit us?' Then this was revealed: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim added: "And that answer was for Muḥammad."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which places are most beloved to Allah, and which are most hateful to Allah?' He said: 'I do not know until I ask.' Then Jibrīl descended, and he had been delayed. He said: 'You delayed me so much that I thought my Lord was displeased with me.' He said: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "Jibrīl was delayed from the Prophet (ﷺ) for forty days, then he descended. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'You did not descend until I longed for you.' Jibrīl said to him: 'I was more longing for you, but I am commanded.' So Allah revealed to Jibrīl: 'Say to him: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾.'" This report is *mursal*, meaning its chain omits the companion who heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "The angels were delayed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibrīl came to him and said: 'What held you back from me?' He said: 'How would we come to you when you do not trim your nails, nor clean your knuckles, nor trim your moustaches, nor use the siwak?' Then he recited: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾." This too is *mursal*.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿لَهُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِينا﴾ (*to Him belongs what is before us*), that it means the matters of the Hereafter. ﴿وما خَلْفَنا﴾ (*and what is behind us*) means the matters of this world. ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ (*and what is between that*) means what is between this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ that it means what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same from Abū al-ʿĀliya.

Al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has been silent about is pardoned. So accept from Allah His pardon, for Allah was never forgetful of anything." Then he recited: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ (Maryam: 64). Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from the hadith of Jābir.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ (Maryam: 65) that he said: "Do you know of any likeness or equal for the Lord?"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from him regarding ﴿هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 65): "No one is named *al-Raḥmān* except Him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, regarding the same verse: "O Muḥammad, do you know of any child for your God?"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ويَقُولُ الإنْسانُ﴾ (*and man says*) that it refers to al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words *jithiyyan* that it means "seated," and regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "disobedience." Ibn Jarīr narrated from him regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "rebellion" (*ʿiṣiyyan*).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنَّ﴾ (*then We will surely drag out*) that it means: "We will surely drag out from the people of every religion their leaders and their heads in evil."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "We will gather the first generation with the last, until the number is complete, then We will raise them all. Then He will begin with the greatest in crime, then the next greatest." Then he recited ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam: 68) to His words *ʿitiyyan*.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَحْنُ أعْلَمُ بِالَّذِينَ هم أوْلى بِها صِلِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 70) that He says they are most deserving of remaining eternally in Hell.

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Sumayya, who said: "We differed about the *wurūd* (coming to). Some of us said: 'No believer will enter it.' Others said: 'They will all enter it.' Then (the verse) ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾. So I met Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and mentioned this to him. He said, pointing with his finger to his ears, 'May my ears be deaf if I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No one, righteous or wicked, will remain but that he will enter it. It will be cool and peaceful for the believer, just as it was for Ibrāhīm, to the extent that the Fire will cry out from its coldness." ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous, and We will leave the wrongdoers in it kneeling﴾.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Hannād, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq disputed with Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās said: '*Al-wurūd* means entering.' Nāfiʿ said: 'No.' Then Ibn ʿAbbās recited ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell; you will be coming to it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ: 98), and said: 'Did they come to it or not?' And he recited ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ (Hūd: 98). 'Did they enter it or not? As for you and me, we will surely enter it. So look, will we come out of it or not?'"

Al-Ḥākim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾ (*and there is none of you but will come to it*) that he said: "There is none of you but will enter it."

Hannād and al-Ṭabarānī narrated from him regarding the verse that *wurūdahā* means the Bridge (*al-Ṣirāṭ*).

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, al-Bayhaqī, Ibn al-Anbārī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'All people will come to the Fire, then they will leave it according to their deeds. The first of them will pass like the blink of lightning, then like the wind, then like a galloping horse, then like a rider on his mount, then like the tightening of the saddle, then like his walking.'" Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Masʿūd through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one who witnessed Badr and al-Ḥudaybiyya will enter the Fire.' Ḥafṣa said: 'Does not Allah say: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾?' She said: 'Did you not hear Him say: ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾?'"

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim who loses three children will enter the Fire, except for the fulfilment of the oath (*taḥillat al-qasam*)." Then Sufyān recited ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh*, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Muʿādh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever guards behind the Muslims in the path of Allah voluntarily, and is not taken by a ruler, will not see the Fire with his eyes except for the fulfilment of the oath, for Allah says: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾." The reports on the interpretation of this verse are very numerous.

Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿ḥatman maqḍiyyan﴾ (a decree already decided) that it is a decree from Allah. Al-Khaṭīb in *Tālī al-Talkhīṣ* narrated from ʿIkrima regarding *ḥatman maqḍiyyan* that it is an obligatory oath. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿ونَذَرُ الظّالِمِينَ فِيها جِثِيًّا﴾ that it means "remaining in it."

[p-897]

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. That is, Allah the Most High said: Say, O Jibril, "And we do not descend..." This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow in receiving the descent of Jibril, so Jibril was commanded to inform him that the angels do not descend upon him except by the command of Allah.

It was said: Jibril withheld himself from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for forty days. It was said: fifteen; it was said: twelve; it was said: three days. It was also said: this is a report about the people of Paradise, who say upon entering it: "And we do not descend [into] these gardens ﴿except by the command of your Lord﴾." The first view is more preferable by the indication of what precedes it. Its meaning admits of two aspects:

The first: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, who commands us to descend."

The second: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, which commands you with what He has legislated for you and for your community." And tanazzul (descending) is descent gradually (ʿalā mahl), though it may also be applied to descent in general.

Then Jibril confirmed what he had informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of, so he said: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that﴾. That is: of directions and places, or of past and future times, and what is between them of the time or place in which we are. So we are not able to move from one direction to another, or from one time to another, except by the command and will of your Lord. It was said: the meaning is: to Him belongs what has passed of the affairs of this world, what is to come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between them, which is what lies between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). It was said: the earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth. It was said: what has passed of our lifetimes, what has changed of them, and the state in which we presently are.

According to all these statements the meaning is that Allah the Most High is the One who encompasses everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and not an atom's weight escapes His knowledge; so we do not proceed to any matter except by His permission. He said "and what is between that" and did not say "between those two" because the intended meaning is "and what is between what we have mentioned," as in His saying: ﴿neither too old nor too young; but between that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 68]. ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾: that is, He has not forgotten you, even if revelation has been delayed from you. It was said: the meaning is that He knows all things and forgets none of them. It was said: the meaning is: your Lord would never forget the sending to you at the time at which He sends His messengers.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾: that is, their Creator and the Creator of what is between them, and their Owner and the Owner of what is between them; and whoever is thus, forgetfulness is impossible for Him.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to worship Him and to be patient in it, so He said: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾. The fa' here indicates causation, because His being Lord of the worlds is a cause necessitating that He be worshipped. The verb "be steadfast" (iṣṭabir) is transitive with lām rather than ʿalā, which it takes with its usual construction, because it includes the meaning of perseverance. ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ The interrogation is for denial.

The meaning: He has no like or equal such that he would share with Him in worship, for that would entail that worship would not be sincerely devoted to Him, the Glorified. So, when the sharer is negated, Allah the Glorified deserves to be singled out for worship and for it to be made purely His. This is based on the view that what is meant by samiyy (namesake) is a partner in the named (the essence). It was also said: what is meant is a partner in the name, as is apparent from the usage of the Arabic language. Thus it was said: the meaning is that no one among the idols or others has ever been named "Allah," meaning after the addition of the alif and lām which replaced the hamzah and became obligatory. It was also said: what is meant is: do you know anyone named "al-Raḥmān" other than Him?

Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation, and Allah knows best: "Do you know of a namesake for Him?" — one who deserves to be called Creator, Powerful, and Knowing of what has been and what will be? On this basis, there is no namesake for Allah in all His names, because others, even if named with some of His names, Allah the Glorified has the true reality of that attribute. The negation of knowledge derived from the interrogation here means the negation of the known in the most eloquent and complete manner.

﴿And man says: "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ The majority read it as an interrogative; Ibn Dhakwan read "idha ma mitu" as a declarative. The "man" here refers to the disbeliever, because this interrogation is for denial, mockery, and denial of resurrection. It was said: the lām in "al-insan" is for the whole species, even though only some, namely the disbelievers, uttered this statement, since what is done by one of them may be attributed to the group. What is meant by "ukhraj" is: from the grave. The element governing the adverbial phrase is a verb indicated by "ukhraj," because what follows the lām does not govern what precedes it.

﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ The hamzah is for reproachful denial, and the waw is for conjoining the clause that follows to the clause that precedes. What is meant by "remember" here is exercising thought: that is, does this denier not reflect upon his first creation and so infer the return from the beginning? The beginning is more wondrous and more strange than the return, because the first creation is the bringing of these created things from non-existence into existence by origination and invention, and nothing preceded it that could serve as an example for it; whereas for the later creation, the first creation has preceded it, so it is like an example for it. The meaning of "before" is: before the state in which he now is. The clause ﴿and he was nothing﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, the state was that he was then not anything among things at all; so his return after he was an existing thing is easier and simpler.

The people of Makkah, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, and the people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "awa-lā yadhdhakkaru" with shaddah; its origin is "yatadhakkaru." Shaybah, Nafiʿ, ʿĀsim, and Ibn ʿĀmir read "yadhkuru" with a lighter form. In the reading of Ubayy: "awa-lā yatadhakkaru."

Then, when the Glorified and Exalted brought this argument, upon which the intelligent have agreed that among the arguments for resurrection there is no stronger argument than it, He confirmed it with an oath by His name, the Glorified, joined to His Messenger, as an honour and exaltation for him, so He said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾. The meaning of "lanahsurannahum" is: We will surely drive them to the place of gathering after bringing them out of their graves alive as they were. The waw in His saying "and the devils" is for conjunction with the object, or is in the sense of "together with."

The meaning: these deniers, Allah will gather them together with their devils who misled and led them astray. This is apparent if the lām in "al-insan" is for the specific (the known disbelieving man). As for taking it to be for the genus, then there exists within the genus someone who will be gathered with his devil.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, on their knees.﴾ "Jithiyy" is the plural of jathin, from their saying: "jathā ʿalā rukbatayhi yajthū juthūwan," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial: that is, kneeling on their knees because of the terror of the station and the awe of the reckoning; or because kneeling is the condition of the people of the station, as in His saying: ﴿And you will see every community kneeling﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. It was also said: what is meant by His saying "jithiyy" is groups, and its origin is the plural of jathwah, and a jathwah is a heap of dust or stones.

Ṭarafah said:
"I see two heaps of dust, upon them slabs, hard, of flat stone, arranged in order."

﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect﴾. The shiʿah is the group that followed a religion among the religions. Al-Zamakhshari specified it, saying: it is the party that followed (shāʿat) a misguided one among the misguided. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ [al-Anʿam: 159]. The meaning of ﴿which of them is most insolent against the Most Merciful﴾ is: whoever was most disobedient to Allah and most defiant. For He draws out from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most disobedient and most defiant of them; then, when they are gathered, He casts them into Hell. The ʿitiyy here is a verbal noun like ʿutuww, which is rebellion in disobedience. It was said: the meaning is: We will draw out from the people of every religion their leaders and chiefs in evil. The reciters agreed on reading "ayyuhum" with a ḍammah except Hārūn al-Ghāzī, who read it with a fatḥah.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding the case of "ayyuhum" there are three views. The first is the view of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: that it is marfūʿ by way of ḥikāyah (quotation). The meaning: then We will surely draw out from every sect those who are said of them: "Which of them is more..." Al-Khalil recited in this regard the poet's verse:

"I have spent a night from the girl in a place, so I have spent (the night) neither in a state of distress nor deprived."

That is: so I have spent the night in the position of one who is said of him: "he is neither distressed nor deprived."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq, meaning al-Zajjaj, preferring this view and considering it good.

The second view is that of Yunus: that "lanazaʿanna" is like verbs that are annulled and suspended (ta'līq), so this verb is, in his view, suspended from acting upon "ayy." Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others restricted suspension to verbs of doubt and the like, which are not certain to occur.

The third view is that of Sibawayh: that "ayyuhum" here is built on ḍammah, because it differs from its sisters in the elision (of the noun). Many grammarians have considered Sibawayh's statement erroneous; indeed al-Zajjaj said: it has not become clear to me that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. The grammarians have a lengthy discussion about the i'rab of "ayyuhum" in this context.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing of those who most deserve to burn therein.﴾ It is said: ṣalā yaṣlā ṣuliyyan, like maḍā al-shay' yamḍī muḍiyyan. Al-Jawhari said: it is said "ṣalaytu al-rajul nāran" when you cause him to enter the fire and make him burn in it; if you throw him in as though intending burning, you say "aṣlaytuhu" with alif, and "ṣallaytahu" and "tuṣlīhi," and from it is His saying: ﴿and he will burn in a blaze﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 12]. Whoever reads it lightly does so from their saying: "ṣaliya fulān al-nār" with kasrah, yaṣlā ṣuliyyan: he was burned. Allah the Most High said: ﴿those who most deserve to burn therein﴾. Al-ʿAjjaj said: "By God, were it not for the fire that you would burn in it..."

The meaning of the verse: those who are most insolent against the Most Merciful are those most deserving of its burning, or their burning is most deserving of the fire.

﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it.﴾ The address is to the people without a shift in grammatical person, or it is to the mentioned man, in which case it is an iltifāt (shift); that is: there is none of you, of any one, but he will come to it, that is, reach it.

People have differed about this coming (wurūd). It was said: the wurūd is entering, and it will be cool and safe upon the believers, as it was upon Ibrahim. A group said: the wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ. It was said: wurūd is not entering; it is as one says: "I came to Basra but did not enter it." Many scholars held back from definitively determining this wurūd and took it according to its apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. They said: then whoever Allah has guaranteed to keep far from it does not enter the Fire. Among what indicates that wurūd does not necessarily imply entering is His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], for what is meant is that he arrived at it, not that he entered it. From the same usage is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So when they came to the water, bluish of its pigeons, they set down the staves of the settled one who had pitched camp."

It is not hidden that the view that wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ, or wurūd upon Hell while it is extinguished, combines the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah; so this verse should be understood accordingly, since the combination is achieved by understanding wurūd as entering the Fire together with the one who enters being among the believers kept far from its punishment, or by understanding it as passing over the bridge erected over it, which is the ṣirāṭ.

﴿It was a decree decided by your Lord.﴾ That is: that their mentioned coming was a matter decreed, which Allah the Glorified had determined that it must occur without fail. The Muʿtazilah have used this verse to argue that punishment is obligatory upon Allah; but according to the Ashʿariyyah, this is likened to what is obligatory, from the aspect of the impossibility of any breach of it occurring.

﴿Then We will deliver those who were pious﴾: that is, those who guarded against what necessitates the Fire, which is disbelief in Allah and His disobedience, and abandoning what He legislated and made obligatory to act upon.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 2 of 2):

ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra read ﴿نُنْجِي﴾ (*nunjī*) with a light (*takhfīf*) pronunciation, from *anjā*. Ḥumayd, Yaʿqūb and al-Kisāʾī also read it this way. The rest read it with the emphatic (*tashdīd*) form. Ibn Abī Layla read ﴿ثَمَّ نَذَرُ﴾ with a fatḥa on the *thāʾ* of *thamma*. By "the wrongdoers" (*al-ẓālimīn*) is meant those who wronged themselves by doing what makes the Fire obligatory, or who wronged others with an injustice against their person, property or honour. *Al-Jithiyy* is the plural of *jāthin* (kneeling). The explanation and grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of *al-jithiyy* were given shortly before.

Al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibrīl: 'What prevents you from visiting us more often than you visit us?' Then this was revealed: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim added: "And that answer was for Muḥammad."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which places are most beloved to Allah, and which are most hateful to Allah?' He said: 'I do not know until I ask.' Then Jibrīl descended, and he had been delayed. He said: 'You delayed me so much that I thought my Lord was displeased with me.' He said: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "Jibrīl was delayed from the Prophet (ﷺ) for forty days, then he descended. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'You did not descend until I longed for you.' Jibrīl said to him: 'I was more longing for you, but I am commanded.' So Allah revealed to Jibrīl: 'Say to him: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾.'" This report is *mursal*, meaning its chain omits the companion who heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "The angels were delayed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibrīl came to him and said: 'What held you back from me?' He said: 'How would we come to you when you do not trim your nails, nor clean your knuckles, nor trim your moustaches, nor use the siwak?' Then he recited: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾." This too is *mursal*.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿لَهُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِينا﴾ (*to Him belongs what is before us*), that it means the matters of the Hereafter. ﴿وما خَلْفَنا﴾ (*and what is behind us*) means the matters of this world. ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ (*and what is between that*) means what is between this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ that it means what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same from Abū al-ʿĀliya.

Al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has been silent about is pardoned. So accept from Allah His pardon, for Allah was never forgetful of anything." Then he recited: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ (Maryam: 64). Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from the hadith of Jābir.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ (Maryam: 65) that he said: "Do you know of any likeness or equal for the Lord?"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from him regarding ﴿هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 65): "No one is named *al-Raḥmān* except Him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, regarding the same verse: "O Muḥammad, do you know of any child for your God?"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ويَقُولُ الإنْسانُ﴾ (*and man says*) that it refers to al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words *jithiyyan* that it means "seated," and regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "disobedience." Ibn Jarīr narrated from him regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "rebellion" (*ʿiṣiyyan*).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنَّ﴾ (*then We will surely drag out*) that it means: "We will surely drag out from the people of every religion their leaders and their heads in evil."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "We will gather the first generation with the last, until the number is complete, then We will raise them all. Then He will begin with the greatest in crime, then the next greatest." Then he recited ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam: 68) to His words *ʿitiyyan*.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَحْنُ أعْلَمُ بِالَّذِينَ هم أوْلى بِها صِلِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 70) that He says they are most deserving of remaining eternally in Hell.

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Sumayya, who said: "We differed about the *wurūd* (coming to). Some of us said: 'No believer will enter it.' Others said: 'They will all enter it.' Then (the verse) ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾. So I met Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and mentioned this to him. He said, pointing with his finger to his ears, 'May my ears be deaf if I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No one, righteous or wicked, will remain but that he will enter it. It will be cool and peaceful for the believer, just as it was for Ibrāhīm, to the extent that the Fire will cry out from its coldness." ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous, and We will leave the wrongdoers in it kneeling﴾.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Hannād, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq disputed with Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās said: '*Al-wurūd* means entering.' Nāfiʿ said: 'No.' Then Ibn ʿAbbās recited ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell; you will be coming to it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ: 98), and said: 'Did they come to it or not?' And he recited ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ (Hūd: 98). 'Did they enter it or not? As for you and me, we will surely enter it. So look, will we come out of it or not?'"

Al-Ḥākim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾ (*and there is none of you but will come to it*) that he said: "There is none of you but will enter it."

Hannād and al-Ṭabarānī narrated from him regarding the verse that *wurūdahā* means the Bridge (*al-Ṣirāṭ*).

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, al-Bayhaqī, Ibn al-Anbārī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'All people will come to the Fire, then they will leave it according to their deeds. The first of them will pass like the blink of lightning, then like the wind, then like a galloping horse, then like a rider on his mount, then like the tightening of the saddle, then like his walking.'" Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Masʿūd through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one who witnessed Badr and al-Ḥudaybiyya will enter the Fire.' Ḥafṣa said: 'Does not Allah say: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾?' She said: 'Did you not hear Him say: ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾?'"

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim who loses three children will enter the Fire, except for the fulfilment of the oath (*taḥillat al-qasam*)." Then Sufyān recited ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh*, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Muʿādh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever guards behind the Muslims in the path of Allah voluntarily, and is not taken by a ruler, will not see the Fire with his eyes except for the fulfilment of the oath, for Allah says: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾." The reports on the interpretation of this verse are very numerous.

Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿ḥatman maqḍiyyan﴾ (a decree already decided) that it is a decree from Allah. Al-Khaṭīb in *Tālī al-Talkhīṣ* narrated from ʿIkrima regarding *ḥatman maqḍiyyan* that it is an obligatory oath. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿ونَذَرُ الظّالِمِينَ فِيها جِثِيًّا﴾ that it means "remaining in it."

[p-897]

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. That is, Allah the Most High said: Say, O Jibril, "And we do not descend..." This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow in receiving the descent of Jibril, so Jibril was commanded to inform him that the angels do not descend upon him except by the command of Allah.

It was said: Jibril withheld himself from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for forty days. It was said: fifteen; it was said: twelve; it was said: three days. It was also said: this is a report about the people of Paradise, who say upon entering it: "And we do not descend [into] these gardens ﴿except by the command of your Lord﴾." The first view is more preferable by the indication of what precedes it. Its meaning admits of two aspects:

The first: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, who commands us to descend."

The second: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, which commands you with what He has legislated for you and for your community." And tanazzul (descending) is descent gradually (ʿalā mahl), though it may also be applied to descent in general.

Then Jibril confirmed what he had informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of, so he said: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that﴾. That is: of directions and places, or of past and future times, and what is between them of the time or place in which we are. So we are not able to move from one direction to another, or from one time to another, except by the command and will of your Lord. It was said: the meaning is: to Him belongs what has passed of the affairs of this world, what is to come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between them, which is what lies between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). It was said: the earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth. It was said: what has passed of our lifetimes, what has changed of them, and the state in which we presently are.

According to all these statements the meaning is that Allah the Most High is the One who encompasses everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and not an atom's weight escapes His knowledge; so we do not proceed to any matter except by His permission. He said "and what is between that" and did not say "between those two" because the intended meaning is "and what is between what we have mentioned," as in His saying: ﴿neither too old nor too young; but between that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 68]. ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾: that is, He has not forgotten you, even if revelation has been delayed from you. It was said: the meaning is that He knows all things and forgets none of them. It was said: the meaning is: your Lord would never forget the sending to you at the time at which He sends His messengers.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾: that is, their Creator and the Creator of what is between them, and their Owner and the Owner of what is between them; and whoever is thus, forgetfulness is impossible for Him.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to worship Him and to be patient in it, so He said: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾. The fa' here indicates causation, because His being Lord of the worlds is a cause necessitating that He be worshipped. The verb "be steadfast" (iṣṭabir) is transitive with lām rather than ʿalā, which it takes with its usual construction, because it includes the meaning of perseverance. ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ The interrogation is for denial.

The meaning: He has no like or equal such that he would share with Him in worship, for that would entail that worship would not be sincerely devoted to Him, the Glorified. So, when the sharer is negated, Allah the Glorified deserves to be singled out for worship and for it to be made purely His. This is based on the view that what is meant by samiyy (namesake) is a partner in the named (the essence). It was also said: what is meant is a partner in the name, as is apparent from the usage of the Arabic language. Thus it was said: the meaning is that no one among the idols or others has ever been named "Allah," meaning after the addition of the alif and lām which replaced the hamzah and became obligatory. It was also said: what is meant is: do you know anyone named "al-Raḥmān" other than Him?

Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation, and Allah knows best: "Do you know of a namesake for Him?" — one who deserves to be called Creator, Powerful, and Knowing of what has been and what will be? On this basis, there is no namesake for Allah in all His names, because others, even if named with some of His names, Allah the Glorified has the true reality of that attribute. The negation of knowledge derived from the interrogation here means the negation of the known in the most eloquent and complete manner.

﴿And man says: "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ The majority read it as an interrogative; Ibn Dhakwan read "idha ma mitu" as a declarative. The "man" here refers to the disbeliever, because this interrogation is for denial, mockery, and denial of resurrection. It was said: the lām in "al-insan" is for the whole species, even though only some, namely the disbelievers, uttered this statement, since what is done by one of them may be attributed to the group. What is meant by "ukhraj" is: from the grave. The element governing the adverbial phrase is a verb indicated by "ukhraj," because what follows the lām does not govern what precedes it.

﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ The hamzah is for reproachful denial, and the waw is for conjoining the clause that follows to the clause that precedes. What is meant by "remember" here is exercising thought: that is, does this denier not reflect upon his first creation and so infer the return from the beginning? The beginning is more wondrous and more strange than the return, because the first creation is the bringing of these created things from non-existence into existence by origination and invention, and nothing preceded it that could serve as an example for it; whereas for the later creation, the first creation has preceded it, so it is like an example for it. The meaning of "before" is: before the state in which he now is. The clause ﴿and he was nothing﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, the state was that he was then not anything among things at all; so his return after he was an existing thing is easier and simpler.

The people of Makkah, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, and the people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "awa-lā yadhdhakkaru" with shaddah; its origin is "yatadhakkaru." Shaybah, Nafiʿ, ʿĀsim, and Ibn ʿĀmir read "yadhkuru" with a lighter form. In the reading of Ubayy: "awa-lā yatadhakkaru."

Then, when the Glorified and Exalted brought this argument, upon which the intelligent have agreed that among the arguments for resurrection there is no stronger argument than it, He confirmed it with an oath by His name, the Glorified, joined to His Messenger, as an honour and exaltation for him, so He said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾. The meaning of "lanahsurannahum" is: We will surely drive them to the place of gathering after bringing them out of their graves alive as they were. The waw in His saying "and the devils" is for conjunction with the object, or is in the sense of "together with."

The meaning: these deniers, Allah will gather them together with their devils who misled and led them astray. This is apparent if the lām in "al-insan" is for the specific (the known disbelieving man). As for taking it to be for the genus, then there exists within the genus someone who will be gathered with his devil.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell, on their knees.﴾ "Jithiyy" is the plural of jathin, from their saying: "jathā ʿalā rukbatayhi yajthū juthūwan," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial: that is, kneeling on their knees because of the terror of the station and the awe of the reckoning; or because kneeling is the condition of the people of the station, as in His saying: ﴿And you will see every community kneeling﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]. It was also said: what is meant by His saying "jithiyy" is groups, and its origin is the plural of jathwah, and a jathwah is a heap of dust or stones.

Ṭarafah said:
"I see two heaps of dust, upon them slabs, hard, of flat stone, arranged in order."

﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect﴾. The shiʿah is the group that followed a religion among the religions. Al-Zamakhshari specified it, saying: it is the party that followed (shāʿat) a misguided one among the misguided. Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ [al-Anʿam: 159]. The meaning of ﴿which of them is most insolent against the Most Merciful﴾ is: whoever was most disobedient to Allah and most defiant. For He draws out from every group of the groups of error and corruption the most disobedient and most defiant of them; then, when they are gathered, He casts them into Hell. The ʿitiyy here is a verbal noun like ʿutuww, which is rebellion in disobedience. It was said: the meaning is: We will draw out from the people of every religion their leaders and chiefs in evil. The reciters agreed on reading "ayyuhum" with a ḍammah except Hārūn al-Ghāzī, who read it with a fatḥah.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding the case of "ayyuhum" there are three views. The first is the view of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: that it is marfūʿ by way of ḥikāyah (quotation). The meaning: then We will surely draw out from every sect those who are said of them: "Which of them is more..." Al-Khalil recited in this regard the poet's verse:

"I have spent a night from the girl in a place, so I have spent (the night) neither in a state of distress nor deprived."

That is: so I have spent the night in the position of one who is said of him: "he is neither distressed nor deprived."

Al-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq, meaning al-Zajjaj, preferring this view and considering it good.

The second view is that of Yunus: that "lanazaʿanna" is like verbs that are annulled and suspended (ta'līq), so this verb is, in his view, suspended from acting upon "ayy." Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others restricted suspension to verbs of doubt and the like, which are not certain to occur.

The third view is that of Sibawayh: that "ayyuhum" here is built on ḍammah, because it differs from its sisters in the elision (of the noun). Many grammarians have considered Sibawayh's statement erroneous; indeed al-Zajjaj said: it has not become clear to me that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them. The grammarians have a lengthy discussion about the i'rab of "ayyuhum" in this context.

﴿Then indeed We are most knowing of those who most deserve to burn therein.﴾ It is said: ṣalā yaṣlā ṣuliyyan, like maḍā al-shay' yamḍī muḍiyyan. Al-Jawhari said: it is said "ṣalaytu al-rajul nāran" when you cause him to enter the fire and make him burn in it; if you throw him in as though intending burning, you say "aṣlaytuhu" with alif, and "ṣallaytahu" and "tuṣlīhi," and from it is His saying: ﴿and he will burn in a blaze﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 12]. Whoever reads it lightly does so from their saying: "ṣaliya fulān al-nār" with kasrah, yaṣlā ṣuliyyan: he was burned. Allah the Most High said: ﴿those who most deserve to burn therein﴾. Al-ʿAjjaj said: "By God, were it not for the fire that you would burn in it..."

The meaning of the verse: those who are most insolent against the Most Merciful are those most deserving of its burning, or their burning is most deserving of the fire.

﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it.﴾ The address is to the people without a shift in grammatical person, or it is to the mentioned man, in which case it is an iltifāt (shift); that is: there is none of you, of any one, but he will come to it, that is, reach it.

People have differed about this coming (wurūd). It was said: the wurūd is entering, and it will be cool and safe upon the believers, as it was upon Ibrahim. A group said: the wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ. It was said: wurūd is not entering; it is as one says: "I came to Basra but did not enter it." Many scholars held back from definitively determining this wurūd and took it according to its apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 101]. They said: then whoever Allah has guaranteed to keep far from it does not enter the Fire. Among what indicates that wurūd does not necessarily imply entering is His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], for what is meant is that he arrived at it, not that he entered it. From the same usage is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So when they came to the water, bluish of its pigeons, they set down the staves of the settled one who had pitched camp."

It is not hidden that the view that wurūd is passing over the ṣirāṭ, or wurūd upon Hell while it is extinguished, combines the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah; so this verse should be understood accordingly, since the combination is achieved by understanding wurūd as entering the Fire together with the one who enters being among the believers kept far from its punishment, or by understanding it as passing over the bridge erected over it, which is the ṣirāṭ.

﴿It was a decree decided by your Lord.﴾ That is: that their mentioned coming was a matter decreed, which Allah the Glorified had determined that it must occur without fail. The Muʿtazilah have used this verse to argue that punishment is obligatory upon Allah; but according to the Ashʿariyyah, this is likened to what is obligatory, from the aspect of the impossibility of any breach of it occurring.

﴿Then We will deliver those who were pious﴾: that is, those who guarded against what necessitates the Fire, which is disbelief in Allah and His disobedience, and abandoning what He legislated and made obligatory to act upon.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 2 of 2):

ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra read ﴿نُنْجِي﴾ (*nunjī*) with a light (*takhfīf*) pronunciation, from *anjā*. Ḥumayd, Yaʿqūb and al-Kisāʾī also read it this way. The rest read it with the emphatic (*tashdīd*) form. Ibn Abī Layla read ﴿ثَمَّ نَذَرُ﴾ with a fatḥa on the *thāʾ* of *thamma*. By "the wrongdoers" (*al-ẓālimīn*) is meant those who wronged themselves by doing what makes the Fire obligatory, or who wronged others with an injustice against their person, property or honour. *Al-Jithiyy* is the plural of *jāthin* (kneeling). The explanation and grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of *al-jithiyy* were given shortly before.

Al-Bukhārī and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibrīl: 'What prevents you from visiting us more often than you visit us?' Then this was revealed: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim added: "And that answer was for Muḥammad."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which places are most beloved to Allah, and which are most hateful to Allah?' He said: 'I do not know until I ask.' Then Jibrīl descended, and he had been delayed. He said: 'You delayed me so much that I thought my Lord was displeased with me.' He said: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from ʿIkrima, who said: "Jibrīl was delayed from the Prophet (ﷺ) for forty days, then he descended. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'You did not descend until I longed for you.' Jibrīl said to him: 'I was more longing for you, but I am commanded.' So Allah revealed to Jibrīl: 'Say to him: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾.'" This report is *mursal*, meaning its chain omits the companion who heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "The angels were delayed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibrīl came to him and said: 'What held you back from me?' He said: 'How would we come to you when you do not trim your nails, nor clean your knuckles, nor trim your moustaches, nor use the siwak?' Then he recited: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾." This too is *mursal*.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿لَهُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِينا﴾ (*to Him belongs what is before us*), that it means the matters of the Hereafter. ﴿وما خَلْفَنا﴾ (*and what is behind us*) means the matters of this world. ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ (*and what is between that*) means what is between this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿وما بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ that it means what is between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the same from Abū al-ʿĀliya.

Al-Bazzār, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has been silent about is pardoned. So accept from Allah His pardon, for Allah was never forgetful of anything." Then he recited: ﴿And your Lord was not forgetful﴾ (Maryam: 64). Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from the hadith of Jābir.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ (Maryam: 65) that he said: "Do you know of any likeness or equal for the Lord?"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated from him regarding ﴿هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُ سَمِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 65): "No one is named *al-Raḥmān* except Him."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, regarding the same verse: "O Muḥammad, do you know of any child for your God?"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ويَقُولُ الإنْسانُ﴾ (*and man says*) that it refers to al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words *jithiyyan* that it means "seated," and regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "disobedience." Ibn Jarīr narrated from him regarding *ʿitiyyan* that it means "rebellion" (*ʿiṣiyyan*).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatāda regarding ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَنْزِعَنَّ﴾ (*then We will surely drag out*) that it means: "We will surely drag out from the people of every religion their leaders and their heads in evil."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "We will gather the first generation with the last, until the number is complete, then We will raise them all. Then He will begin with the greatest in crime, then the next greatest." Then he recited ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam: 68) to His words *ʿitiyyan*.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words ﴿ثُمَّ لَنَحْنُ أعْلَمُ بِالَّذِينَ هم أوْلى بِها صِلِيًّا﴾ (Maryam: 70) that He says they are most deserving of remaining eternally in Hell.

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Sumayya, who said: "We differed about the *wurūd* (coming to). Some of us said: 'No believer will enter it.' Others said: 'They will all enter it.' Then (the verse) ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾. So I met Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and mentioned this to him. He said, pointing with his finger to his ears, 'May my ears be deaf if I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No one, righteous or wicked, will remain but that he will enter it. It will be cool and peaceful for the believer, just as it was for Ibrāhīm, to the extent that the Fire will cry out from its coldness." ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous, and We will leave the wrongdoers in it kneeling﴾.'"

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Hannād, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq disputed with Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās said: '*Al-wurūd* means entering.' Nāfiʿ said: 'No.' Then Ibn ʿAbbās recited ﴿Indeed you, and what you worship besides Allah, are fuel for Hell; you will be coming to it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ: 98), and said: 'Did they come to it or not?' And he recited ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ (Hūd: 98). 'Did they enter it or not? As for you and me, we will surely enter it. So look, will we come out of it or not?'"

Al-Ḥākim narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾ (*and there is none of you but will come to it*) that he said: "There is none of you but will enter it."

Hannād and al-Ṭabarānī narrated from him regarding the verse that *wurūdahā* means the Bridge (*al-Ṣirāṭ*).

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who graded it authentic, al-Bayhaqī, Ibn al-Anbārī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Masʿūd regarding His words ﴿وإنْ مِنكم إلّا وارِدُها﴾: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'All people will come to the Fire, then they will leave it according to their deeds. The first of them will pass like the blink of lightning, then like the wind, then like a galloping horse, then like a rider on his mount, then like the tightening of the saddle, then like his walking.'" Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Masʿūd through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No one who witnessed Badr and al-Ḥudaybiyya will enter the Fire.' Ḥafṣa said: 'Does not Allah say: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾?' She said: 'Did you not hear Him say: ﴿Then We will save those who were righteous﴾?'"

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim who loses three children will enter the Fire, except for the fulfilment of the oath (*taḥillat al-qasam*)." Then Sufyān recited ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh*, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Muʿādh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever guards behind the Muslims in the path of Allah voluntarily, and is not taken by a ruler, will not see the Fire with his eyes except for the fulfilment of the oath, for Allah says: ﴿and there is none of you but will come to it﴾." The reports on the interpretation of this verse are very numerous.

Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿ḥatman maqḍiyyan﴾ (a decree already decided) that it is a decree from Allah. Al-Khaṭīb in *Tālī al-Talkhīṣ* narrated from ʿIkrima regarding *ḥatman maqḍiyyan* that it is an obligatory oath. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿ونَذَرُ الظّالِمِينَ فِيها جِثِيًّا﴾ that it means "remaining in it."

[p-897]

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 64–72 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾. That is, Allah the Most High said: Say, O Jibril, "And we do not descend..." This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow in receiving the descent of Jibril, so Jibril was commanded to inform him that the angels do not descend upon him except by the command of Allah.

It was said: Jibril withheld himself from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for forty days. It was said: fifteen; it was said: twelve; it was said: three days. It was also said: this is a report about the people of Paradise, who say upon entering it: "And we do not descend [into] these gardens ﴿except by the command of your Lord﴾." The first view is more preferable by the indication of what precedes it. Its meaning admits of two aspects:

The first: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, who commands us to descend."

The second: "And we do not descend to you except by the command of your Lord, which commands you with what He has legislated for you and for your community." And tanazzul (descending) is descent gradually (ʿalā mahl), though it may also be applied to descent in general.

Then Jibril confirmed what he had informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of, so he said: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that﴾. That is: of directions and places, or of past and future times, and what is between them of the time or place in which we are. So we are not able to move from one direction to another, or from one time to another, except by the command and will of your Lord. It was said: the meaning is: to Him belongs what has passed of the affairs of this world, what is to come of the affairs of the Hereafter, and what is between them, which is what lies between the two blasts (of the Trumpet). It was said: the earth that is before us when we descend, the sky that is behind us, and what is between the sky and the earth. It was said: what has passed of our lifetimes, what has changed of them, and the state in which we presently are.

According to all these statements the meaning is that Allah the Most High is the One who encompasses everything; nothing is hidden from Him, and not an atom's weight escapes His knowledge; so we do not proceed to any matter except by His permission. He said "and what is between that" and did not say "between those two" because the intended meaning is "and what is between what we have mentioned," as in His saying: ﴿neither too old nor too young; but between that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 68]. ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾: that is, He has not forgotten you, even if revelation has been delayed from you. It was said: the meaning is that He knows all things and forgets none of them. It was said: the meaning is: your Lord would never forget the sending to you at the time at which He sends His messengers.

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾: that is, their Creator and the Creator of what is between them, and their Owner and the Owner of what is between them; and whoever is thus, forgetfulness is impossible for Him.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to worship Him and to be patient in it, so He said: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾. The fa' here indicates causation, because His being Lord of the worlds is a cause necessitating that He be worshipped. The verb "be steadfast" (iṣṭabir) is transitive with lām rather than ʿalā, which it takes with its usual construction, because it includes the meaning of perseverance. ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ The interrogation is for denial.
