Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established the matter of the Gathering and answered the doubt of those who denied it, He wished to describe the condition of the accountable at that time, so He said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The time-clause is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, the Day of Gathering. It was also said: it is governed by the verb that follows it. The meaning of "gathering them to the Most Merciful" is gathering them to His Garden and the abode of His honor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ (al-Saffat 37:99). The word wafd is the plural of wafid, as rakb is the plural of rakib and sahb is the plural of sahib. It is said: wafada yafidu wafdan when he went out to a king or to a grave matter; so said al-Jawhari.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾: sawq is urging to move, and wird means thirsty, as said al-Akhfash and others. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: they are those walking on foot. Al-Azhari said: they are those walking on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water. It was also said: wirdan means "for the watering," as when you say "I came to you out of honor," meaning "for honor." It was also said: "individually." It was said: there is no contradiction among these sayings, for they are driven on foot, thirsty and individually. The root of wird is the group that comes to water of birds, camels, people or otherwise, and wird is also the water that is approached.

The clause ﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾ is a new clause explaining some of what will happen on that Day. The pronoun in "they will have" refers to both groups. It was said: to the God-fearing only; and it was said: to the criminals only. The first is preferred. The meaning of "not having power of intercession" is that they will not be able to intercede for others. It was said: no one else will be able to intercede for them. The first is preferred.

﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. This exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation: that is, neither of the two mentioned groups has power of intercession except one who has prepared himself for it by that which makes him among those who intercede for others, by being a believer and God-fearing. This is the meaning of "taking a covenant with Allah." It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is that Allah commanded him to do so, as they say: "The commander made a covenant with so-and-so" when he ordered him to do it. It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was said: other than that.

According to the connected reading of this exception, the case of (man) in "one who has taken" is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original case of the exception. As for the second interpretation, the exception is disconnected (munqati') because the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession, ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and these are the Muslims. It was said: it is connected also according to this interpretation, and the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession except one of them who was a Muslim.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wuldan﴾ with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read in the four places mentioned in this surah with a fatha on the waw and the lam. We have already mentioned the difference between the two readings. The sentence is a new clause explaining the saying of the Jews and Christians, and of whoever among the Arabs claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

In His words: ﴿Indeed, you have brought a monstrous thing﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the second person, and in it is a rejection of this hideous statement. Idd, as al-Jawhari said, is a calamity and a terrible matter, and likewise idda. The plural of idda is idad. It is said: the calamity afflicted so-and-so (addathu), it afflicts him (ya'udduhu) with ada'an, with a fatha.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿addan﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. The majority read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿'addan﴾ like madd. It is derived from heaviness; it is said: the load burdened him (addahu al-himlu, ya'uddu-hu) when it made him heavy.

Al-Wahidi said: ﴿You have brought a monstrous thing﴾, meaning a great thing according to all. The meaning of the verse is: You have said a great saying. It was said: idd means wonder, and idda means severity, and the meanings are close, and the root revolves around severity and heaviness.

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿yakādu﴾ with the yā' (third person). The rest read it with the tā' (second person). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with the tā'. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the yā', from infitar. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ (al-Infitar 82:1) and His saying: ﴿The sky will be split by it﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:18). Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasadda'na﴾. Infitar and tafattur mean splitting apart.

﴿And the earth splits open﴾: that is, and it is almost that the earth splits open. The verb is repeated for emphasis, because "they are torn apart" (yatafattarna) and "splits open" (tashuqqu) have the same meaning.

﴿And the mountains fall down in ruin﴾: that is, they fall and collapse. The word hadda is in the accusative either as an emphatic verbal noun, because falling (khurur) is included in its meaning, or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, meaning: "and they will be utterly ruined" (wa-tanhaddu hadda), or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning: "ruined" (mahdudatan), or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "because they will be ruined." Al-Harawi said: It is said: the matter broke me (haddani al-amru) and broke my support (hadda rukni), meaning it broke me and reached me. Al-Jawhari said: hadda al-bina' yahuddu-hu hadda means he broke it and crushed it; the calamity weakened its support (hadda-tu al-musibatu awhanat rukna-hu); and al-jabal (the mountain) inhadda, meaning it broke. Al-hadda is the sound of the fall of a wall, as Ibn al-A'rabi said.

The phrase ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the genitive position as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative position, with the meaning of li-anna (because). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by an implied preposition. It was also said: it is in the nominative position as the subject of hadda. Ad-du'a' (calling) in the sense of naming: that is, they named a son for the Most Merciful; or in the sense of attribution: that is, they attributed a son to Him.

﴿And it is not proper for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾: that is, it is not fitting for Him and does not befit Him, because it is impossible for Him, since a son implies kinship of kind and temporal origin. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "that they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son," while the situation is that it does not befit Him, glory be to Him, to have that.

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: that is, there is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging servitude, humbly and submissively, as He said: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾ (al-Naml 27:87), that is, abased. The meaning is: all creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him? It was read ﴿ātin﴾ according to the original form.

﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾: that is, He has restricted them and known their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾: that is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, without a helper and without wealth with him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:88).

[End of part 1]

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th*, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and they will become adversaries to them﴾ (ﷺ, Q 19:82), said: "Helpers." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him that ﴿ḍiddan﴾ (ضِدًّا) means "grief." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ (Q 19:83), that it means "leading them astray with misguidance." Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ that it means "inciting the polytheists against Muhammad and his companions." 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding the verse that it means "urging them, with a sharp push, toward the disobedience of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ (وفدًا, "as a delegation," Q 19:85) that it means "riders." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ that it means "upon camels."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: those who are eager and those who are fearful; two on one camel, three on one camel, four on one camel, and ten on one camel. And the Fire will gather their remainder; it will rest where they rest and it will spend the night where they spend the night." The hadiths on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wirdan﴾ (وِرْدًا, Q 19:86) that it means "thirsty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ (Q 19:87) that it means: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah, and disavowing power and might, and hoping only in Allah." Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding the verse that it means: "Whoever dies without associating anything with Allah enters Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ and said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up. None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to my own deeds, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant for me with You that You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever brings joy to a believer has pleased me, and whoever pleases me has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, and whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, the Fire will not touch him. Indeed Allah does not break the promise."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever comes to us on the Day of Resurrection with the five prayers, having guarded their ablution, their times, their bowing and their prostration, without diminishing any of them, will come having a covenant with Allah that He will not punish him. And whoever comes having fallen short in any of them has no covenant with Allah; if He wills He will have mercy on him, and if He wills He will punish him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿you have certainly brought something monstrous﴾ (Q 19:89) that it means "a grave statement." And regarding His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ (Q 19:90), he said: "Because of shirk the heavens, the earth, the mountains, and all creatures have been emptied of it, except for the two weights (jinn and humankind); and they were almost ceasing to exist from it because of the greatness of Allah, glory be to Him. Just as the good deeds of a polytheist do not benefit him along with shirk, so likewise he hopes that Allah will forgive the sins of those who affirm His oneness." And regarding His words ﴿and the mountains crumble into pieces﴾ (Q 19:90) he said: "Demolition."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related through the chain of 'Awn from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed a mountain calls out to another mountain by its name: 'O so-and-so, has anyone passed by you today who remembered Allah?' If he says, 'Yes,' it rejoices." 'Awn said: "Will it hear falsehood when it is spoken and not hear goodness? They are more attentive to goodness." Then he recited ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾ (Q 19:88) and the verses that follow.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 81–95 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Farra' said: Its meaning is: so that they might be intercessors for them in the Hereafter. It was also said: Its meaning is: so that they might strengthen themselves through them against the punishment of Allah and be protected by them.

﴿Nay! They will deny their worship﴾: that is, the matter is not as they supposed and imagined. The pronoun in the verb may refer to the gods: that is, these idols will deny the worship of the disbelievers toward them on the Day when Allah makes them speak, because when they were worshipped they were lifeless objects that did not perceive that. Or it may refer to the polytheists: that is, the polytheists will deny that they worshipped the idols. The first interpretation is supported by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They did not worship us﴾ (al-Qasas 28:63), and His words: ﴿Then they will throw to them the saying: Indeed, you are liars﴾ (al-Nahl 16:86). The second interpretation is supported by His words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23).

Ibn Abi Nuhayk read ﴿Nay﴾ (kallan) with tanwin. It is also narrated from him, along with this, that the kaf was read with a damma and with a fatha. With the damma, it means "all together," and it is governed by a hidden verb, as if it had said: "They will all deny [their worship]." With the fatha, it is a verbal noun for a deleted verb, whose implied sense is: "This opinion is rejected, rejected." The reading of the majority is the correct one, and it is a particle of repulsion and rebuke.

﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾: that is, these gods that they supposed to be a source of might for them will be opposed to them, meaning opposed to might; and the opposite of might is humiliation. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the second interpretation, the polytheists will be opposed to the gods and enemies of them, disbelieving in them after they had loved them and believed in them.

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ Al-Zajjaj mentioned two interpretations of this. The second interpretation is that they were sent against them and were assigned to them because of their disbelief. He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36). So the meaning of "sending" here is "empowering." From this is His saying, glory be to Him, to Iblis: ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice﴾ (al-Isra' 17:64). The second interpretation is supported by the completion of the verse, which is ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ (ta'uzzuhum azza). Indeed, azz, hazz and istifzaz mean moving, stirring and provoking. So Allah, glory be to Him, informed that the devils move the disbelievers, stir them up and lead them astray, and that is their empowerment over them. It was also said: The meaning of azz is "hastening," and this is close to what we have mentioned, because hastening is moving, stirring, provoking and disturbing.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ (وفدًا, "as a delegation," Q 19:85) that it means "riders." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ that it means "upon camels."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: those who are eager and those who are fearful; two on one camel, three on one camel, four on one camel, and ten on one camel. And the Fire will gather their remainder; it will rest where they rest and it will spend the night where they spend the night." The hadiths on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ and said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up. None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to my own deeds, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant for me with You that You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.'"

Indeed Allah does not break the promise."

And regarding His words ﴿and the mountains crumble into pieces﴾ (Q 19:90) he said: "Demolition."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 81–95 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 900]

Allah, glory be to Him, relates what these disbelievers were doing. They wished for what they did not deserve, and they swore by Allah, glory be to Him, [claiming] that they had taken gods besides Allah in order to gain strength through them. Al-Harawi said: The meaning of ﴿so that they might be a source of might for them﴾ is: so that they might be helpers for them. Al-Farra' said: Its meaning is: so that they might be intercessors for them in the Hereafter. It was also said: Its meaning is: so that they might strengthen themselves through them against the punishment of Allah and be protected by them.

﴿Nay! They will deny their worship﴾: that is, the matter is not as they supposed and imagined. The pronoun in the verb may refer to the gods: that is, these idols will deny the worship of the disbelievers toward them on the Day when Allah makes them speak, because when they were worshipped they were lifeless objects that did not perceive that. Or it may refer to the polytheists: that is, the polytheists will deny that they worshipped the idols. The first interpretation is supported by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They did not worship us﴾ (al-Qasas 28:63), and His words: ﴿Then they will throw to them the saying: Indeed, you are liars﴾ (al-Nahl 16:86). The second interpretation is supported by His words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23).

Ibn Abi Nuhayk read ﴿Nay﴾ (kallan) with tanwin. It is also narrated from him, along with this, that the kaf was read with a damma and with a fatha. With the damma, it means "all together," and it is governed by a hidden verb, as if it had said: "They will all deny [their worship]." With the fatha, it is a verbal noun for a deleted verb, whose implied sense is: "This opinion is rejected, rejected." The reading of the majority is the correct one, and it is a particle of repulsion and rebuke.

﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾: that is, these gods that they supposed to be a source of might for them will be opposed to them, meaning opposed to might; and the opposite of might is humiliation. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the second interpretation, the polytheists will be opposed to the gods and enemies of them, disbelieving in them after they had loved them and believed in them.

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ Al-Zajjaj mentioned two interpretations of this. One is that its meaning is: We left the disbelievers between themselves and the devils, and did not protect them from them nor shield them, unlike the believers, of whom it was said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Isra' 17:65). The second interpretation is that they were sent against them and were assigned to them because of their disbelief. He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36). So the meaning of "sending" here is "empowering." From this is His saying, glory be to Him, to Iblis: ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice﴾ (al-Isra' 17:64). The second interpretation is supported by the completion of the verse, which is ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ (ta'uzzuhum azza). Indeed, azz, hazz and istifzaz mean moving, stirring and provoking. So Allah, glory be to Him, informed that the devils move the disbelievers, stir them up and lead them astray, and that is their empowerment over them. It was also said: The meaning of azz is "hastening," and this is close to what we have mentioned, because hastening is moving, stirring, provoking and disturbing.

The context of this verse is to make the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) marvel at their condition, and to alert him that all of that is due to the misguidance and seduction of the devils. The clause ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ is in the position of an accusative circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new clause, on the assumption of a question indicated by the context, as if it had been said: "What do the devils do with them?"

﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾: that is, do not ask Allah to destroy them because of their insistence on disbelief, their obstinacy against the truth and their rebellion against the call of Allah, glory be to Him. Then Allah, glory be to Him, gave the reason for this prohibition in His words: ﴿Indeed, We are counting for them a count﴾. That is: We count for them the days, nights, months and years of their lives until the end of their terms. It was also said: We count their breaths. It was also said: their steps. It was also said: their glances. It was also said: the hours. Qutrub said: We count their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is: Do not be hasty against them, for We only delay them so that they may increase in sin.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established the matter of the Gathering and answered the doubt of those who denied it, He wished to describe the condition of the accountable at that time, so He said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The time-clause is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, the Day of Gathering. It was also said: it is governed by the verb that follows it. The meaning of "gathering them to the Most Merciful" is gathering them to His Garden and the abode of His honor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ (al-Saffat 37:99). The word wafd is the plural of wafid, as rakb is the plural of rakib and sahb is the plural of sahib. It is said: wafada yafidu wafdan when he went out to a king or to a grave matter; so said al-Jawhari.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾: sawq is urging to move, and wird means thirsty, as said al-Akhfash and others. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: they are those walking on foot. Al-Azhari said: they are those walking on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water. It was also said: wirdan means "for the watering," as when you say "I came to you out of honor," meaning "for honor." It was also said: "individually." It was said: there is no contradiction among these sayings, for they are driven on foot, thirsty and individually. The root of wird is the group that comes to water of birds, camels, people or otherwise, and wird is also the water that is approached.

The clause ﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾ is a new clause explaining some of what will happen on that Day. The pronoun in "they will have" refers to both groups. It was said: to the God-fearing only; and it was said: to the criminals only. The first is preferred. The meaning of "not having power of intercession" is that they will not be able to intercede for others. It was said: no one else will be able to intercede for them. The first is preferred.

﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. This exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation: that is, neither of the two mentioned groups has power of intercession except one who has prepared himself for it by that which makes him among those who intercede for others, by being a believer and God-fearing. This is the meaning of "taking a covenant with Allah." It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is that Allah commanded him to do so, as they say: "The commander made a covenant with so-and-so" when he ordered him to do it. It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was said: other than that.

According to the connected reading of this exception, the case of (man) in "one who has taken" is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original case of the exception. As for the second interpretation, the exception is disconnected (munqati') because the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession, ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and these are the Muslims. It was said: it is connected also according to this interpretation, and the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession except one of them who was a Muslim.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wuldan﴾ with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read in the four places mentioned in this surah with a fatha on the waw and the lam. We have already mentioned the difference between the two readings. The sentence is a new clause explaining the saying of the Jews and Christians, and of whoever among the Arabs claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

In His words: ﴿Indeed, you have brought a monstrous thing﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the second person, and in it is a rejection of this hideous statement. Idd, as al-Jawhari said, is a calamity and a terrible matter, and likewise idda. The plural of idda is idad. It is said: the calamity afflicted so-and-so (addathu), it afflicts him (ya'udduhu) with ada'an, with a fatha.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿addan﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. The majority read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿'addan﴾ like madd. It is derived from heaviness; it is said: the load burdened him (addahu al-himlu, ya'uddu-hu) when it made him heavy.

Al-Wahidi said: ﴿You have brought a monstrous thing﴾, meaning a great thing according to all. The meaning of the verse is: You have said a great saying. It was said: idd means wonder, and idda means severity, and the meanings are close, and the root revolves around severity and heaviness.

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿yakādu﴾ with the yā' (third person). The rest read it with the tā' (second person). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with the tā'. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the yā', from infitar. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ (al-Infitar 82:1) and His saying: ﴿The sky will be split by it﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:18). Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasadda'na﴾. Infitar and tafattur mean splitting apart.

﴿And the earth splits open﴾: that is, and it is almost that the earth splits open. The verb is repeated for emphasis, because "they are torn apart" (yatafattarna) and "splits open" (tashuqqu) have the same meaning.

﴿And the mountains fall down in ruin﴾: that is, they fall and collapse. The word hadda is in the accusative either as an emphatic verbal noun, because falling (khurur) is included in its meaning, or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, meaning: "and they will be utterly ruined" (wa-tanhaddu hadda), or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning: "ruined" (mahdudatan), or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "because they will be ruined." Al-Harawi said: It is said: the matter broke me (haddani al-amru) and broke my support (hadda rukni), meaning it broke me and reached me. Al-Jawhari said: hadda al-bina' yahuddu-hu hadda means he broke it and crushed it; the calamity weakened its support (hadda-tu al-musibatu awhanat rukna-hu); and al-jabal (the mountain) inhadda, meaning it broke. Al-hadda is the sound of the fall of a wall, as Ibn al-A'rabi said.

The phrase ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the genitive position as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative position, with the meaning of li-anna (because). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by an implied preposition. It was also said: it is in the nominative position as the subject of hadda. Ad-du'a' (calling) in the sense of naming: that is, they named a son for the Most Merciful; or in the sense of attribution: that is, they attributed a son to Him.

﴿And it is not proper for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾: that is, it is not fitting for Him and does not befit Him, because it is impossible for Him, since a son implies kinship of kind and temporal origin. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "that they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son," while the situation is that it does not befit Him, glory be to Him, to have that.

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: that is, there is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging servitude, humbly and submissively, as He said: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾ (al-Naml 27:87), that is, abased. The meaning is: all creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him? It was read ﴿ātin﴾ according to the original form.

﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾: that is, He has restricted them and known their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾: that is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, without a helper and without wealth with him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:88).

[End of part 1]

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th*, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and they will become adversaries to them﴾ (ﷺ, Q 19:82), said: "Helpers." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him that ﴿ḍiddan﴾ (ضِدًّا) means "grief." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ (Q 19:83), that it means "leading them astray with misguidance." That is: We count for them the days, nights, months and years of their lives until the end of their terms. It was also said: We count their breaths. It was also said: their steps. It was also said: their glances. It was also said: the hours. Qutrub said: We count their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is: Do not be hasty against them, for We only delay them so that they may increase in sin.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established the matter of the Gathering and answered the doubt of those who denied it, He wished to describe the condition of the accountable at that time, so He said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The time-clause is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, the Day of Gathering. It was also said: it is governed by the verb that follows it. The meaning of "gathering them to the Most Merciful" is gathering them to His Garden and the abode of His honor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ (al-Saffat 37:99). The word wafd is the plural of wafid, as rakb is the plural of rakib and sahb is the plural of sahib. It is said: wafada yafidu wafdan when he went out to a king or to a grave matter; so said al-Jawhari.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾: sawq is urging to move, and wird means thirsty, as said al-Akhfash and others. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: they are those walking on foot. Al-Azhari said: they are those walking on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water. It was also said: wirdan means "for the watering," as when you say "I came to you out of honor," meaning "for honor." It was also said: "individually." It was said: there is no contradiction among these sayings, for they are driven on foot, thirsty and individually. The root of wird is the group that comes to water of birds, camels, people or otherwise, and wird is also the water that is approached.

The clause ﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾ is a new clause explaining some of what will happen on that Day. The pronoun in "they will have" refers to both groups. It was said: to the God-fearing only; and it was said: to the criminals only. The first is preferred. The meaning of "not having power of intercession" is that they will not be able to intercede for others. It was said: no one else will be able to intercede for them. The first is preferred.

﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. This exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation: that is, neither of the two mentioned groups has power of intercession except one who has prepared himself for it by that which makes him among those who intercede for others, by being a believer and God-fearing. This is the meaning of "taking a covenant with Allah." It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is that Allah commanded him to do so, as they say: "The commander made a covenant with so-and-so" when he ordered him to do it. It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was said: other than that.

According to the connected reading of this exception, the case of (man) in "one who has taken" is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original case of the exception. As for the second interpretation, the exception is disconnected (munqati') because the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession, ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and these are the Muslims. It was said: it is connected also according to this interpretation, and the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession except one of them who was a Muslim.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wuldan﴾ with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read in the four places mentioned in this surah with a fatha on the waw and the lam. We have already mentioned the difference between the two readings. The sentence is a new clause explaining the saying of the Jews and Christians, and of whoever among the Arabs claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

In His words: ﴿Indeed, you have brought a monstrous thing﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the second person, and in it is a rejection of this hideous statement. Idd, as al-Jawhari said, is a calamity and a terrible matter, and likewise idda. The plural of idda is idad. It is said: the calamity afflicted so-and-so (addathu), it afflicts him (ya'udduhu) with ada'an, with a fatha.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿addan﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. The majority read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿'addan﴾ like madd. It is derived from heaviness; it is said: the load burdened him (addahu al-himlu, ya'uddu-hu) when it made him heavy.

Al-Wahidi said: ﴿You have brought a monstrous thing﴾, meaning a great thing according to all. The meaning of the verse is: You have said a great saying. It was said: idd means wonder, and idda means severity, and the meanings are close, and the root revolves around severity and heaviness.

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿yakādu﴾ with the yā' (third person). The rest read it with the tā' (second person). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with the tā'. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the yā', from infitar. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ (al-Infitar 82:1) and His saying: ﴿The sky will be split by it﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:18). Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasadda'na﴾. Infitar and tafattur mean splitting apart.

﴿And the earth splits open﴾: that is, and it is almost that the earth splits open. The verb is repeated for emphasis, because "they are torn apart" (yatafattarna) and "splits open" (tashuqqu) have the same meaning.

﴿And the mountains fall down in ruin﴾: that is, they fall and collapse. The word hadda is in the accusative either as an emphatic verbal noun, because falling (khurur) is included in its meaning, or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, meaning: "and they will be utterly ruined" (wa-tanhaddu hadda), or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning: "ruined" (mahdudatan), or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "because they will be ruined." Al-Harawi said: It is said: the matter broke me (haddani al-amru) and broke my support (hadda rukni), meaning it broke me and reached me. Al-Jawhari said: hadda al-bina' yahuddu-hu hadda means he broke it and crushed it; the calamity weakened its support (hadda-tu al-musibatu awhanat rukna-hu); and al-jabal (the mountain) inhadda, meaning it broke. Al-hadda is the sound of the fall of a wall, as Ibn al-A'rabi said.

The phrase ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the genitive position as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative position, with the meaning of li-anna (because). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by an implied preposition. It was also said: it is in the nominative position as the subject of hadda. Ad-du'a' (calling) in the sense of naming: that is, they named a son for the Most Merciful; or in the sense of attribution: that is, they attributed a son to Him.

﴿And it is not proper for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾: that is, it is not fitting for Him and does not befit Him, because it is impossible for Him, since a son implies kinship of kind and temporal origin. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "that they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son," while the situation is that it does not befit Him, glory be to Him, to have that.

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: that is, there is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging servitude, humbly and submissively, as He said: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾ (al-Naml 27:87), that is, abased. The meaning is: all creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him? It was read ﴿ātin﴾ according to the original form.

﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾: that is, He has restricted them and known their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾: that is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, without a helper and without wealth with him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:88).

[End of part 1]

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th*, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and they will become adversaries to them﴾ (ﷺ, Q 19:82), said: "Helpers." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him that ﴿ḍiddan﴾ (ضِدًّا) means "grief." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ (Q 19:83), that it means "leading them astray with misguidance." Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ that it means "inciting the polytheists against Muhammad and his companions." 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding the verse that it means "urging them, with a sharp push, toward the disobedience of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ (وفدًا, "as a delegation," Q 19:85) that it means "riders." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ that it means "upon camels."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: those who are eager and those who are fearful; two on one camel, three on one camel, four on one camel, and ten on one camel. And the Fire will gather their remainder; it will rest where they rest and it will spend the night where they spend the night." The hadiths on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wirdan﴾ (وِرْدًا, Q 19:86) that it means "thirsty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ (Q 19:87) that it means: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah, and disavowing power and might, and hoping only in Allah." Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding the verse that it means: "Whoever dies without associating anything with Allah enters Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ and said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up. None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to my own deeds, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant for me with You that You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever brings joy to a believer has pleased me, and whoever pleases me has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, and whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, the Fire will not touch him. Indeed Allah does not break the promise."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever comes to us on the Day of Resurrection with the five prayers, having guarded their ablution, their times, their bowing and their prostration, without diminishing any of them, will come having a covenant with Allah that He will not punish him. And whoever comes having fallen short in any of them has no covenant with Allah; if He wills He will have mercy on him, and if He wills He will punish him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿you have certainly brought something monstrous﴾ (Q 19:89) that it means "a grave statement." And regarding His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ (Q 19:90), he said: "Because of shirk the heavens, the earth, the mountains, and all creatures have been emptied of it, except for the two weights (jinn and humankind); and they were almost ceasing to exist from it because of the greatness of Allah, glory be to Him. Just as the good deeds of a polytheist do not benefit him along with shirk, so likewise he hopes that Allah will forgive the sins of those who affirm His oneness." And regarding His words ﴿and the mountains crumble into pieces﴾ (Q 19:90) he said: "Demolition."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related through the chain of 'Awn from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed a mountain calls out to another mountain by its name: 'O so-and-so, has anyone passed by you today who remembered Allah?' If he says, 'Yes,' it rejoices." 'Awn said: "Will it hear falsehood when it is spoken and not hear goodness? They are more attentive to goodness." Then he recited ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾ (Q 19:88) and the verses that follow.

Al-Farra' said: Its meaning is: so that they might be intercessors for them in the Hereafter. It was also said: Its meaning is: so that they might strengthen themselves through them against the punishment of Allah and be protected by them.

﴿Nay! They will deny their worship﴾: that is, the matter is not as they supposed and imagined. The pronoun in the verb may refer to the gods: that is, these idols will deny the worship of the disbelievers toward them on the Day when Allah makes them speak, because when they were worshipped they were lifeless objects that did not perceive that. Or it may refer to the polytheists: that is, the polytheists will deny that they worshipped the idols. The first interpretation is supported by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They did not worship us﴾ (al-Qasas 28:63), and His words: ﴿Then they will throw to them the saying: Indeed, you are liars﴾ (al-Nahl 16:86). The second interpretation is supported by His words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23).

Ibn Abi Nuhayk read ﴿Nay﴾ (kallan) with tanwin. It is also narrated from him, along with this, that the kaf was read with a damma and with a fatha. With the damma, it means "all together," and it is governed by a hidden verb, as if it had said: "They will all deny [their worship]." With the fatha, it is a verbal noun for a deleted verb, whose implied sense is: "This opinion is rejected, rejected." The reading of the majority is the correct one, and it is a particle of repulsion and rebuke.

﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾: that is, these gods that they supposed to be a source of might for them will be opposed to them, meaning opposed to might; and the opposite of might is humiliation. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the second interpretation, the polytheists will be opposed to the gods and enemies of them, disbelieving in them after they had loved them and believed in them.

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ Al-Zajjaj mentioned two interpretations of this. The second interpretation is that they were sent against them and were assigned to them because of their disbelief. He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36). So the meaning of "sending" here is "empowering." From this is His saying, glory be to Him, to Iblis: ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice﴾ (al-Isra' 17:64). The second interpretation is supported by the completion of the verse, which is ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ (ta'uzzuhum azza). Indeed, azz, hazz and istifzaz mean moving, stirring and provoking. So Allah, glory be to Him, informed that the devils move the disbelievers, stir them up and lead them astray, and that is their empowerment over them. It was also said: The meaning of azz is "hastening," and this is close to what we have mentioned, because hastening is moving, stirring, provoking and disturbing.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him that ﴿ḍiddan﴾ (ضِدًّا) means "grief." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ (Q 19:83), that it means "leading them astray with misguidance." Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ that it means "inciting the polytheists against Muhammad and his companions." 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding the verse that it means "urging them, with a sharp push, toward the disobedience of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ (وفدًا, "as a delegation," Q 19:85) that it means "riders." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ that it means "upon camels."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: those who are eager and those who are fearful; two on one camel, three on one camel, four on one camel, and ten on one camel. And the Fire will gather their remainder; it will rest where they rest and it will spend the night where they spend the night." The hadiths on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding the verse that it means: "Whoever dies without associating anything with Allah enters Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ and said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up. None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to my own deeds, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant for me with You that You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 81–95 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 900]

Allah, glory be to Him, relates what these disbelievers were doing. They wished for what they did not deserve, and they swore by Allah, glory be to Him, [claiming] that they had taken gods besides Allah in order to gain strength through them. Al-Harawi said: The meaning of ﴿so that they might be a source of might for them﴾ is: so that they might be helpers for them. Al-Farra' said: Its meaning is: so that they might be intercessors for them in the Hereafter. It was also said: Its meaning is: so that they might strengthen themselves through them against the punishment of Allah and be protected by them.

﴿Nay! They will deny their worship﴾: that is, the matter is not as they supposed and imagined. The pronoun in the verb may refer to the gods: that is, these idols will deny the worship of the disbelievers toward them on the Day when Allah makes them speak, because when they were worshipped they were lifeless objects that did not perceive that. Or it may refer to the polytheists: that is, the polytheists will deny that they worshipped the idols. The first interpretation is supported by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They did not worship us﴾ (al-Qasas 28:63), and His words: ﴿Then they will throw to them the saying: Indeed, you are liars﴾ (al-Nahl 16:86). The second interpretation is supported by His words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ (al-An'am 6:23).

Ibn Abi Nuhayk read ﴿Nay﴾ (kallan) with tanwin. It is also narrated from him, along with this, that the kaf was read with a damma and with a fatha. With the damma, it means "all together," and it is governed by a hidden verb, as if it had said: "They will all deny [their worship]." With the fatha, it is a verbal noun for a deleted verb, whose implied sense is: "This opinion is rejected, rejected." The reading of the majority is the correct one, and it is a particle of repulsion and rebuke.

﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾: that is, these gods that they supposed to be a source of might for them will be opposed to them, meaning opposed to might; and the opposite of might is humiliation. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the second interpretation, the polytheists will be opposed to the gods and enemies of them, disbelieving in them after they had loved them and believed in them.

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ Al-Zajjaj mentioned two interpretations of this. One is that its meaning is: We left the disbelievers between themselves and the devils, and did not protect them from them nor shield them, unlike the believers, of whom it was said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Isra' 17:65). The second interpretation is that they were sent against them and were assigned to them because of their disbelief. He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:36). So the meaning of "sending" here is "empowering." From this is His saying, glory be to Him, to Iblis: ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice﴾ (al-Isra' 17:64). The second interpretation is supported by the completion of the verse, which is ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ (ta'uzzuhum azza). Indeed, azz, hazz and istifzaz mean moving, stirring and provoking. So Allah, glory be to Him, informed that the devils move the disbelievers, stir them up and lead them astray, and that is their empowerment over them. It was also said: The meaning of azz is "hastening," and this is close to what we have mentioned, because hastening is moving, stirring, provoking and disturbing.

The context of this verse is to make the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) marvel at their condition, and to alert him that all of that is due to the misguidance and seduction of the devils. The clause ﴿driving them with a driving﴾ is in the position of an accusative circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a new clause, on the assumption of a question indicated by the context, as if it had been said: "What do the devils do with them?"

﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾: that is, do not ask Allah to destroy them because of their insistence on disbelief, their obstinacy against the truth and their rebellion against the call of Allah, glory be to Him. Then Allah, glory be to Him, gave the reason for this prohibition in His words: ﴿Indeed, We are counting for them a count﴾. That is: We count for them the days, nights, months and years of their lives until the end of their terms. It was also said: We count their breaths. It was also said: their steps. It was also said: their glances. It was also said: the hours. Qutrub said: We count their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is: Do not be hasty against them, for We only delay them so that they may increase in sin.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established the matter of the Gathering and answered the doubt of those who denied it, He wished to describe the condition of the accountable at that time, so He said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The time-clause is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, the Day of Gathering. It was also said: it is governed by the verb that follows it. The meaning of "gathering them to the Most Merciful" is gathering them to His Garden and the abode of His honor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ (al-Saffat 37:99). The word wafd is the plural of wafid, as rakb is the plural of rakib and sahb is the plural of sahib. It is said: wafada yafidu wafdan when he went out to a king or to a grave matter; so said al-Jawhari.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾: sawq is urging to move, and wird means thirsty, as said al-Akhfash and others. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: they are those walking on foot. Al-Azhari said: they are those walking on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water. It was also said: wirdan means "for the watering," as when you say "I came to you out of honor," meaning "for honor." It was also said: "individually." It was said: there is no contradiction among these sayings, for they are driven on foot, thirsty and individually. The root of wird is the group that comes to water of birds, camels, people or otherwise, and wird is also the water that is approached.

The clause ﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾ is a new clause explaining some of what will happen on that Day. The pronoun in "they will have" refers to both groups. It was said: to the God-fearing only; and it was said: to the criminals only. The first is preferred. The meaning of "not having power of intercession" is that they will not be able to intercede for others. It was said: no one else will be able to intercede for them. The first is preferred.

﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. This exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation: that is, neither of the two mentioned groups has power of intercession except one who has prepared himself for it by that which makes him among those who intercede for others, by being a believer and God-fearing. This is the meaning of "taking a covenant with Allah." It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is that Allah commanded him to do so, as they say: "The commander made a covenant with so-and-so" when he ordered him to do it. It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was said: other than that.

According to the connected reading of this exception, the case of (man) in "one who has taken" is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original case of the exception. As for the second interpretation, the exception is disconnected (munqati') because the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession, ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and these are the Muslims. It was said: it is connected also according to this interpretation, and the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession except one of them who was a Muslim.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wuldan﴾ with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read in the four places mentioned in this surah with a fatha on the waw and the lam. We have already mentioned the difference between the two readings. The sentence is a new clause explaining the saying of the Jews and Christians, and of whoever among the Arabs claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

In His words: ﴿Indeed, you have brought a monstrous thing﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the second person, and in it is a rejection of this hideous statement. Idd, as al-Jawhari said, is a calamity and a terrible matter, and likewise idda. The plural of idda is idad. It is said: the calamity afflicted so-and-so (addathu), it afflicts him (ya'udduhu) with ada'an, with a fatha.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿addan﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. The majority read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿'addan﴾ like madd. It is derived from heaviness; it is said: the load burdened him (addahu al-himlu, ya'uddu-hu) when it made him heavy.

Al-Wahidi said: ﴿You have brought a monstrous thing﴾, meaning a great thing according to all. The meaning of the verse is: You have said a great saying. It was said: idd means wonder, and idda means severity, and the meanings are close, and the root revolves around severity and heaviness.

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿yakādu﴾ with the yā' (third person). The rest read it with the tā' (second person). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with the tā'. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the yā', from infitar. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ (al-Infitar 82:1) and His saying: ﴿The sky will be split by it﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:18). Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasadda'na﴾. Infitar and tafattur mean splitting apart.

﴿And the earth splits open﴾: that is, and it is almost that the earth splits open. The verb is repeated for emphasis, because "they are torn apart" (yatafattarna) and "splits open" (tashuqqu) have the same meaning.

﴿And the mountains fall down in ruin﴾: that is, they fall and collapse. The word hadda is in the accusative either as an emphatic verbal noun, because falling (khurur) is included in its meaning, or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, meaning: "and they will be utterly ruined" (wa-tanhaddu hadda), or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning: "ruined" (mahdudatan), or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "because they will be ruined." Al-Harawi said: It is said: the matter broke me (haddani al-amru) and broke my support (hadda rukni), meaning it broke me and reached me. Al-Jawhari said: hadda al-bina' yahuddu-hu hadda means he broke it and crushed it; the calamity weakened its support (hadda-tu al-musibatu awhanat rukna-hu); and al-jabal (the mountain) inhadda, meaning it broke. Al-hadda is the sound of the fall of a wall, as Ibn al-A'rabi said.

The phrase ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the genitive position as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative position, with the meaning of li-anna (because). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by an implied preposition. It was also said: it is in the nominative position as the subject of hadda. Ad-du'a' (calling) in the sense of naming: that is, they named a son for the Most Merciful; or in the sense of attribution: that is, they attributed a son to Him.

﴿And it is not proper for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾: that is, it is not fitting for Him and does not befit Him, because it is impossible for Him, since a son implies kinship of kind and temporal origin. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "that they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son," while the situation is that it does not befit Him, glory be to Him, to have that.

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: that is, there is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging servitude, humbly and submissively, as He said: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾ (al-Naml 27:87), that is, abased. The meaning is: all creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him? It was read ﴿ātin﴾ according to the original form.

﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾: that is, He has restricted them and known their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾: that is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, without a helper and without wealth with him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:88).

﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾: that is, do not ask Allah to destroy them because of their insistence on disbelief, their obstinacy against the truth and their rebellion against the call of Allah, glory be to Him. Then Allah, glory be to Him, gave the reason for this prohibition in His words: ﴿Indeed, We are counting for them a count﴾. That is: We count for them the days, nights, months and years of their lives until the end of their terms. It was also said: We count their breaths. It was also said: their steps. It was also said: their glances. It was also said: the hours. Qutrub said: We count their deeds. It was also said: the meaning is: Do not be hasty against them, for We only delay them so that they may increase in sin.

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established the matter of the Gathering and answered the doubt of those who denied it, He wished to describe the condition of the accountable at that time, so He said: ﴿On the Day We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. The time-clause is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, meaning: Remember, O Muhammad, the Day of Gathering. It was also said: it is governed by the verb that follows it. The meaning of "gathering them to the Most Merciful" is gathering them to His Garden and the abode of His honor, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord﴾ (al-Saffat 37:99). The word wafd is the plural of wafid, as rakb is the plural of rakib and sahb is the plural of sahib. It is said: wafada yafidu wafdan when he went out to a king or to a grave matter; so said al-Jawhari.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾: sawq is urging to move, and wird means thirsty, as said al-Akhfash and others. Al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: they are those walking on foot. Al-Azhari said: they are those walking on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water. It was also said: wirdan means "for the watering," as when you say "I came to you out of honor," meaning "for honor." It was also said: "individually." It was said: there is no contradiction among these sayings, for they are driven on foot, thirsty and individually. The root of wird is the group that comes to water of birds, camels, people or otherwise, and wird is also the water that is approached.

The clause ﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾ is a new clause explaining some of what will happen on that Day. The pronoun in "they will have" refers to both groups. It was said: to the God-fearing only; and it was said: to the criminals only. The first is preferred. The meaning of "not having power of intercession" is that they will not be able to intercede for others. It was said: no one else will be able to intercede for them. The first is preferred.

﴿Except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. This exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation: that is, neither of the two mentioned groups has power of intercession except one who has prepared himself for it by that which makes him among those who intercede for others, by being a believer and God-fearing. This is the meaning of "taking a covenant with Allah." It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is that Allah commanded him to do so, as they say: "The commander made a covenant with so-and-so" when he ordered him to do it. It was said: the meaning of "taking a covenant" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was said: other than that.

According to the connected reading of this exception, the case of (man) in "one who has taken" is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original case of the exception. As for the second interpretation, the exception is disconnected (munqati') because the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession, ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, and these are the Muslims. It was said: it is connected also according to this interpretation, and the meaning is: The criminals will not have power of intercession except one of them who was a Muslim.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wuldan﴾ with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read in the four places mentioned in this surah with a fatha on the waw and the lam. We have already mentioned the difference between the two readings. The sentence is a new clause explaining the saying of the Jews and Christians, and of whoever among the Arabs claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

In His words: ﴿Indeed, you have brought a monstrous thing﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the second person, and in it is a rejection of this hideous statement. Idd, as al-Jawhari said, is a calamity and a terrible matter, and likewise idda. The plural of idda is idad. It is said: the calamity afflicted so-and-so (addathu), it afflicts him (ya'udduhu) with ada'an, with a fatha.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read ﴿addan﴾ with a fatha on the hamza. The majority read it with a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah read ﴿'addan﴾ like madd. It is derived from heaviness; it is said: the load burdened him (addahu al-himlu, ya'uddu-hu) when it made him heavy.

Al-Wahidi said: ﴿You have brought a monstrous thing﴾, meaning a great thing according to all. The meaning of the verse is: You have said a great saying. It was said: idd means wonder, and idda means severity, and the meanings are close, and the root revolves around severity and heaviness.

﴿The heavens are almost torn apart because of it﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿yakādu﴾ with the yā' (third person). The rest read it with the tā' (second person). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with the tā'. Hamzah, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the yā', from infitar. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading because of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ (al-Infitar 82:1) and His saying: ﴿The sky will be split by it﴾ (al-Muzzammil 73:18). Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasadda'na﴾. Infitar and tafattur mean splitting apart.

﴿And the earth splits open﴾: that is, and it is almost that the earth splits open. The verb is repeated for emphasis, because "they are torn apart" (yatafattarna) and "splits open" (tashuqqu) have the same meaning.

﴿And the mountains fall down in ruin﴾: that is, they fall and collapse. The word hadda is in the accusative either as an emphatic verbal noun, because falling (khurur) is included in its meaning, or it is a verbal noun for a hidden verb, meaning: "and they will be utterly ruined" (wa-tanhaddu hadda), or it is in the accusative of circumstance, meaning: "ruined" (mahdudatan), or it is an object of purpose, meaning: "because they will be ruined." Al-Harawi said: It is said: the matter broke me (haddani al-amru) and broke my support (hadda rukni), meaning it broke me and reached me. Al-Jawhari said: hadda al-bina' yahuddu-hu hadda means he broke it and crushed it; the calamity weakened its support (hadda-tu al-musibatu awhanat rukna-hu); and al-jabal (the mountain) inhadda, meaning it broke. Al-hadda is the sound of the fall of a wall, as Ibn al-A'rabi said.

The phrase ﴿that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the genitive position as a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative position, with the meaning of li-anna (because). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by an implied preposition. It was also said: it is in the nominative position as the subject of hadda. Ad-du'a' (calling) in the sense of naming: that is, they named a son for the Most Merciful; or in the sense of attribution: that is, they attributed a son to Him.

The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, they said: "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "that they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son," while the situation is that it does not befit Him, glory be to Him, to have that.

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: that is, there is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging servitude, humbly and submissively, as He said: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾ (al-Naml 27:87), that is, abased. The meaning is: all creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him? It was read ﴿ātin﴾ according to the original form.

﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾: that is, He has restricted them and known their number. ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾: that is, each one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, without a helper and without wealth with him, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:88).

[End of part 1]

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th*, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿and they will become adversaries to them﴾ (ﷺ, Q 19:82), said: "Helpers." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him that ﴿ḍiddan﴾ (ضِدًّا) means "grief." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ (Q 19:83), that it means "leading them astray with misguidance." Ibn Abi Hatim related from him as well regarding ﴿driving them with agitation﴾ that it means "inciting the polytheists against Muhammad and his companions." 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding the verse that it means "urging them, with a sharp push, toward the disobedience of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ (وفدًا, "as a delegation," Q 19:85) that it means "riders." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Abu Hurayrah regarding ﴿wafdan﴾ that it means "upon camels."

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: those who are eager and those who are fearful; two on one camel, three on one camel, four on one camel, and ten on one camel. And the Fire will gather their remainder; it will rest where they rest and it will spend the night where they spend the night." The hadiths on this subject are very numerous.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿wirdan﴾ (وِرْدًا, Q 19:86) that it means "thirsty." Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ (Q 19:87) that it means: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah, and disavowing power and might, and hoping only in Allah." Ibn Mardawayh related from him regarding the verse that it means: "Whoever dies without associating anything with Allah enters Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited ﴿except those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ and said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up. None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to my own deeds, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant for me with You that You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break the promise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever brings joy to a believer has pleased me, and whoever pleases me has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, and whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, the Fire will not touch him. Indeed Allah does not break the promise."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever comes to us on the Day of Resurrection with the five prayers, having guarded their ablution, their times, their bowing and their prostration, without diminishing any of them, will come having a covenant with Allah that He will not punish him. And whoever comes having fallen short in any of them has no covenant with Allah; if He wills He will have mercy on him, and if He wills He will punish him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿you have certainly brought something monstrous﴾ (Q 19:89) that it means "a grave statement." And regarding His words ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ (Q 19:90), he said: "Because of shirk the heavens, the earth, the mountains, and all creatures have been emptied of it, except for the two weights (jinn and humankind); and they were almost ceasing to exist from it because of the greatness of Allah, glory be to Him. Just as the good deeds of a polytheist do not benefit him along with shirk, so likewise he hopes that Allah will forgive the sins of those who affirm His oneness." And regarding His words ﴿and the mountains crumble into pieces﴾ (Q 19:90) he said: "Demolition."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* related through the chain of 'Awn from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Indeed a mountain calls out to another mountain by its name: 'O so-and-so, has anyone passed by you today who remembered Allah?' If he says, 'Yes,' it rejoices." 'Awn said: "Will it hear falsehood when it is spoken and not hear goodness? They are more attentive to goodness." Then he recited ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾ (Q 19:88) and the verses that follow.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 19, verses 81–95 (part 1 of 2):
